lessons.title: V3·TC1 — Migrating a JavaScript codebase incrementally
lessons.summary: Nobody gets to stop shipping for three months to add types. Migration is something you do to a codebase that is live, on a Tuesday, one directory at a time. This sector is the mechanics of that: allowJs and checkJs, the shim you write at every untyped seam, ratchets that stop the debt growing back, @ts-expect-error with a reason and an owner, and the ordering question of which file to convert next.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TC1 — Migrating a JavaScript codebase incrementally

Every TypeScript tutorial starts with an empty directory. No real migration
ever does. You inherit two hundred thousand lines of JavaScript that pays the
bills, a test suite of uncertain quality, and a product manager who is not
interested in a three-month typing sprint. The interesting engineering is not
"how do I write a type" — you learned that in the first twelve sectors — it is
"how do I add types to a moving system without stopping it, and how do I stop
the untyped part growing back".

The compiler is on your side here more than people expect. `allowJs` lets a
program contain both languages at once. `checkJs` turns the JavaScript half
into a checked program that reads JSDoc as types, so you can find real bugs
before you rename a single file. `strict` is not one switch but eight, and they
can be turned on one at a time. Declaration merging lets you describe a
third-party module that has no types without forking it. None of this is
exotic; all of it is the difference between a migration that lands and one that
becomes a permanent half-finished branch.

The part nobody warns you about is the **seam**. A migration is a moving
boundary between checked and unchecked code, and every value that crosses it
arrives as a lie. TypeScript will happily believe that `require("./cart")`
returns `Cart` because you said so in a `.d.ts` you wrote from memory. It is
not lying to you — you lied to it. So the single most valuable habit in a
migration is to treat the seam like a network boundary: values arrive as
`unknown`, you narrow them with real runtime checks, and typed code downstream
gets a type it has actually earned. Sector 10's guards and sector 19's
`unknown` discipline are not academic exercises; they are the migration
toolkit.

The second thing nobody warns you about is that migrations regress. You convert
`src/billing` to strict TypeScript on Monday; on Thursday somebody adds
`function applyCoupon(order: any)` because they were in a hurry and the build
was green. A migration without a **ratchet** is a migration that oscillates.
The ratchet is a boring piece of CI: count the bad things per file, store the
counts in a checked-in baseline, and fail the build when a count goes up. It
does not demand that anyone fix anything. It only forbids getting worse, which
turns out to be almost all of the value.

The third is the ordering question. Which file do you convert next? The
tempting answer is "whatever I am working on", and that is not wrong, but it
scales badly: convert a leaf utility used by ninety files and every one of
those ninety gets better inference for free. Convert an entry point and you
have typed a file nobody imports. Fan-in is the cheap proxy for value, and the
number of `any`s and `@ts-expect-error`s you would have to write is the cheap
proxy for cost. You want the high-fan-in, low-cost files first, and you want a
scoreboard so the team can see the line move.

This sector is eight pieces of that machinery, written as ordinary TypeScript
functions so that you can test them. Some of them are simplified models of
tools you already use — a suppression-comment parser, a JSDoc reader, a
config-inheritance resolver. Building the model is how you learn what the tool
is actually doing, and the models here are small enough to hold in your head
and close enough to real that you would recognise the production version.

One convention for the whole sector: everything is pure. No filesystem, no
process exit, no `console.log` inside the functions. Migration tooling that
reads the disk is untestable, and untestable CI tooling is CI tooling that
silently stops working. Take the data in, return the report, and let the thin
outer shell do the I/O.

## ex1 — the seam is a network boundary

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The first thing you write in any migration is the shim
that turns a value from the JavaScript half into something you can trust. Four
exports:

- `asRecord(value: unknown): Record<string, unknown> | undefined` — a real
  plain object only. `null`, arrays, functions, strings and numbers all give
  `undefined`.
- `readString(value: unknown, key: string): string | undefined`
- `readNumber(value: unknown, key: string): number | undefined` — finite
  numbers only, and **no coercion**: `"3"` is not a number.
- `requireString(value: unknown, key: string, where: string): string` — throws
  an `Error` whose message is `where`, a colon and a space, then
  `expected string at "key"`, with the key in double quotes.

Examples:

- `asRecord({ a: 1 })` → `{ a: 1 }`; `asRecord([1, 2])` → `undefined`;
  `asRecord(null)` → `undefined`
- `readString({ name: "ada" }, "name")` → `"ada"`
- `readString({ name: 7 }, "name")` → `undefined`
- `readNumber({ n: NaN }, "n")` → `undefined`; `readNumber({ n: "3" }, "n")` →
  `undefined`; `readNumber({ n: 0 }, "n")` → `0`
- `requireString(undefined, "id", "loadCart")` throws with the message
  `loadCart: expected string at "id"`

The parameter type is `unknown`, not `any`, and it must stay that way. `any` at
a seam is not a shim; it is a hole with a comment on it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex1
```

## ex2 — an adapter around a legacy module

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `legacy-cart` is a fifteen-year-old CommonJS module
with snake_case methods and no types. You are not going to rewrite it today.
You are going to put one typed adapter in front of it so that nothing else in
the codebase ever needs to know it exists.

```ts
export interface CartApi {
  addItem(sku: string, quantity: number): void;
  total(): number;
}

export function createCartAdapter(legacy: unknown): CartApi;
```

The legacy object is expected to have `add_item(sku, qty)` and `get_total()`.
The rules:

- If `legacy` is not an object, or either method is missing or is not a
  function, throw `Error("legacy-cart: incompatible module shape")` — at
  construction time, not on first use.
- `addItem` forwards to `add_item(sku, quantity)`, and rejects a `quantity`
  that is not a positive integer with
  `Error("legacy-cart: quantity must be a positive integer")`.
- `total()` calls `get_total()` and validates the result: a finite number, or
  `Error("legacy-cart: get_total returned a non-number")`.
- The adapter must call the legacy methods **with the legacy object as `this`**
  — it is old code and it reads `this` internally.

Examples:

- `createCartAdapter({ add_item() {}, get_total: () => 12 }).total()` → `12`
- `createCartAdapter({})` throws `legacy-cart: incompatible module shape`
- an adapter whose `get_total` returns `"12"` throws on `total()`, not before

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex2
```

## ex3 — the day you turn on strictNullChecks

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Turning on `strictNullChecks` and
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in a converted directory produces a wave of errors
that all have the same shape: a value the old code assumed was there. Three
exports that give the codebase a vocabulary for that.

- `firstMatching<T>(items: readonly T[], predicate: (item: T, index: number) => boolean): T | undefined`
- `mustFind<T>(items: readonly T[], predicate: (item: T, index: number) => boolean, label: string): T`
  — throws an `Error` with message `no match for ` followed by `label`.
- `at<T>(items: readonly T[], index: number): T | undefined` — supports
  negative indices counting from the end, and returns `undefined` for any index
  out of range, including a non-integer one.

Examples, with `nums = [10, 20, 30]`:

- `firstMatching(nums, (n) => n > 15)` → `20`
- `firstMatching(nums, () => false)` → `undefined`
- `firstMatching(nums, (_, i) => i === 2)` → `30`
- `mustFind(nums, (n) => n > 99, "big number")` throws `no match for big number`
- `at(nums, -1)` → `30`; `at(nums, -4)` → `undefined`; `at(nums, 1.5)` →
  `undefined`; `at([], 0)` → `undefined`

`mustFind` must be usable as an expression of type `T` with no non-null
assertion at the call site — that is the whole point of it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex3
```

## ex4 — a ratchet, so it cannot get worse

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The counts come from somewhere else — a type-coverage
tool, a grep, whatever you have. Your job is the policy.

```ts
export type RatchetViolation =
  | { kind: "increase"; file: string; was: number; now: number }
  | { kind: "unlisted"; file: string; now: number };

export interface RatchetReport {
  ok: boolean;
  violations: RatchetViolation[];
  improvements: { file: string; was: number; now: number }[];
  nextBaseline: Record<string, number>;
}

export function ratchet(
  baseline: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
  current: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
): RatchetReport;
```

Rules:

- A file in the baseline whose count went **up** is an `increase` violation.
- A file **not** in the baseline with a count above zero is `unlisted` — new
  code does not get a free allowance.
- A file whose count went **down** is an improvement.
- `nextBaseline` contains every current file with a count above zero, and
  nothing else: files deleted or fully cleaned drop out, which is what makes
  the ratchet tighten.
- Both `violations` and `improvements` are sorted by file name, ascending.
  `ok` is true when there are no violations.

Examples:

- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{ "a.ts": 3 }` → ok, no violations, no
  improvements, next baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`
- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{ "a.ts": 4 }` → one `increase` violation
- baseline `{}`, current `{ "b.ts": 1 }` → one `unlisted` violation
- baseline `{}`, current `{ "b.ts": 0 }` → ok, and `b.ts` is not in the next
  baseline
- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{}` → ok, no improvement recorded, and the
  next baseline is empty

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex4
```

## ex5 — suppressions with a reason and an owner

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `@ts-expect-error` is a legitimate migration tool and
an appalling habit, and the difference between the two is whether anyone can
tell why it is there six months later. Two exports.

```ts
export interface Suppression {
  line: number;                                    // 1-based
  directive: "ts-expect-error" | "ts-ignore";
  owner: string | null;                            // from owner:@handle
  reason: string;                                  // "" when absent
}

export function parseSuppressions(source: string): Suppression[];
export function auditSuppressions(source: string): string[];
```

`parseSuppressions` scans line comments only — a line whose first non-space
characters are `//` followed by optional space and `@ts-expect-error` or
`@ts-ignore`. Anything after the directive is metadata:

- an `owner:@handle` token anywhere in the remainder sets `owner` to the handle
  without the `@`; the handle is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`
- what is left, after removing that token and stripping leading `-` or `—`
  separators and surrounding whitespace, is the `reason`

Results come back in line order.

`auditSuppressions` returns diagnostic strings, in line order and, within a
line, in this order:

- `line N: use @ts-expect-error instead of @ts-ignore`
- `line N: suppression needs a reason`
- `line N: suppression needs owner:@handle`

Example — for the source

```ts
// @ts-expect-error owner:@ada - legacy cart returns any
const total = cart.total();
// @ts-ignore
const other = cart.other();
```

`parseSuppressions` gives `[{ line: 1, directive: "ts-expect-error", owner: "ada",
reason: "legacy cart returns any" }, { line: 3, directive: "ts-ignore", owner: null,
reason: "" }]`, and `auditSuppressions` gives three diagnostics, all for line 3.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex5
```

## ex6 — reading the types that are already there

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Before you rename anything, turn on `checkJs` and read
the JSDoc the previous team left behind. It is more accurate than you expect,
and it is the cheapest source of signatures you will ever get.

```ts
export interface JsDocParam {
  name: string;
  type: string;
  optional: boolean;
  defaultValue: string | null;
  description: string;
}

export interface JsDocSignature {
  params: JsDocParam[];
  returns: string | null;
}

export function parseJsDoc(block: string): JsDocSignature;
```

The block arrives as raw text including the `/**`, the leading `*` on each line
and the closing `*/`. Strip that decoration first. Then, for each line that
starts with `@param`:

- the type is the balanced-brace group immediately after the tag — **balanced**,
  because `{{ id: string, tags: string[] }}` is one type and a naive
  `/\{(.*?)\}/` cuts it in half
- the name follows, either bare (`sku`), bracketed for optional (`[sku]`), or
  bracketed with a default (`[quantity=1]`)
- the rest of the line is the description, with a leading `-` or `—` and
  surrounding whitespace removed

`@returns` (or `@return`) contributes only its type to `returns`; when the tag
is absent, `returns` is `null`. Tags that are neither are ignored. Only
single-line tags need to be handled.

Worked example — this block

```
/**
 * Adds an item to the cart.
 * @param {string} sku - stock code
 * @param {number} [quantity=1] how many
 * @param {{ id: string }} [meta]
 * @returns {Promise<void>} nothing useful
 */
```

gives three params — `{ name: "sku", type: "string", optional: false,
defaultValue: null, description: "stock code" }`, then `quantity` with
`optional: true` and `defaultValue: "1"`, then `meta` with type `{ id: string }`,
`optional: true`, `defaultValue: null` and an empty description — and
`returns` of `"Promise<void>"`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex6
```

## ex7 — the scoreboard, and what to convert next

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. A migration that nobody can measure stalls, and a
migration where everyone picks their own next file converts the wrong things.

```ts
export interface FileStat {
  path: string;
  lines: number;
  typed: boolean;
  anyCount: number;
  importedBy: number;
}

export interface MigrationSummary {
  totalFiles: number;
  typedFiles: number;
  totalLines: number;
  typedLines: number;
  percentTyped: number;   // by lines, one decimal place
}

export function summarize(files: readonly FileStat[]): MigrationSummary;
export function nextTargets(files: readonly FileStat[], count: number): string[];
```

`summarize` counts by lines, not by files — a thousand-line module and a
four-line constants file are not the same progress. `percentTyped` is
`typedLines / totalLines * 100` rounded to one decimal place, and is `0` when
there are no lines at all.

`nextTargets` considers **untyped files only** and ranks them by

```
score = importedBy * 10 - anyCount * 2 - Math.floor(lines / 50)
```

descending, ties broken by path ascending. It returns at most `count` paths,
and returns `[]` for a `count` of zero or less.

Example — with

```ts
[
  { path: "src/util/money.js", lines: 60,  typed: false, anyCount: 2, importedBy: 9 },
  { path: "src/app.js",        lines: 400, typed: false, anyCount: 1, importedBy: 0 },
  { path: "src/util/date.ts",  lines: 80,  typed: true,  anyCount: 0, importedBy: 9 },
]
```

`summarize` gives `{ totalFiles: 3, typedFiles: 1, totalLines: 540,
typedLines: 80, percentTyped: 14.8 }`, and `nextTargets(files, 2)` gives
`["src/util/money.js", "src/app.js"]` — scores `85` and `-10`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex7
```

## ex8 — a typed bridge over the callback half

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Half of a legacy Node codebase is error-first
callbacks, and rewriting it all at once is not on the table. You need a bridge
that is typed well enough that callers never see the callback, and a bridge in
the other direction for the legacy code that still expects one.

```ts
export type Callback<T> = (error: Error | null, value?: T) => void;
export type NodeStyle<A extends readonly unknown[], T> =
  (...args: [...A, Callback<T>]) => void;

export function promisify<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(
  fn: NodeStyle<A, T>,
): (...args: A) => Promise<T>;

export function callbackify<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(
  fn: (...args: A) => Promise<T>,
): NodeStyle<A, T>;
```

`promisify`:

- resolves with the callback's value when `error` is `null` or `undefined`
- rejects with the error otherwise
- rejects if `fn` throws **synchronously** — a legacy function that validates
  its arguments before doing any work is common, and an un-caught throw there
  turns an async API into a sometimes-sync one
- settles once; a legacy function that calls its callback twice does not break
  the caller

`callbackify`:

- calls the callback with `(null, value)` on success and `(error)` on failure
- normalises a non-`Error` rejection into `new Error(String(reason))`, because
  legacy code will call `error.message` and a rejected string has none
- must **not** treat a throw from inside the callback as a rejection

Example:

```ts
const readOnce = promisify<[string], string>((path, done) => done(null, path.toUpperCase()));
await readOnce("a.txt");            // "A.TXT", and the type is string
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration ex8
```

## challenge — the migration gate (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Everything in this sector so far has been one
rule. CI needs all of them at once, in one report, with one exit code.

```ts
export interface FileReport {
  path: string;
  anyCount: number;
  suppressions: number;
  owner: string | null;
}

export interface Baselines {
  any: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  suppressions: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}

export interface GateOptions {
  maxNewSuppressions: number;
  requireOwnerUnder: readonly string[];   // path prefixes
}

export interface GateResult {
  exitCode: number;
  lines: string[];
}

export function runGate(
  baselines: Baselines,
  current: readonly FileReport[],
  options: GateOptions,
): GateResult;
```

Errors, each on its own line:

- `E any-ratchet <path>: <was> -> <now>` when `anyCount` exceeds
  `baselines.any[path]`, treating a missing baseline entry as `0`
- `E owner-missing <path>` when `owner` is `null` and the path starts with any
  of the `requireOwnerUnder` prefixes
- `E suppression-budget: <n> new, limit <max>` — emitted at most once, when the
  total of `max(0, now - baseline)` across every file exceeds
  `maxNewSuppressions`. A file that removed suppressions does not fund another
  file adding them; that is what the `max(0, ...)` is for.

Information lines: `I any-ratchet <path>: <was> -> <now>` when the count went
down against a baseline entry that exists.

Output order: every `E` line sorted ascending, then every `I` line sorted
ascending, then exactly one summary line:

```
SUMMARY files=<count> any=<total anyCount> suppressions=<total suppressions>
```

`exitCode` is `1` when there is at least one `E` line and `0` otherwise.

Worked example — baselines `{ any: { "src/a.ts": 2 }, suppressions: {} }`,
options `{ maxNewSuppressions: 1, requireOwnerUnder: ["src/billing/"] }`, and
current

```ts
[
  { path: "src/a.ts", anyCount: 1, suppressions: 0, owner: "ada" },
  { path: "src/billing/tax.ts", anyCount: 1, suppressions: 2, owner: null },
]
```

produces, in order: `E any-ratchet src/billing/tax.ts: 0 -> 1`,
`E owner-missing src/billing/tax.ts`, `E suppression-budget: 2 new, limit 1`,
`I any-ratchet src/a.ts: 2 -> 1`, `SUMMARY files=2 any=2 suppressions=2`, with
an exit code of `1`.

Honest difficulty note: no single rule here is hard. The work is in the
ordering and in the fact that the sort is over rendered strings, so
`E any-ratchet` sorts before `E owner-missing` before `E suppression-budget`
without you doing anything — check that this is true for your rule names before
you rely on it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration challenge
```

## review1 — what `strict` actually means here

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Every migration argument eventually becomes an
argument about which flags are on in which directory, and nobody can answer it
because the answer is spread across four `tsconfig.json` files that extend each
other. Compute it.

```ts
export const STRICT_FAMILY = [
  "alwaysStrict",
  "noImplicitAny",
  "noImplicitThis",
  "strictBindCallApply",
  "strictFunctionTypes",
  "strictNullChecks",
  "strictPropertyInitialization",
  "useUnknownInCatchVariables",
] as const;

export type StrictFlag = (typeof STRICT_FAMILY)[number];

export interface RawConfig {
  extends?: string;
  compilerOptions?: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>;
}

export function effectiveStrictFlags(
  configs: Readonly<Record<string, RawConfig>>,
  entry: string,
): Record<StrictFlag, boolean>;
```

The rules TypeScript actually uses:

- `extends` names another key in `configs`. Options merge with the **more
  derived config winning**, key by key.
- Each family flag resolves to its own explicit boolean if one appears anywhere
  in the merged options; otherwise it takes the value of the merged `strict`,
  and `strict` itself defaults to `false`.
- Only boolean values count. `"true"` and `1` are ignored as if absent — a
  string in a config file is a typo, not a setting.
- An `extends` naming a config that does not exist throws
  `Error("unknown config: <name>")`.
- A cycle throws `Error("circular extends: <chain>")`, where the chain is the
  names visited from the entry to the repeat, joined with `" -> "`, ending with
  the repeated name.

Example — with

```ts
{
  "base.json":    { compilerOptions: { strict: true } },
  "legacy.json":  { extends: "base.json", compilerOptions: { noImplicitAny: false } },
}
```

`effectiveStrictFlags(configs, "legacy.json")` gives every flag `true` except
`noImplicitAny`, which is `false`. With `"a.json"` extending `"b.json"`
extending `"a.json"`, the call throws
`circular extends: a.json -> b.json -> a.json`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc01_incremental_migration review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/v3tc01_incremental_migration

Migration is the part of TypeScript that no handbook chapter covers, because it
is not a language feature — it is a project management problem with a compiler
attached. These are the notes.

## Notes

**`allowJs` and `checkJs` are the two switches that make a mixed program
possible.** `allowJs` lets `.js` files be part of the program at all, so a
`.ts` file can import them and get *some* type information back — TypeScript
infers from the JavaScript source. `checkJs` goes further and reports errors in
those files, reading JSDoc as type annotations. The order that works is:
`allowJs` first so the program compiles, then `checkJs` on one directory at a
time via `// @ts-check` at the top of individual files, then renames. Turning
on `checkJs` repository-wide as step one produces ten thousand errors and a
reverted commit.

**The seam is where the lies live.** In a mixed program every value crossing
from unchecked to checked code has a type you asserted rather than proved.
There are only three honest options: validate at the boundary (`ex1`, `ex2`),
type the boundary as `unknown` and force callers to narrow, or accept the risk
knowingly and write it down. The dishonest fourth option — a hand-written
`.d.ts` that says what you hope the module returns — is where most migration
bugs come from, because it is indistinguishable from a checked type at every
call site.

**`strict` is eight flags, and they have very different costs.**
`noImplicitAny` is usually the cheapest and highest-value: it finds the places
where the compiler gave up. `strictNullChecks` is the expensive one, and it is
expensive because it is finding real bugs — every error is a place the old code
assumed a value existed. `strictPropertyInitialization` mostly annoys people
with dependency-injected classes. `useUnknownInCatchVariables` breaks every
`catch (e) { e.message }` in the codebase, which is exactly the point. Sequence
them; do not take all eight at once.

**Ratchets beat deadlines.** A rule that says "no new `any`" is enforceable
today with a baseline file and no cleanup work at all. A rule that says "no
`any` by Q3" requires someone to do the work and someone else to chase them.
The first one ships; the second one becomes a slide. The mechanism in `ex4` —
counts per file, checked in, compare and refuse to increase — is what
type-coverage baselines, ESLint suppression files and tools like `betterer` all
implement, and the `unlisted` rule is the part that makes it airtight.

**`@ts-expect-error` beats `@ts-ignore`, always.** Both suppress. Only
`@ts-expect-error` fails the build when the error underneath disappears, which
means your suppressions clean themselves up as the surrounding code gets typed.
A migration that uses `@ts-ignore` accumulates permanent debt that nothing will
ever remind you about.

**Migrate from the leaves up.** Converting a low-level utility improves
inference in every file that imports it, and those files are still JavaScript —
they get better hover information and better `checkJs` errors for free.
Converting an entry point improves nothing downstream, because nothing is
downstream. Fan-in is the metric; `ex7` is that argument made executable.

## ex1 — the seam

The three-part object check — `typeof`, `!== null`, `!Array.isArray` — is one
of the small number of snippets worth memorising outright, and every part of it
is defending against a JavaScript wart. `typeof null === "object"` is the 1995
bug that could not be fixed. Arrays being objects is not a bug but it surprises
people at exactly the wrong moment, because JSON payloads are full of them.

The no-coercion rule in `readNumber` deserves a moment. A shim that accepts
`"3"` and returns `3` feels friendly and is a disaster: it means a caller can
never tell whether the upstream system changed its schema, because your shim
papers over it. Boundaries should be strict and loudly wrong, not helpful.

## ex2 — the adapter

Adapters are the reason a migration can be incremental at all. The typed world
grows outwards from adapters, and the untyped world shrinks; the interface in
the middle is what lets both sides change independently. Notice that the
adapter validates twice for two different reasons — shape at construction,
values on every call — and that the split maps exactly onto "what can only be
wrong once" versus "what can be wrong every time".

The `this` requirement is not artificial. Legacy JavaScript is full of methods
that read `this`, and a migration that extracts methods into standalone
functions breaks them silently — the failure is `undefined is not an object`
at a call site three modules away.

## ex3 — after strictNullChecks

The `find` versus `mustFind` distinction is a vocabulary, and vocabularies are
how teams stop arguing. `firstMatching` returns `T | undefined` and says
absence is normal. `mustFind` returns `T` and says absence is a bug. The
non-null assertion `!` says neither — it says "trust me" with no information
about who, why or what happens when the trust is misplaced.

`at` with negative indices is worth implementing once because it makes
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` bearable. The flag's real complaint is that
`items[i]` might be a hole, and a helper that returns `T | undefined` honestly
is better than a `!` at every index.

## ex4 and the challenge — ratchets

The interesting design decision in `ratchet` is that it returns `nextBaseline`
rather than writing it. A function that decides and a function that acts are
two functions, and CI needs to run the deciding one without ever running the
acting one. Every ratchet that has silently stopped working did so because
somebody wired the update path into the check path.

The challenge adds the thing real gates have: several rules with different
shapes — per-file, global budget, and a policy scoped to a path prefix — folded
into one deterministic report. The determinism is not a nicety. A gate whose
output reorders between runs produces diffs nobody reads.

## ex5 and ex6 — reading what is already there

The suppression audit and the JSDoc reader are the same idea from two
directions: the codebase already contains structured information, in comments,
and treating comments as data is what turns a migration from guesswork into
measurement. The balanced-brace scan in `ex6` is the small piece of real
engineering — a regex cannot count, and JSDoc types nest.

## ex8 — the callback bridge

Variadic tuple types (`[...A, Callback<T>]`) are the feature that makes a
correctly typed `promisify` possible at all; before TypeScript 4.0 the answer
was a stack of overloads for zero through seven arguments, which is what
`@types/node` still carries for historical reasons. The runtime details — catch
the synchronous throw, normalise non-`Error` rejections, use two-argument
`then` so the callback's own bugs do not become rejections — are the parts that
get written wrong in production every time.

## review1 — flags across a chain

`strict` as a default rather than an override is the design that makes partial
adoption possible, and knowing that rule is a genuinely useful thing to have in
your head during a code review. The cycle detection is there because
`extends` chains in monorepos get long and somebody eventually points one back
at itself.

## Further reading

- [TypeScript handbook: migrating from JavaScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/migrating-from-javascript.html) — the official sequence, including `allowJs` and per-file `// @ts-check`.
- [tsconfig reference: `strict`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#strict) — the eight flags it implies, each with its own page and its own escape hatch.
- [JSDoc supported types in TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/jsdoc-supported-types.html) — exactly what `checkJs` understands, which is far more than most people assume.
- [Airbnb's TypeScript migration write-up](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P-J9Eg7hJwE) — a large real migration, including the codemod and the ratchet.
- [`type-coverage`](https://github.com/plantain-00/type-coverage) — the tool the `ex4` model is a miniature of, including its `--detail` and baseline behaviour.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·TC1 — Migrating a JavaScript codebase incrementally

Every TypeScript tutorial starts with an empty directory. No real migration
ever does. You inherit two hundred thousand lines of JavaScript that pays the
bills, a test suite of uncertain quality, and a product manager who is not
interested in a three-month typing sprint. The interesting engineering is not
"how do I write a type" — you learned that in the first twelve sectors — it is
"how do I add types to a moving system without stopping it, and how do I stop
the untyped part growing back".

The compiler is on your side here more than people expect. `allowJs` lets a
program contain both languages at once. `checkJs` turns the JavaScript half
into a checked program that reads JSDoc as types, so you can find real bugs
before you rename a single file. `strict` is not one switch but eight, and they
can be turned on one at a time. Declaration merging lets you describe a
third-party module that has no types without forking it. None of this is
exotic; all of it is the difference between a migration that lands and one that
becomes a permanent half-finished branch.

The part nobody warns you about is the **seam**. A migration is a moving
boundary between checked and unchecked code, and every value that crosses it
arrives as a lie. TypeScript will happily believe that `require("./cart")`
returns `Cart` because you said so in a `.d.ts` you wrote from memory. It is
not lying to you — you lied to it. So the single most valuable habit in a
migration is to treat the seam like a network boundary: values arrive as
`unknown`, you narrow them with real runtime checks, and typed code downstream
gets a type it has actually earned. Sector 10's guards and sector 19's
`unknown` discipline are not academic exercises; they are the migration
toolkit.

The second thing nobody warns you about is that migrations regress. You convert
`src/billing` to strict TypeScript on Monday; on Thursday somebody adds
`function applyCoupon(order: any)` because they were in a hurry and the build
was green. A migration without a **ratchet** is a migration that oscillates.
The ratchet is a boring piece of CI: count the bad things per file, store the
counts in a checked-in baseline, and fail the build when a count goes up. It
does not demand that anyone fix anything. It only forbids getting worse, which
turns out to be almost all of the value.

The third is the ordering question. Which file do you convert next? The
tempting answer is "whatever I am working on", and that is not wrong, but it
scales badly: convert a leaf utility used by ninety files and every one of
those ninety gets better inference for free. Convert an entry point and you
have typed a file nobody imports. Fan-in is the cheap proxy for value, and the
number of `any`s and `@ts-expect-error`s you would have to write is the cheap
proxy for cost. You want the high-fan-in, low-cost files first, and you want a
scoreboard so the team can see the line move.

This sector is eight pieces of that machinery, written as ordinary TypeScript
functions so that you can test them. Some of them are simplified models of
tools you already use — a suppression-comment parser, a JSDoc reader, a
config-inheritance resolver. Building the model is how you learn what the tool
is actually doing, and the models here are small enough to hold in your head
and close enough to real that you would recognise the production version.

One convention for the whole sector: everything is pure. No filesystem, no
process exit, no `console.log` inside the functions. Migration tooling that
reads the disk is untestable, and untestable CI tooling is CI tooling that
silently stops working. Take the data in, return the report, and let the thin
outer shell do the I/O.

## ex1 — the seam is a network boundary

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The first thing you write in any migration is the shim
that turns a value from the JavaScript half into something you can trust. Four
exports:

- `asRecord(value: unknown): Record<string, unknown> | undefined` — a real
  plain object only. `null`, arrays, functions, strings and numbers all give
  `undefined`.
- `readString(value: unknown, key: string): string | undefined`
- `readNumber(value: unknown, key: string): number | undefined` — finite
  numbers only, and **no coercion**: `"3"` is not a number.
- `requireString(value: unknown, key: string, where: string): string` — throws
  an `Error` whose message is `where`, a colon and a space, then
  `expected string at "key"`, with the key in double quotes.

Examples:

- `asRecord({ a: 1 })` → `{ a: 1 }`; `asRecord([1, 2])` → `undefined`;
  `asRecord(null)` → `undefined`
- `readString({ name: "ada" }, "name")` → `"ada"`
- `readString({ name: 7 }, "name")` → `undefined`
- `readNumber({ n: NaN }, "n")` → `undefined`; `readNumber({ n: "3" }, "n")` →
  `undefined`; `readNumber({ n: 0 }, "n")` → `0`
- `requireString(undefined, "id", "loadCart")` throws with the message
  `loadCart: expected string at "id"`

The parameter type is `unknown`, not `any`, and it must stay that way. `any` at
a seam is not a shim; it is a hole with a comment on it.


## ex2 — an adapter around a legacy module

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `legacy-cart` is a fifteen-year-old CommonJS module
with snake_case methods and no types. You are not going to rewrite it today.
You are going to put one typed adapter in front of it so that nothing else in
the codebase ever needs to know it exists.

```ts
export interface CartApi {
  addItem(sku: string, quantity: number): void;
  total(): number;
}

export function createCartAdapter(legacy: unknown): CartApi;
```

The legacy object is expected to have `add_item(sku, qty)` and `get_total()`.
The rules:

- If `legacy` is not an object, or either method is missing or is not a
  function, throw `Error("legacy-cart: incompatible module shape")` — at
  construction time, not on first use.
- `addItem` forwards to `add_item(sku, quantity)`, and rejects a `quantity`
  that is not a positive integer with
  `Error("legacy-cart: quantity must be a positive integer")`.
- `total()` calls `get_total()` and validates the result: a finite number, or
  `Error("legacy-cart: get_total returned a non-number")`.
- The adapter must call the legacy methods **with the legacy object as `this`**
  — it is old code and it reads `this` internally.

Examples:

- `createCartAdapter({ add_item() {}, get_total: () => 12 }).total()` → `12`
- `createCartAdapter({})` throws `legacy-cart: incompatible module shape`
- an adapter whose `get_total` returns `"12"` throws on `total()`, not before

## ex3 — the day you turn on strictNullChecks

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Turning on `strictNullChecks` and
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in a converted directory produces a wave of errors
that all have the same shape: a value the old code assumed was there. Three
exports that give the codebase a vocabulary for that.

- `firstMatching<T>(items: readonly T[], predicate: (item: T, index: number) => boolean): T | undefined`
- `mustFind<T>(items: readonly T[], predicate: (item: T, index: number) => boolean, label: string): T`
  — throws an `Error` with message `no match for ` followed by `label`.
- `at<T>(items: readonly T[], index: number): T | undefined` — supports
  negative indices counting from the end, and returns `undefined` for any index
  out of range, including a non-integer one.

Examples, with `nums = [10, 20, 30]`:

- `firstMatching(nums, (n) => n > 15)` → `20`
- `firstMatching(nums, () => false)` → `undefined`
- `firstMatching(nums, (_, i) => i === 2)` → `30`
- `mustFind(nums, (n) => n > 99, "big number")` throws `no match for big number`
- `at(nums, -1)` → `30`; `at(nums, -4)` → `undefined`; `at(nums, 1.5)` →
  `undefined`; `at([], 0)` → `undefined`

`mustFind` must be usable as an expression of type `T` with no non-null
assertion at the call site — that is the whole point of it.

## ex4 — a ratchet, so it cannot get worse

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The counts come from somewhere else — a type-coverage
tool, a grep, whatever you have. Your job is the policy.

```ts
export type RatchetViolation =
  | { kind: "increase"; file: string; was: number; now: number }
  | { kind: "unlisted"; file: string; now: number };

export interface RatchetReport {
  ok: boolean;
  violations: RatchetViolation[];
  improvements: { file: string; was: number; now: number }[];
  nextBaseline: Record<string, number>;
}

export function ratchet(
  baseline: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
  current: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
): RatchetReport;
```

Rules:

- A file in the baseline whose count went **up** is an `increase` violation.
- A file **not** in the baseline with a count above zero is `unlisted` — new
  code does not get a free allowance.
- A file whose count went **down** is an improvement.
- `nextBaseline` contains every current file with a count above zero, and
  nothing else: files deleted or fully cleaned drop out, which is what makes
  the ratchet tighten.
- Both `violations` and `improvements` are sorted by file name, ascending.
  `ok` is true when there are no violations.

Examples:

- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{ "a.ts": 3 }` → ok, no violations, no
  improvements, next baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`
- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{ "a.ts": 4 }` → one `increase` violation
- baseline `{}`, current `{ "b.ts": 1 }` → one `unlisted` violation
- baseline `{}`, current `{ "b.ts": 0 }` → ok, and `b.ts` is not in the next
  baseline
- baseline `{ "a.ts": 3 }`, current `{}` → ok, no improvement recorded, and the
  next baseline is empty

```

```

## ex5 — suppressions with a reason and an owner

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `@ts-expect-error` is a legitimate migration tool and
an appalling habit, and the difference between the two is whether anyone can
tell why it is there six months later. Two exports.

```ts
export interface Suppression {
  line: number;                                    // 1-based
  directive: "ts-expect-error" | "ts-ignore";
  owner: string | null;                            // from owner:@handle
  reason: string;                                  // "" when absent
}

export function parseSuppressions(source: string): Suppression[];
export function auditSuppressions(source: string): string[];
```

`parseSuppressions` scans line comments only — a line whose first non-space
characters are `//` followed by optional space and `@ts-expect-error` or
`@ts-ignore`. Anything after the directive is metadata:

- an `owner:@handle` token anywhere in the remainder sets `owner` to the handle
  without the `@`; the handle is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`
- what is left, after removing that token and stripping leading `-` or `—`
  separators and surrounding whitespace, is the `reason`

Results come back in line order.

`auditSuppressions` returns diagnostic strings, in line order and, within a
line, in this order:

- `line N: use @ts-expect-error instead of @ts-ignore`
- `line N: suppression needs a reason`
- `line N: suppression needs owner:@handle`

Example — for the source

```ts
// @ts-expect-error owner:@ada - legacy cart returns any
const total = cart.total();
// @ts-ignore
const other = cart.other();
```

`parseSuppressions` gives `[{ line: 1, directive: "ts-expect-error", owner: "ada",
reason: "legacy cart returns any" }, { line: 3, directive: "ts-ignore", owner: null,
reason: "" }]`, and `auditSuppressions` gives three diagnostics, all for line 3.

## ex6 — reading the types that are already there

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Before you rename anything, turn on `checkJs` and read
the JSDoc the previous team left behind. It is more accurate than you expect,
and it is the cheapest source of signatures you will ever get.

```ts
export interface JsDocParam {
  name: string;
  type: string;
  optional: boolean;
  defaultValue: string | null;
  description: string;
}

export interface JsDocSignature {
  params: JsDocParam[];
  returns: string | null;
}

export function parseJsDoc(block: string): JsDocSignature;
```

The block arrives as raw text including the `/**`, the leading `*` on each line
and the closing `*/`. Strip that decoration first. Then, for each line that
starts with `@param`:

- the type is the balanced-brace group immediately after the tag — **balanced**,
  because `{{ id: string, tags: string[] }}` is one type and a naive
  `/\{(.*?)\}/` cuts it in half
- the name follows, either bare (`sku`), bracketed for optional (`[sku]`), or
  bracketed with a default (`[quantity=1]`)
- the rest of the line is the description, with a leading `-` or `—` and
  surrounding whitespace removed

`@returns` (or `@return`) contributes only its type to `returns`; when the tag
is absent, `returns` is `null`. Tags that are neither are ignored. Only
single-line tags need to be handled.

Worked example — this block

```
/**
 * Adds an item to the cart.
 * @param {string} sku - stock code
 * @param {number} [quantity=1] how many
 * @param {{ id: string }} [meta]
 * @returns {Promise<void>} nothing useful
 */
```

gives three params — `{ name: "sku", type: "string", optional: false,
defaultValue: null, description: "stock code" }`, then `quantity` with
`optional: true` and `defaultValue: "1"`, then `meta` with type `{ id: string }`,
`optional: true`, `defaultValue: null` and an empty description — and
`returns` of `"Promise<void>"`.


## ex7 — the scoreboard, and what to convert next

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. A migration that nobody can measure stalls, and a
migration where everyone picks their own next file converts the wrong things.

```ts
export interface FileStat {
  path: string;
  lines: number;
  typed: boolean;
  anyCount: number;
  importedBy: number;
}

export interface MigrationSummary {
  totalFiles: number;
  typedFiles: number;
  totalLines: number;
  typedLines: number;
  percentTyped: number;   // by lines, one decimal place
}

export function summarize(files: readonly FileStat[]): MigrationSummary;
export function nextTargets(files: readonly FileStat[], count: number): string[];
```

`summarize` counts by lines, not by files — a thousand-line module and a
four-line constants file are not the same progress. `percentTyped` is
`typedLines / totalLines * 100` rounded to one decimal place, and is `0` when
there are no lines at all.

`nextTargets` considers **untyped files only** and ranks them by

```
score = importedBy * 10 - anyCount * 2 - Math.floor(lines / 50)
```

descending, ties broken by path ascending. It returns at most `count` paths,
and returns `[]` for a `count` of zero or less.

Example — with

```ts
[
  { path: "src/util/money.js", lines: 60,  typed: false, anyCount: 2, importedBy: 9 },
  { path: "src/app.js",        lines: 400, typed: false, anyCount: 1, importedBy: 0 },
  { path: "src/util/date.ts",  lines: 80,  typed: true,  anyCount: 0, importedBy: 9 },
]
```

`summarize` gives `{ totalFiles: 3, typedFiles: 1, totalLines: 540,
typedLines: 80, percentTyped: 14.8 }`, and `nextTargets(files, 2)` gives
`["src/util/money.js", "src/app.js"]` — scores `85` and `-10`.

```

```

## ex8 — a typed bridge over the callback half

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Half of a legacy Node codebase is error-first
callbacks, and rewriting it all at once is not on the table. You need a bridge
that is typed well enough that callers never see the callback, and a bridge in
the other direction for the legacy code that still expects one.

```ts
export type Callback<T> = (error: Error | null, value?: T) => void;
export type NodeStyle<A extends readonly unknown[], T> =
  (...args: [...A, Callback<T>]) => void;

export function promisify<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(
  fn: NodeStyle<A, T>,
): (...args: A) => Promise<T>;

export function callbackify<A extends readonly unknown[], T>(
  fn: (...args: A) => Promise<T>,
): NodeStyle<A, T>;
```

`promisify`:

- resolves with the callback's value when `error` is `null` or `undefined`
- rejects with the error otherwise
- rejects if `fn` throws **synchronously** — a legacy function that validates
  its arguments before doing any work is common, and an un-caught throw there
  turns an async API into a sometimes-sync one
- settles once; a legacy function that calls its callback twice does not break
  the caller

`callbackify`:

- calls the callback with `(null, value)` on success and `(error)` on failure
- normalises a non-`Error` rejection into `new Error(String(reason))`, because
  legacy code will call `error.message` and a rejected string has none
- must **not** treat a throw from inside the callback as a rejection

Example:

```ts
const readOnce = promisify<[string], string>((path, done) => done(null, path.toUpperCase()));
await readOnce("a.txt");            // "A.TXT", and the type is string
```

```

```

## challenge — the migration gate (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Everything in this sector so far has been one
rule. CI needs all of them at once, in one report, with one exit code.

```ts
export interface FileReport {
  path: string;
  anyCount: number;
  suppressions: number;
  owner: string | null;
}

export interface Baselines {
  any: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  suppressions: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}

export interface GateOptions {
  maxNewSuppressions: number;
  requireOwnerUnder: readonly string[];   // path prefixes
}

export interface GateResult {
  exitCode: number;
  lines: string[];
}

export function runGate(
  baselines: Baselines,
  current: readonly FileReport[],
  options: GateOptions,
): GateResult;
```

Errors, each on its own line:

- `E any-ratchet <path>: <was> -> <now>` when `anyCount` exceeds
  `baselines.any[path]`, treating a missing baseline entry as `0`
- `E owner-missing <path>` when `owner` is `null` and the path starts with any
  of the `requireOwnerUnder` prefixes
- `E suppression-budget: <n> new, limit <max>` — emitted at most once, when the
  total of `max(0, now - baseline)` across every file exceeds
  `maxNewSuppressions`. A file that removed suppressions does not fund another
  file adding them; that is what the `max(0, ...)` is for.

Information lines: `I any-ratchet <path>: <was> -> <now>` when the count went
down against a baseline entry that exists.

Output order: every `E` line sorted ascending, then every `I` line sorted
ascending, then exactly one summary line:

```
SUMMARY files=<count> any=<total anyCount> suppressions=<total suppressions>
```

`exitCode` is `1` when there is at least one `E` line and `0` otherwise.

Worked example — baselines `{ any: { "src/a.ts": 2 }, suppressions: {} }`,
options `{ maxNewSuppressions: 1, requireOwnerUnder: ["src/billing/"] }`, and
current

```ts
[
  { path: "src/a.ts", anyCount: 1, suppressions: 0, owner: "ada" },
  { path: "src/billing/tax.ts", anyCount: 1, suppressions: 2, owner: null },
]
```

produces, in order: `E any-ratchet src/billing/tax.ts: 0 -> 1`,
`E owner-missing src/billing/tax.ts`, `E suppression-budget: 2 new, limit 1`,
`I any-ratchet src/a.ts: 2 -> 1`, `SUMMARY files=2 any=2 suppressions=2`, with
an exit code of `1`.

Honest difficulty note: no single rule here is hard. The work is in the
ordering and in the fact that the sort is over rendered strings, so
`E any-ratchet` sorts before `E owner-missing` before `E suppression-budget`
without you doing anything — check that this is true for your rule names before
you rely on it.
