# Reading - typescript/v3tc02_async_cancellation

Promises model results. Cancellation is about work, and the gap between those
two sentences is where the bugs live. These are the notes.

## Notes

**A promise cannot be cancelled, and this is deliberate.** The TC39 committee
considered cancellable promises and dropped them, because a promise can be
observed by many consumers and letting any one of them cancel it is a shared
mutable state problem with no good answer. `AbortController` moves cancellation
where it belongs: to the party that started the work. The consequence you have
to internalise is that a wrapper like `ex1`'s `abortable` does not stop
anything — it stops *waiting*. To actually stop work, the signal must reach the
code doing the work, which is why every function in this sector passes it down.

**`AbortSignal` is bigger than most people know.** `signal.aborted`,
`signal.reason`, `signal.throwIfAborted()`, the `"abort"` event, and the
statics `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any(signals)`. `reason` is
typed `any` and defaults to a `DOMException` whose `name` is `"AbortError"` —
so the standard "was this a cancellation?" check is
`error instanceof DOMException && error.name === "AbortError"`, or, in code
that controls its own aborts, comparing against a sentinel you passed to
`abort()` yourself.

**Listener cleanup is not optional.** A signal outlives the operation. Attach a
listener per request to a page-lifetime signal and you have a list that grows
until navigation. The discipline is: every wrapper has exactly one `cleanup`,
it is called from every terminal path, and it is idempotent. `{ once: true }`
helps on the abort path only, which is the path that is least likely to be the
common one.

**Three outcomes, not two.** Fulfilled, rejected, cancelled. Encoding the third
as a rejection is a category error with real operational consequences: retries
of work nobody wants, cancelled requests in the error rate, alerting on user
navigation. `Settled<T>` in `ex6` and `Timed<T>` in `review1` are the same idea
twice, and both are discriminated unions because that is what makes the
compiler demand a decision at every consumer.

**Determinism comes from injection.** Every waiting primitive in this sector is
a parameter: `delay` in `ex8`, `timer` in `review1`, deferred promises in the
gates. A module that reaches for `setTimeout` internally has tests that take
real time, flake under load, and cannot exercise the ordering that matters.
This is the async equivalent of taking a clock as a dependency, and it is the
single highest-leverage habit in testing async code.

**Concurrency limits belong in a pool, not in chunks.** A chunked
`Promise.all` runs at the speed of the slowest member of each chunk and idles
in between; a worker pool over a shared cursor keeps every slot busy. Five
lines either way — the pool is the one to memorise.

## ex1 — abortable

The three requirements — early return when already aborted, cleanup on all
paths, no unhandled rejection — are each a real production bug in miniature.
The last one is the subtlest: after you reject for abort, the underlying
promise is still going to settle, and if you never attached a rejection handler
to it, Node prints an unhandled rejection warning (and, since v15, can
terminate the process). `promise.then(resolve, reject)` attaches the handler
even though the second call to `reject` does nothing.

## ex2 — anySignal

`AbortSignal.any()` shipped in Node 20 and the 2023 browsers, and the
interesting part of its specification is the memory model: the combined signal
must not keep its sources alive, and the sources must not accumulate listeners
from dead combinations. Your `dispose()` is the manual version of that
guarantee. The already-aborted fast path matters for the same reason — a
combination built from a signal that fired last week should not subscribe to
anything.

## ex3 — deferred

Two ideas worth keeping. First, `state` derived from the promise rather than
from the resolve call, so that resolving with a pending thenable does not lie.
Second, the conditional parameter tuple that makes `resolve()` legal for
`void` and illegal for `number`. That trick — `[T] extends [void] ? [] : [T]` —
appears in the real `Promise.withResolvers` typings and in every event-emitter
library, and the bracket wrapping is what prevents distribution over a union.

## ex4 — takeUntil

Async iteration has a cleanup protocol most people never read. `return()` on
the iterator means "the consumer is done"; for a generator it resumes execution
at the `yield` as though a `return` statement ran, so `finally` blocks fire.
That is what lets a generator close a file handle when its consumer breaks out
of a loop. Calling `return()` on the source when you stop early is the polite
half of that contract, and forgetting it is how a paginated fetch keeps
fetching after the component unmounts.

## ex5 — mapWithLimit

The pre-sized results array is the detail that separates working code from
code that works in tests. Pushing results as they complete gives you completion
order, which equals input order whenever everything resolves immediately —
which is precisely what a test with stubbed tasks does. Then production
reorders your data.

## ex6 and review1 — outcomes as types

Both exercises replace an exception with a value, and both do it because the
consumer needs to distinguish cases the `catch` block flattens. Note the shape
of `{ status: "aborted" }`: a variant with no payload. Resisting the urge to
give every variant the same fields is what keeps the union honest.

## ex7 — typed once

`K extends keyof M` plus a return type of `M[K]` is the entire mechanism, and
it is worth contrasting with Node's `events.once`, which returns
`Promise<any[]>` because `EventEmitter` carries no type information at all.
Modern Node has a typed `EventEmitter<T>` generic for exactly this reason, and
the DOM's one-payload-per-event model is why the browser side was typeable
first.

## ex8 and the challenge

The retry loop's real content is one line: check `signal.aborted` inside the
`catch` before deciding to retry. Everything else is arithmetic. The challenge
is the sector's synthesis — shared work, per-caller cancellation, reference
counting, and the identity check before deleting a map entry that a newer
caller may already own. That last one is a genuine concurrency bug in a
single-threaded language, which surprises people who think races require
threads.

## Further reading

- [MDN: `AbortController`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController) — including `reason`, `throwIfAborted`, and the statics.
- [WHATWG DOM: aborting ongoing activities](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#aborting-ongoing-activities) — the normative text, short and readable, and the source of the "abort algorithms" model.
- [Node.js: `events.once` and `AbortSignal` support](https://nodejs.org/api/events.html#eventsonceemitter-name-options) — how the platform threads signals through its own APIs.
- [V8: promise combinators](https://v8.dev/features/promise-combinators) — `all`, `allSettled`, `any`, `race`, and what each does on the first rejection.
- [TC39: the cancellable promises proposal, withdrawn](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-cancelable-promises) — why the language does not have `promise.cancel()`, in the committee's own words.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·TC2 — Async, promises and cancellation

Sector 11 and drill set d21 taught you the types: `Promise<T>` is not `T`, an
`async` function always returns a promise, `Awaited<T>` unwraps as many layers
as there are. That is the vocabulary. This sector is about the sentence nobody
teaches you to write, which is how an async operation *stops*.

Cancellation is where async code gets genuinely hard, and the reason is that a
promise has no cancel method and never will. A promise is a handle on a result
that will exist; it is not a handle on the work. Once you have called
`fetch(url)` the request is in flight, and the promise you are holding is
downstream of it. Whatever you do to that promise — ignore it, race it, wrap it
— the socket stays open, the timer stays armed, the database keeps churning.
Cancellation has to be arranged *upstream*, and the standard way to arrange it
is an `AbortSignal` that you pass down and everyone honours on the way.

That is why the shape of every function in this sector is the same: work goes
in, a signal goes in beside it, and the signal is threaded down to whatever
does the actual waiting. It looks like ceremony until the first time you have
to cancel a request that is six layers deep, at which point you discover that
the layer in the middle dropped the signal and there is nothing you can do from
the outside.

There are three rejections at play and confusing them is the most common
category of async bug in a typed codebase. The task failed. The task was
cancelled. The task is still running and you stopped waiting. Those are three
different facts about the world, they demand three different responses — retry,
do nothing, log a warning — and a `catch (error)` block that treats them alike
will retry a request the user cancelled by navigating away. Half of this
sector's exercises are about giving those three states distinct, typed
representations, which is the discriminated union habit from sector 04 applied
where it is worth the most.

The second theme is **cleanup**. `signal.addEventListener("abort", ...)` inside
a wrapper is a listener attached to an object that may outlive your promise by
minutes. Attach it and forget to remove it and you have a leak whose symptom is
a slow memory climb in a long-lived process, which is the least debuggable class
of production problem there is. Every wrapper here has two exit paths — the work
finished, or the signal fired — and both of them have to tidy up. Writing the
removal on both paths is a habit, and the exercises will not let you skip it.

The third theme is **determinism in tests**. Not one exercise in this sector
uses a real timer. Where something needs to be pending, you get a deferred
promise and the gate settles it by hand; where something needs a delay, the
delay is a function you are handed. This is not a testing convenience, it is
the design. A module that calls `setTimeout` internally is a module whose tests
take real seconds and fail on a loaded CI box; a module that takes its waiting
as a parameter is a module whose tests run in microseconds and never flake.
Once you have written a few functions this way you will find it difficult to go
back.

A note on `AbortSignal` itself, because it has grown since the version most
tutorials describe. It has `aborted`, a `"abort"` event, and — since Node 17
and the equivalent browser releases — `reason`, which is whatever was passed to
`controller.abort(...)` and defaults to a `DOMException` named `AbortError`.
It also has `throwIfAborted()`, and the static helpers `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`
and `AbortSignal.any(signals)`. You will build simplified versions of the last
two here, because building them is how you learn what they promise about
listener cleanup and what they do not.

Everything in this sector is written against `AbortSignal` and
`AbortController` from the standard library, with no dependencies. The types
come from `lib.dom.d.ts` or from `@types/node`, and they are close enough to
identical that the code compiles unchanged in both.

## ex1 — abortable, and tidy about it

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The primitive everything else is built from: take a
promise you cannot cancel and give the caller a promise that stops waiting.

```ts
export function throwIfAborted(signal: AbortSignal): void;
export function abortable<T>(promise: Promise<T>, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<T>;
```

`throwIfAborted` throws `signal.reason` when the signal is already aborted and
does nothing otherwise.

`abortable`:

- if `signal.aborted` is already true, rejects with `signal.reason` — and never
  subscribes to anything
- otherwise resolves or rejects exactly as `promise` does
- if the signal aborts first, rejects with `signal.reason`
- **removes its abort listener on every path**, including the path where the
  promise settles normally
- never produces an unhandled rejection: if the underlying promise rejects
  after you have already rejected for abort, that rejection must be handled

Examples:

- with a controller that has not aborted,
  `abortable(Promise.resolve(1), controller.signal)` resolves to `1`
- `controller.abort("nope")` then `abortable(pending, controller.signal)`
  rejects with the string `"nope"`
- a promise that settles first, followed by `controller.abort()`, must leave no
  listener behind — the gate reads `listenerCount` on a stub signal

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex1
```

## ex2 — one signal from many

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. A request has three reasons to stop: the user
navigated away, the component unmounted, and the overall deadline expired.
Three signals, one operation. Combine them.

```ts
export interface CombinedSignal {
  readonly signal: AbortSignal;
  dispose(): void;
}

export function anySignal(signals: readonly AbortSignal[]): CombinedSignal;
```

Rules:

- the returned signal aborts as soon as **any** input aborts, with that input's
  `reason`
- if any input is already aborted when you are called, the returned signal is
  already aborted — with the reason of the **first** such input in array order
  — and no listeners are attached at all
- `dispose()` removes every listener the function attached, and is safe to call
  more than once
- after the combined signal aborts, its own listeners are removed automatically:
  the caller should not have to call `dispose()` on the normal path
- an empty array gives a signal that never aborts, and a `dispose()` that does
  nothing

Examples:

- `anySignal([a.signal, b.signal])`, then `b.abort("late")` → the combined
  signal is aborted with reason `"late"`
- `a.abort("first")` before the call → the combined signal is already aborted
  with `"first"`, and `a` has no new listeners
- after `b.abort()`, neither `a` nor `b` has any remaining listener from this
  function

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex2
```

## ex3 — a deferred you can inspect

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Every test in this sector needs a promise somebody
else settles. Build the primitive, and give it the one extra thing the platform
version lacks.

```ts
export type DeferredState = "pending" | "fulfilled" | "rejected";

export interface Deferred<T> {
  readonly promise: Promise<T>;
  resolve: (
    ...args: [T] extends [void]
      ? [value?: T | PromiseLike<T>]
      : [value: T | PromiseLike<T>]
  ) => void;
  reject: (reason?: unknown) => void;
  readonly state: DeferredState;
}

export function deferred<T>(): Deferred<T>;
```

Requirements:

- `state` is a **live** view, not a snapshot: reading it after the promise
  settles gives `"fulfilled"` or `"rejected"`
- `state` changes only when the promise **actually settles**. Resolving with a
  pending thenable leaves the state `"pending"` until that thenable settles,
  because that is what resolving with a thenable means.
- calling `resolve` or `reject` a second time changes nothing
- `deferred<void>()` must allow `d.resolve()` with no argument, and
  `deferred<number>()` must **not** — that is what the conditional parameter
  tuple in the signature buys you

Examples:

- `const d = deferred<number>(); d.state` → `"pending"`; `d.resolve(1)`; after
  one microtask, `d.state` → `"fulfilled"`
- `const d = deferred<void>(); d.resolve()` compiles
- `d.reject(new Error("x")); d.resolve(1)` leaves the state `"rejected"`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex3
```

## ex4 — stop pulling

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. An async iterable is a pull-based stream, and the
consumer decides when to stop. Wire a signal to that decision.

```ts
export async function* takeUntil<T>(
  source: AsyncIterable<T>,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): AsyncGenerator<T, void, undefined>;
```

Rules:

- yields items from `source` until the signal aborts, then **returns cleanly**
  — this is a stop, not an error, and it must not throw
- if the signal is already aborted, yields nothing and calls nothing on the
  source
- when it stops early, it calls `source`'s iterator `return()` if the iterator
  has one, so the producer can release whatever it is holding
- an abort that arrives while `next()` is pending stops the iteration as soon
  as the abort fires, without waiting for that `next()` to settle
- if `source` throws, the error propagates unchanged

Examples, with a source that yields `"a"`, `"b"`, `"c"`:

- with a signal that never aborts, collecting gives `["a", "b", "c"]`
- aborting after `"a"` gives `["a"]`, and the source's `return()` has been
  called exactly once
- an already-aborted signal gives `[]`, and the source's iterator was never
  requested

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex4
```

## ex5 — a concurrency limit that respects the signal

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `Promise.all` over five hundred items opens five
hundred connections. A limit fixes that, and a limit that ignores cancellation
keeps starting work after the user has left.

```ts
export function mapWithLimit<T, R>(
  items: readonly T[],
  limit: number,
  fn: (item: T, index: number, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<R>,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<R[]>;
```

Rules:

- at most `limit` calls to `fn` are in flight at any moment
- results come back in **input order**, regardless of completion order
- `fn` receives the same signal, so it can cancel its own work
- when the signal aborts, **no further calls to `fn` are started**, and the
  returned promise rejects with `signal.reason`
- an already-aborted signal rejects without calling `fn` at all
- the first rejection from `fn` rejects the whole call — like `Promise.all`,
  and unlike `allSettled`
- `limit` below `1` throws `RangeError("limit must be at least 1")`
  synchronously
- `mapWithLimit([], 2, fn, signal)` resolves to `[]`

Examples:

- three items, limit `2`, with deferred tasks: exactly two calls have happened
  before anything settles; resolving the first starts the third
- aborting after two starts leaves the third never called, and the returned
  promise rejects with the reason

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex5
```

## ex6 — three outcomes, not two

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. `Promise.allSettled` knows about fulfilled and
rejected. Real systems have a third outcome — we stopped waiting — and

budget.

```ts
export type Settled<T> =
  | { status: "fulfilled"; value: T }
  | { status: "rejected"; reason: unknown }
  | { status: "aborted" };

export function settleAll<T>(
  promises: readonly Promise<T>[],
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<Settled<T>[]>;
```

Rules:

- the returned promise **never rejects**
- one entry per input, in input order
- an input that settles before the abort keeps its real outcome, even if the
  abort arrives a moment later
- an input still pending when the signal aborts becomes `{ status: "aborted" }`
- the returned promise resolves as soon as every entry is decided — it does not
  wait for pending inputs after an abort
- an already-aborted signal resolves immediately with every entry `"aborted"`
- `settleAll([], signal)` resolves to `[]`

Examples:

- two inputs, the first resolved with `1`, the second pending, then
  `controller.abort()` → `[{ status: "fulfilled", value: 1 }, { status: "aborted" }]`
- an input that rejects with `"boom"` → `{ status: "rejected", reason: "boom" }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex6
```

## ex7 — one event, typed, with an escape

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Waiting for a single event is the most common
promise-from-callback conversion there is, and the version everyone writes
first leaks a listener whenever the event never fires.

```ts
export interface Emitter<M> {
  addEventListener<K extends keyof M>(
    type: K,
    listener: (payload: M[K]) => void,
  ): void;
  removeEventListener<K extends keyof M>(
    type: K,
    listener: (payload: M[K]) => void,
  ): void;
}

export function once<M, K extends keyof M>(
  emitter: Emitter<M>,
  type: K,
  options?: { signal?: AbortSignal },
): Promise<M[K]>;
```

Rules:

- resolves with the first payload for `type`, and removes the listener
- with a signal that aborts first, rejects with `signal.reason` and removes the
  listener
- an already-aborted signal rejects **without ever subscribing** to the emitter
- no `options`, or `options` without a `signal`, means it waits forever — which
  is legitimate and must still compile
- the abort listener is removed on the resolve path too

The typing is half the exercise. Given

```ts
interface SocketEvents { data: string; error: Error; end: void }
declare const socket: Emitter<SocketEvents>;
```

`once(socket, "data")` must have type `Promise<string>`, `once(socket, "error")`
must be `Promise<Error>`, and `once(socket, "close")` must not compile.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex7
```

## ex8 — retry, without a real timer in sight

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Retrying is easy. Retrying without retrying a
cancellation, and without a test suite that takes eleven seconds, is the
exercise.

```ts
export interface RetryOptions {
  attempts: number;
  delay: (attempt: number) => Promise<void>;
  signal: AbortSignal;
}

export function retry<T>(
  task: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<T>,
  options: RetryOptions,
): Promise<T>;
```

Rules:

- calls `task(signal)` up to `attempts` times in total
- between a failed attempt `n` and the next one, awaits `delay(n)` — `n` is
  1-based and names the attempt that just failed, so a first failure awaits
  `delay(1)`
- after the last attempt fails, rejects with **that attempt's** reason
- a successful attempt resolves immediately and no delay is awaited
- when the signal aborts, rejects with `signal.reason`: no further attempt is
  started, and a delay in progress is not waited out
- an already-aborted signal rejects without calling `task`
- `attempts` below `1` throws `RangeError("attempts must be at least 1")`
  synchronously

Examples, with a task that fails twice and then succeeds:

- `attempts: 3` resolves on the third call; `delay` was called with `1` and
  then `2`
- `attempts: 2` rejects with the second failure's reason, and `delay` was
  called once
- a task that succeeds immediately is called once and `delay` never

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex8
```

## challenge — one request, many callers (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Ten components ask for the same user at the same
moment. You want one request. Then three of those components unmount, and you
want the request to survive — until the last one leaves, at which point you
want it gone.

```ts
export interface Loader<K, V> {
  load(key: K, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<V>;
  readonly inFlight: number;
}

export function createLoader<K, V>(
  fetcher: (key: K, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<V>,
  keyOf: (key: K) => string,
): Loader<K, V>;
```

Rules:

- concurrent `load` calls whose `keyOf` results are equal share **one**
  `fetcher` call, and all of them resolve with its value or reject with its
  reason
- each caller's returned promise rejects with **that caller's own**
  `signal.reason` when that caller aborts, and the other callers are unaffected
- when every caller of an in-flight key has aborted, the shared `fetcher` call
  is aborted too — with the reason of the last caller to leave — and the entry
  is removed
- when the shared call settles, the entry is removed. This is request
  deduplication, not a cache: a `load` after settlement starts a new fetch.
- a caller whose signal is already aborted rejects immediately and never joins
  or creates an entry
- `inFlight` is the number of distinct keys currently being fetched

Worked example:

```ts
const loader = createLoader(fetchUser, (id: string) => id)
const a = loader.load("u1", first.signal)
const b = loader.load("u1", second.signal)
// fetchUser has been called exactly once; loader.inFlight === 1
first.abort("gone")        // a rejects with "gone"; b is still pending
second.abort("also gone")  // b rejects; the shared fetch's signal is aborted
// loader.inFlight === 0
```

Honest difficulty note: the reference counting is the easy part. The part
people get wrong is that the shared promise now has a rejection handler
attached per caller and *also* needs one of its own for the case where every
caller has already walked away — otherwise the shared rejection is unhandled
and the process prints a warning about a promise nobody owns.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation challenge
```

## review1 — a timeout that is a value, not an exception

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Timeouts are the cancellation everyone writes
first and almost everyone writes wrong, usually by throwing an error that is
indistinguishable from the operation genuinely failing.

```ts
export type Timed<T> =
  | { status: "ok"; value: T }
  | { status: "timeout" }
  | { status: "failed"; reason: unknown };

export function withTimeout<T>(
  task: (signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<T>,
  ms: number,
  timer: (ms: number, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<void>,
): Promise<Timed<T>>;
```

Rules:

- `task` receives a signal that is aborted with the string `"timeout"` when the
  timer resolves first
- the returned promise **never rejects**
- if the timer wins, the result is `{ status: "timeout" }` — whatever the task
  does afterwards is ignored, including a later success
- if `task` resolves first, the result is `{ status: "ok", value }` and the
  timer's own signal is aborted, so the timer can clean up
- if `task` rejects first, the result is `{ status: "failed", reason }`, and
  the timer's signal is aborted as well
- `timer` is a parameter for the same reason `delay` was in `ex8`: there is no
  `setTimeout` anywhere in your code

Examples, with a `timer` you control:

- resolving the task's deferred first gives `{ status: "ok", value }` and the
  timer's signal is aborted
- resolving the timer first gives `{ status: "timeout" }`, and resolving the
  task afterwards changes nothing
- a task that rejects with `"boom"` gives `{ status: "failed", reason: "boom" }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation review1
```

## Concepts, in the order you will need them

### The three questions to ask of any async API

1. **Who can stop it?** If the answer is "nobody", the API needs a signal
   parameter before it goes any further.
2. **What does failure mean?** If cancellation and failure arrive through the
   same channel with the same type, callers cannot tell them apart.
3. **Where does it wait?** If the waiting is a `setTimeout` inside the
   function, the function is untestable without fake timers.

Every exercise in this sector is one of those three questions made concrete.

### The cancellation contract, written out

A function that accepts a signal is promising four things:

- it checks `signal.aborted` before starting work
- it passes the signal to anything it calls that accepts one
- it rejects with `signal.reason` when the signal fires, promptly
- it removes every listener it added, on every exit path

Functions that do three of the four are the ones that produce mysterious
behaviour. The commonest omission is the second: a middle layer that takes a
signal, uses it for its own bookkeeping, and calls `fetch(url)` without it.

### Why `reason` and not an error class

`controller.abort()` with no argument produces a `DOMException` named
`"AbortError"`. `controller.abort("timeout")` produces the string. Both are
legitimate, and the choice is about who reads it:

```ts
if (signal.reason === TIMEOUT) { /* our own sentinel, exact comparison */ }
if (error instanceof DOMException && error.name === "AbortError") { /* anyone's */ }
```

A codebase that aborts with sentinels it defines gets exact comparisons and no
string matching. A library that must interoperate with everyone else's aborts
has to handle the `DOMException` form as well.

## Worked example — the whole stack, threaded

```ts
async function loadDashboard(userId: string, signal: AbortSignal) {
  throwIfAborted(signal)

  const [profile, orders] = await Promise.all([
    fetchJson(`/users/${userId}`, signal),
    fetchJson(`/users/${userId}/orders`, signal),
  ])

  const enriched = await mapWithLimit(
    orders,
    4,
    (order, _index, inner) => fetchJson(`/orders/${order.id}`, inner),
    signal,
  )

  return { profile, orders: enriched }
}
```

Count the places the signal appears: seven, and every one is load-bearing.
Remove it from `mapWithLimit`'s callback and an abort stops the pool from
starting new work but leaves four requests running to completion. Remove it
from `fetchJson` and nothing is ever cancelled at all; the pool merely stops
scheduling. That gradient — from "fully cancelled" to "stopped waiting" — is
worth being able to describe precisely, because most real codebases are
somewhere in the middle and do not know it.

## Common mistakes

**`Promise.race([work, timeout])` and nothing else.** The work keeps running,
the timer keeps ticking (so a Node process will not exit), and the loser's
rejection may be unhandled. Race is a building block, not a solution.

**Treating an abort as a failure.** Retries of cancelled work, error-rate
alerts that fire when users navigate, and log noise that trains everyone to
ignore the logs.

**Listeners without removal.** The leak is invisible until the process has been
up for a day. Look for `addEventListener("abort"` with no matching
`removeEventListener` in the same function.

**`async` executors.** `new Promise(async (resolve) => { ... })` swallows any
throw inside the executor, because the executor's returned promise is
discarded. It is one of the few things ESLint bans outright, and it is right
to.

**Awaiting in a loop when you meant concurrency**, and its mirror,
`Promise.all` over five hundred items when you meant a limit. Both are one line
away from correct and neither shows up in a test with three items.

**Forgetting that the pending work still holds resources** after you have
decided its outcome. `settleAll` marks an entry `"aborted"`; the promise behind
it is still running unless the signal reached it.

## The interview answer

"How do you cancel a promise?" — the question is a trap, and the answer is that
you do not. Promises are results; cancellation is about the work that produces
them. You pass an `AbortSignal` into the operation, the operation honours it,
and callers get a rejection with `signal.reason`. Then add the part that shows
you have done it for real: the signal has to be threaded all the way down, and
a single layer that drops it makes the whole chain uncancellable; every wrapper
must remove its abort listener on both exit paths or you leak; and cancellation
should be distinguishable from failure at the type level, because otherwise
retry logic retries things the user cancelled.

If they push further, `AbortSignal.any` for combining, `AbortSignal.timeout`
for deadlines, and reference counting when several callers share one in-flight
request.

## Check yourself

1. Why does `promise.cancel()` not exist, and what did TC39 conclude?
2. What exactly does `abortable(promise, signal)` stop?
3. Give the two-line check for "was this error a cancellation" when the abort
   came from someone else's code.
4. Why must a wrapper remove its abort listener on the *success* path?
5. What happens to the underlying promise's rejection after you reject for
   abort, and how do you avoid an unhandled rejection?
6. Why is a worker pool better than chunked `Promise.all` for a concurrency
   limit?
7. Why must `mapWithLimit` write results by index rather than pushing?
8. What does calling `return()` on an async iterator do to a generator?
9. Why does `deferred` derive its state from the promise instead of setting it
   in `resolve`?
10. Explain the `[T] extends [void] ? ... : ...` trick and why the brackets are
    there.
11. What is the operational consequence of representing cancellation as a
    rejection?
12. Why is `timer` a parameter of `withTimeout` rather than a `setTimeout`
    inside it?
13. In a shared-request loader, what goes wrong if you delete the map entry
    without checking identity?
14. Why is `new Promise(async (resolve) => ...)` a bug?
15. Which of `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `any` and `race` reject on the first
    failure, and which never reject at all?
lessons.fullReading:
# Long read — cancellation, from the committee's minutes to your call stack

## Why the language does not help you

In 2016 there was a serious proposal for cancellable promises. It reached stage
1, accumulated a `CancelToken` design borrowed from C#, and was withdrawn by
its champion in 2017. The reasoning is worth reading in the original, but the
core is this: a promise is a value that many parties can hold, and giving any
holder the power to cancel it is a shared-mutable-state problem. If two
components await the same promise and one cancels, what does the other see? If
the answer is "a rejection", you have let one consumer break another. If the
answer is "nothing, it keeps waiting", the cancellation did not cancel
anything.

The resolution was to separate the *result* from the *work*. A promise stays a
read-only view of an outcome. Cancellation becomes a message you send to
whoever started the work, and `AbortController` is the standard envelope for
that message. Once you see the split, the design of every API in this sector
follows: the signal goes in with the request, not out with the promise.

This also explains a persistent confusion. People ask why `abortable(p, signal)`
does not cancel `p`. It cannot. It never had a handle on the work — only on the
outcome. What it does is stop *you* waiting, which is genuinely useful and
genuinely different, and a codebase that does not distinguish the two ends up
with "cancelled" requests that still hit the database.

## The anatomy of AbortSignal

`AbortController` is deliberately tiny: a `signal` property and an `abort()`
method. The signal is an `EventTarget` with an `aborted` boolean, a `reason`,
and an `"abort"` event that fires at most once. That "at most once" is
load-bearing — it is why `{ once: true }` is safe and why an aborted signal
never fires again for a listener added later.

`reason` arrived later than the rest and changed the ergonomics. Before it,
every codebase invented its own way to say *why*: a flag on the controller, a
custom error thrown at the check site, a wrapper class. Now `abort(x)` carries
`x` through to every listener, and its default is a `DOMException` with
`name === "AbortError"`, chosen so that `fetch` rejections were already
matching the convention. In Node the same object is available and the same name
is used, which is one of the quieter platform-convergence wins of the last few
years.

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` and `AbortSignal.any(signals)` are the two statics
worth knowing. `timeout` produces a signal that aborts with a
`TimeoutError` `DOMException` — note, *not* `AbortError`, so the two are
distinguishable, which is precisely the three-outcomes lesson baked into the
platform. `any` combines, and the specification work on it was mostly about
memory: an implementation that keeps every source signal alive for the lifetime
of the combined one leaks in exactly the way `ex2`'s `dispose()` exists to
prevent.

## Structured concurrency, and why JavaScript has none

Other ecosystems have an answer to a question JavaScript ducks: when a function
returns, is its work finished? In Kotlin's coroutines, Swift's task groups, and
Trio's nurseries, the answer is yes by construction — a scope cannot exit while
its children are running, and cancelling a scope cancels the tree. That is
"structured concurrency", and it makes the entire class of bug this sector is
about impossible to write.

JavaScript has no such thing. An `async` function can start work and return
without awaiting it, the work continues, and nothing in the language notices.
Every leak in this sector is a version of that: a pool worker still running
after the pool rejected, a source iterator still producing after the consumer
walked away, a shared fetch nobody is waiting for. The nearest thing to a fix
is discipline — a signal per scope, aborted when the scope ends, threaded to
everything the scope starts — and it is worth knowing that you are hand-rolling
what other languages give you for free, because it tells you where to look when
something is still running that should not be.

There is an ergonomic version of this arriving in the language: explicit
resource management, `using` and `await using` with `Symbol.dispose` and
`Symbol.asyncDispose`, shipped in TypeScript 5.2. It gives you deterministic
cleanup at the end of a block, which is the half of structured concurrency that
concerns resources rather than tasks. An `AbortController` with a `[Symbol.dispose]`
that aborts it is a small pattern with a very good ratio of value to novelty.

## Performance notes

Three things cost more than people expect.

**Creating a promise per item.** `mapWithLimit` over a hundred thousand items
allocates a hundred thousand promises, plus the closures they capture. That is
usually fine; it stops being fine in a hot loop, and the fix is to batch the
work rather than the promises.

**`Promise.all` over a large array.** It subscribes to everything immediately,
which means every one of those operations is in flight at once. The limit is
not politeness, it is the difference between a healthy connection pool and a
thundering herd against a service that then rate-limits you and turns a slow
page into an outage.

**Listeners on a long-lived signal.** Adding and removing is cheap; forgetting
to remove is not, because the closure captures the whole operation's state.
A page-level signal accumulating one listener per request will hold megabytes
within a few minutes of interaction.

Against those, the cost of the abort machinery itself is negligible. An
`AbortController` is a small object and an event target; you can create one per
request without thinking about it.

## When not to reach for cancellation

Not every async operation should take a signal, and adding one where it does
not belong is its own kind of noise.

If the operation is genuinely instantaneous — a cache read, a local
computation wrapped in a promise for interface reasons — a signal parameter is
ceremony that every caller has to satisfy and nobody benefits from. If the
operation *must* complete for correctness, cancellation is actively wrong: a
write that has already been sent cannot be un-sent, and a signal parameter
invites a caller to believe otherwise. The honest shape there is a
non-cancellable function with a comment saying why, and a cancellable wrapper
around the *waiting* if callers need to stop watching.

And if the work is idempotent, cheap, and already in flight, letting it finish
is often better than cancelling: the connection is open, the response is on its
way, and the cost of cancellation — a wasted round trip and a cache entry you
did not fill — can exceed the cost of the bytes. Request deduplication with
reference counting, the sector's challenge, exists exactly at this boundary. It
keeps the work alive while anyone still wants it and drops it the moment nobody
does, which is the most defensible policy available in a language that will not
manage the lifetime for you.

## ex1 — abortable, and tidy about it

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The primitive everything else is built from: take a
promise you cannot cancel and give the caller a promise that stops waiting.

```ts
export function throwIfAborted(signal: AbortSignal): void;
export function abortable<T>(promise: Promise<T>, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<T>;
```

`throwIfAborted` throws `signal.reason` when the signal is already aborted and
does nothing otherwise.

`abortable`:

- if `signal.aborted` is already true, rejects with `signal.reason` — and never
  subscribes to anything
- otherwise resolves or rejects exactly as `promise` does
- if the signal aborts first, rejects with `signal.reason`
- **removes its abort listener on every path**, including the path where the
  promise settles normally
- never produces an unhandled rejection: if the underlying promise rejects
  after you have already rejected for abort, that rejection must be handled

Examples:

- with a controller that has not aborted,
  `abortable(Promise.resolve(1), controller.signal)` resolves to `1`
- `controller.abort("nope")` then `abortable(pending, controller.signal)`
  rejects with the string `"nope"`
- a promise that settles first, followed by `controller.abort()`, must leave no
  listener behind — the gate reads `listenerCount` on a stub signal

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The already-aborted check comes first and returns early, before any listener
exists. Getting that order wrong is not a correctness bug in most tests —
adding a listener to an aborted signal never fires — but it is a leak, and the
gate looks for it.

## Hint 2

The body is a `new Promise` with two subscriptions, one to the work and one to
the signal:

```ts
return new Promise<T>((resolve, reject) => {
  const onAbort = () => reject(signal.reason);
  signal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort);
  promise.then(resolve, reject);
});
```

That version is correct about outcomes and wrong about cleanup. Both `then`
handlers and `onAbort` need to remove the listener, which is one shared
function called from three places — or `finally`, which runs on both.

## Hint 3

The unhandled-rejection rule is the subtle one. If you reject for abort and the
underlying promise rejects a tick later, that second rejection has no handler
unless you attached one. You already did — `promise.then(resolve, reject)`
attaches a rejection handler, and calling `reject` twice is a no-op.

Left to you: `signal.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true })` also
removes the listener, but only on the abort path. Decide whether you still need
explicit removal, and be able to say why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what `abortable` does not do: it does not stop the work. The promise you
wrapped is still running, the request is still open, and the only thing you
changed is that your caller stopped waiting. That distinction is the single
most important idea in this sector, and this function is the clearest place to
see it, because the honest name for it is `stopWaiting`.

## Hint 2

`signal.reason` is typed `any` in the DOM library, which means it flows into
your `reject` without complaint and out to a `catch` block as whatever it is.
That is one of the few places the standard library hands you an `any` on
purpose: the reason really is arbitrary, because `controller.abort(x)` accepts
anything. Treat it as `unknown` in your own code the moment you inspect it.

## Hint 3

Test yourself on this sequence before you write the code. A signal aborts.
Three seconds later, the underlying promise rejects. What does the runtime
print? If your answer is "nothing, if the wrapper attached a rejection handler
before it walked away", you have understood why `promise.then(resolve, reject)`
belongs in the body even on the abort path.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — one signal from many

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. A request has three reasons to stop: the user
navigated away, the component unmounted, and the overall deadline expired.
Three signals, one operation. Combine them.

```ts
export interface CombinedSignal {
  readonly signal: AbortSignal;
  dispose(): void;
}

export function anySignal(signals: readonly AbortSignal[]): CombinedSignal;
```

Rules:

- the returned signal aborts as soon as **any** input aborts, with that input's
  `reason`
- if any input is already aborted when you are called, the returned signal is
  already aborted — with the reason of the **first** such input in array order
  — and no listeners are attached at all
- `dispose()` removes every listener the function attached, and is safe to call
  more than once
- after the combined signal aborts, its own listeners are removed automatically:
  the caller should not have to call `dispose()` on the normal path
- an empty array gives a signal that never aborts, and a `dispose()` that does
  nothing

Examples:

- `anySignal([a.signal, b.signal])`, then `b.abort("late")` → the combined
  signal is aborted with reason `"late"`
- `a.abort("first")` before the call → the combined signal is already aborted
  with `"first"`, and `a` has no new listeners
- after `b.abort()`, neither `a` nor `b` has any remaining listener from this
  function

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc02_async_cancellation ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The returned object is a controller you own, seen from the outside. Create an
`AbortController` inside, hand out its `signal`, and abort it from every
listener. The whole exercise is about who removes what and when.

## Hint 2

One listener per input, and every listener does the same three things:

```ts
const onAbort = (source: AbortSignal) => () => {
  dispose();
  controller.abort(source.reason);
};
```

Take the closure seriously — you need the *source* signal's reason, not a
generic one, and you need the exact function reference back later to remove it.
Store the pairs in an array.

## Hint 3

`dispose()` being idempotent is easiest if it clears the array it iterates:
remove each listener, then set the array to empty. Then calling it from an
abort handler and again from the caller costs nothing.

Left to you: whether to scan for an already-aborted input in a first pass
before attaching anything, or to attach as you go and rely on the abort
handler to clean up. One of those attaches listeners that immediately have to
be removed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`AbortSignal.any()` exists in modern runtimes and does exactly this. Building
it once is still worth an hour, because the interesting part is the memory
behaviour: a combined signal holds strong references to its sources' listener
lists, and a long-lived source signal — a page-level one, say — accumulates
listeners from every short-lived operation that ever combined with it. That is
the leak the `dispose()` contract exists to prevent, and it is why the platform
version took several revisions to get right.

## Hint 2

Think about the ordering rule for already-aborted inputs. "The first such input
in array order" is a deterministic choice, and determinism is the point:
without a rule, the reason you get depends on iteration order, and a caller
writing `if (reason === "timeout")` gets flaky behaviour that reproduces once a
week.

## Hint 3

There is a subtle interaction between the two cleanup paths. When an input
aborts, your handler runs, calls `dispose()`, and *then* aborts the controller.
If you abort first and dispose second, any listener that the caller attached to
the combined signal runs while your input listeners are still attached — which
is harmless here, but is exactly the sort of ordering detail that becomes a bug
when someone later adds logic to the handler.
