## challenge — a harness whose context grows (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Every modern runner has a version of this: a
`beforeEach` that returns something, and every test after it sees that
something in its argument, typed. Build it.

```ts
export interface TestResult {
  name: string;
  ok: boolean;
  error: unknown;
}

export interface Suite<C> {
  beforeEach<E extends object>(
    hook: (context: C) => E | Promise<E>,
  ): Suite<C & E>;
  it(name: string, body: (context: C) => void | Promise<void>): Suite<C>;
  run(): Promise<TestResult[]>;
}

export function describe(name: string): Suite<Record<never, never>>;
```

Behaviour:

- hooks run **before each test**, in registration order, each receiving the
  context built so far and merging its result into it
- a test registered before a hook still sees only the context that existed when
  it was registered — at runtime, that means each test remembers how many hooks
  were registered at the time and runs only those
- tests run sequentially, in registration order
- a test's `name` in the result is the suite name, `" > "`, then the test name
- a passing test is `{ name, ok: true, error: null }`
- a test that throws or rejects is `{ name, ok: false, error }` with the thrown
  value
- a **hook** that throws fails the test with that error and does not run the
  test body
- every method returns a suite so calls chain, and the object is mutable
  underneath — `beforeEach` returns the same suite with a wider type

The typing is the point:

```ts
const suite = describe("cart")
  .beforeEach(() => ({ cart: [] as string[] }))
  .beforeEach(({ cart }) => ({ total: cart.length }))
  .it("starts empty", ({ cart, total }) => {
    // cart is string[], total is number, with no annotations
  })
```

Honest difficulty note: the runtime is thirty lines and mostly bookkeeping. The
type-level move — `beforeEach` returning `Suite<C & E>` while the underlying
object is the same one — is a deliberate, sound-ish lie, and being able to say
exactly why it is safe here is the part worth having.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types challenge
```

## review1 — a case table the compiler audits

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. The last idea of the sector, and the cheapest: a
test table whose *type* forces you to cover every case.

```ts
export type Kind = "credit" | "debit" | "refund";

export interface Entry {
  kind: Kind;
  amount: number;
}

export interface Case<K extends Kind> {
  input: { kind: K; amount: number };
  expected: string;
}

export type CaseTable = { [K in Kind]: Case<K> };

export function describeEntry(entry: Entry): string;
export const CASES: CaseTable;
export function runTable(table: CaseTable): string[];
```

`describeEntry` formats an entry, with the amount always to two decimal places:

- `{ kind: "credit", amount: 12 }` → `"+12.00"`
- `{ kind: "debit", amount: 3.5 }` → `"-3.50"`
- `{ kind: "refund", amount: 8 }` → `"refund of 8.00"`
- the `switch` must end with an exhaustiveness assertion that throws
  `Error("unhandled kind: " + JSON.stringify(entry))` for a value smuggled past
  the compiler

`CASES` is a table with one case per kind — and because `CaseTable` is a mapped
type over the union, adding a fourth kind is a **compile error at the table**,
which is the whole point.

`runTable` runs every case and returns a failure description for each mismatch,
in the key order of the table:

```
<kind>: expected <expected>, got <actual>
```

An all-passing table gives `[]`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types review1
```

## Concepts, in the order you will need them

### The five kinds of double, named properly

- **Dummy** — passed to satisfy a signature, never used.
- **Stub** — returns canned answers. No assertions on it.
- **Spy** — a stub that records how it was called.
- **Mock** — a spy with expectations built in; the assertion is on the
  interaction.
- **Fake** — a real, simplified implementation. In-memory repository, fake
  clock, fake filesystem.

Tests that assert on mocks are testing how your code works. Tests that assert
on outcomes through a fake are testing what it does. Prefer the second unless
the interaction genuinely is the behaviour — a retry policy, an audit log, an
idempotency key.

### Where type-level tests belong

Not everywhere. The types worth testing are the ones with behaviour:

- published API surface, where a widening is a breaking change nobody notices
- inference-heavy helpers, where the *result* type is the feature
- conditional and mapped types you wrote yourself
- anything where `any` creeping in would be silent

The types not worth testing are the ones with no behaviour — an interface with
six fields is not going to regress, and `Expect<Equal<User["id"], string>>` is
a restatement of the declaration two lines above.

### Type-level tests do not need a test runner

```ts
// user.types.test.ts - never imported, never executed
import type { Equal, Expect } from "./assert"
import { parseUser } from "./user"

type Result = ReturnType<typeof parseUser>
type _checks = [
  Expect<Equal<Result, { id: string; name: string } | undefined>>,
]
```

`tsc --noEmit` is the runner. The file is in the program, it type-checks, and a
failure is a build failure. That is the cheapest test you will ever add, and it
runs on every keystroke in the editor.

## Worked example — what a widening regression looks like

```ts
export function toLookup<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K) {
  const out = new Map<T[K], T>()
  for (const item of items) out.set(item[key], item)
  return out
}
```

Return type: `Map<T[K], T>`. Now someone "simplifies" the signature to
`key: keyof T` and every call site still compiles — but the map's key type is
now `T[keyof T]`, a union of every property type in the object. Nothing at
runtime changed. No test fails. Autocomplete gets worse, `.get(id)` starts
accepting a `number` where it used to demand a string, and six weeks later
somebody passes the wrong field and finds out in production.

```ts
type Users = { id: string; age: number }[]
type _check = Expect<Equal<
  ReturnType<typeof toLookup<Users[number], "id">>,
  Map<string, { id: string; age: number }>
>>
```

Three lines, caught at the commit that introduced it.

## Common mistakes

**Using mutual assignability for equality.** It cannot see `any`, cannot see
optional-versus-absent, and distributes over unions. This is the single most
common home-made bug in type testing.

**A predicate that returns `boolean`.** Always a distribution you did not want.
Bracket the check type.

**Doubles typed as `any`.** They compile forever, including after the interface
changed underneath them. The whole point of typing a fake is that it breaks.

**Shared fixture objects.** One test mutates, the next fails, and only in a
suite. Copy on the way out.

**Restoring a spy with an assignment.** Leaves an own property where the
prototype's method used to be, and the symptom appears in a different file.

**Mocking what you own.** If you can inject a fake of your own interface, do
that instead — it type-checks, it survives refactors, and it does not need a
framework.

**Testing types that have no behaviour.** A type test that restates a
declaration is a maintenance cost with no coverage.

## The interview answer

"How do you test TypeScript types?" — the answer has three parts. First, the
mechanism: a compile-time assertion, `Expect<Equal<Actual, Expected>>`, in a
file that is type-checked but never executed, so `tsc --noEmit` is the runner.
Second, the subtlety: exact equality is not mutual assignability, because
mutual assignability cannot distinguish `any` from anything, and the standard
`Equal` works by comparing two deferred conditional function types, which the
compiler relates by identity. Third, the judgement: you test types that have
behaviour — public API surface, inference-heavy generics, conditional types —
and you do not write type tests that restate a declaration.

If the conversation turns to doubles, the beat to hit is that a double must be
typed against the real interface so that it stops compiling when the interface
changes, and that a fake usually beats a mock because it lets you assert on
outcomes rather than on interactions.

## Check yourself

1. Write `Equal<A, B>` from memory and explain why it needs two function types.
2. Give two concrete pairs that mutual assignability wrongly calls equal.
3. Why does `Expect` constrain its parameter to `true` rather than returning a
   boolean?
4. Why does `IsNever<T>` need brackets, and what does the naked version return?
5. How does `0 extends 1 & T` detect `any`?
6. Why must `IsUnknown` check for `any` first?
7. What does the `U = T` default parameter do in `IsUnion`?
8. Why is `expectExact<string>()(value)` two calls instead of one?
9. Why does `DeepPartial` test for functions before objects?
10. Why must a fixture builder deep-copy on the way out?
11. What does `-?` do in `MethodKeys`, and what breaks without it?
12. Why must a Proxy-based mock special-case `"then"`?
13. When restoring a spy, when must you `delete` rather than assign, and what
    goes wrong if you get it backwards?
14. What does a `const` type parameter buy you in `forAll`?
15. Why does a mapped-type case table catch a missing case that an array of
    cases does not?
lessons.fullReading:
# Long read — proving things about programs you have not run

## Two kinds of evidence

A unit test is an existence proof: for these inputs, this output. Run enough of
them and you have covered the cases you thought of. A type is a universal
claim: for every input of this shape, the output has that shape, and the
compiler checks it against every call site in the program including the ones
written next year.

Testing types is the practice of putting the second kind of evidence under
version control. The claim "`parseUser` returns `User | undefined`" is already
enforced everywhere it is used — but nothing pins it, so a change that widens it
to `any` is invisible until something downstream misbehaves. A type test pins
it, in one place, at the cost of three lines.

The economics are unusually good. There is no runner to configure, no fixtures,
no setup, and the feedback is immediate — the error appears in the editor as
you type. The cost is that a badly chosen type test is a restatement of a
declaration, and a file full of those is noise that someone will eventually
delete along with the useful ones.

## How `Equal` actually works

The trick deserves more than the two lines it usually gets.

TypeScript's assignability relation is structural and lossy for this purpose:
`any` is assignable in both directions to everything, so any check built on
`extends` in both directions cannot see it. What you need is *identity*, and
the checker does have an identity relation — it just does not expose it.

Where it leaks is deferred conditional types. When the compiler asks whether
`(<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2)` is assignable to
`(<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)`, it has to relate two conditional types whose
check type is an unresolved type parameter. It cannot evaluate them, so it
falls back to a structural comparison of the conditionals themselves — and that
comparison requires the check types, extends types and branches to be
*identical*. Wrap `A` and `B` in that position and assignability of the wrappers
becomes identity of the wrapped.

This is, unambiguously, an exploit. The behaviour is not specified anywhere;
it is a consequence of how `isRelatedTo` handles deferred conditionals. It has
been stable across every release since TypeScript 2.8 introduced conditional
types, the compiler team is aware that half the ecosystem depends on it, and
the practical risk is low — but it is why every serious codebase puts `Equal`
in one file behind one import.

There are variants worth knowing. Some libraries add a branded object in the
false branch so the error message says something useful. Some add a second
check for `any` explicitly, because the deferred-conditional trick is correct
about `any` but the error is confusing. `expect-type` builds a whole fluent API
on top so that `expectTypeOf(x).toEqualTypeOf<Y>()` reports which side is
wrong. All of them are the same six-line core.

## The distribution rule, which explains half the surprises

A conditional type `T extends U ? X : Y` distributes when `T` is a *naked* type
parameter — appearing alone as the check type. Distribution means: if `T` is a
union, the conditional runs once per member and the results are unioned.

That rule is responsible for almost every confusing type-level result:

- `IsNever<never>` written naked gives `never`, because a union of zero members
  produces zero results.
- `IsUnion<"a" | "b">` written naked gives `boolean`, because one member says
  `true` and another says... also `true`, but a similar predicate can easily
  produce both.
- `NonNullable<T>` is defined with distribution *on purpose*, so that
  `NonNullable<string | null>` is `string` rather than `never`.

Wrapping the check type in a tuple — `[T] extends [U]` — turns distribution
off, because `[T]` is not a naked type parameter. When you want it, leave the
parameter naked; when you want the union treated as a whole, bracket it. That
one sentence is the mental model, and it takes about three encounters with a
`boolean` where you expected `true` before it sticks.

## The doubles argument, and where it comes from

Martin Fowler's 2007 essay named the distinction that the industry still argues
about: mockist and classicist testing. A mockist isolates every unit and
asserts on interactions; a classicist uses real collaborators where possible
and asserts on outcomes. Neither is wrong, and the trade is well understood
now: mock-heavy suites are precise about how code works and break on every
refactor that changes how without changing what.

TypeScript shifts the balance towards fakes, for a specific reason. A fake of a
typed interface is checked by the compiler: when the interface gains a method,
the fake stops compiling and you fix it in one place. A mock library that
stubs by string name has no such property — `mock.method("fnid", ...)` compiles
after `fnid` has been renamed to `findById`, and the test passes because
nothing calls the stub. Typed fakes convert a class of silent test rot into a
build error, and that is worth the extra thirty lines.

There is a second reason, less often stated: a fake is reusable across a whole
suite, and it accumulates capability. `failNext` in `ex7` is the kind of thing
you add once and use in forty tests. A mock's setup is per test and is
rewritten each time.

## Performance, and the cost of clever types

Type-level tests are checked by the same compiler that checks your program, and
they are not free. A file full of deeply recursive conditional types can add
seconds to a build, and the `Equal` trick in particular instantiates function
types that the checker must relate structurally.

Three practical rules. Keep the assertion types shallow — assert on the
`ReturnType` of a function, not on a twelve-level-deep mapped transformation of
it. Do not put type tests in files that are imported by application code; put
them in `*.types.test.ts` files that nothing imports, so an editor only checks
them when they are open. And if a type test is slow, that is information about
the type, not only about the test: sector TC6 is about what makes the compiler
slow, and a type that takes half a second to check in a test takes half a
second at every call site too.

## When not to do any of this

Type-level tests on a codebase with no exported generic API are ceremony.
If the types in question are interfaces with fields, the declaration *is* the
test, and a `Expect<Equal<...>>` restating it adds a second place to update
when the field changes. The signal that you need them is inference: whenever
the interesting type is *computed* rather than written, pin it.

Test doubles have a similar boundary. If a dependency is fast, deterministic
and in-process — a pure function, a formatter, an in-memory cache — use the
real one. Every double is a claim that the real thing behaves in a certain way,
and that claim can be wrong; a suite full of doubles can pass completely while
the system does not work at all. The doubles worth having are for the slow, the
non-deterministic and the expensive: clocks, networks, filesystems, payment
providers, and anything with a rate limit.

And there is a threshold below which none of this pays. A four-hundred-line
tool with no public API and two contributors does not need a fixture builder, a
spy library and a property tester. It needs a handful of tests that run fast.
The machinery in this sector earns its keep in codebases where types are part
of the product — libraries, shared packages, anything other teams import — and
knowing which kind of codebase you are in is most of the judgement.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## ex1 — an equality you can trust

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Build the assertion primitive the rest of the sector
uses.

```ts
export type Equal<A, B> = /* ... */;
export type NotEqual<A, B> = /* ... */;
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;
export type MutuallyAssignable<A, B> = /* the naive version, for comparison */;

export const TYPE_CHECKS: [
  Expect<Equal<string, string>>,
  Expect<NotEqual<string, "a">>,
  Expect<NotEqual<any, string>>,
  Expect<NotEqual<{ a: string }, { a: string; b?: number }>>,
  Expect<Equal<{ a: string }, { a: string }>>,
  Expect<Equal<MutuallyAssignable<any, string>, true>>,
];
```

Requirements:

- `Expect<T extends true>` accepts only `true`, so `Expect<false>` is a compile
  error rather than a silently passing check
- `Equal` must distinguish `any` from every other type, and must distinguish an
  optional property from an absent one
- `MutuallyAssignable<A, B>` is `A extends B ? (B extends A ? true : false) : false`
  — it exists so that the last entry in the table documents exactly how the
  naive version fails
- `TYPE_CHECKS` is exported with a value: an array of six `true`s

That last table entry is the point of the exercise. `MutuallyAssignable<any,
string>` is `true`, and `Equal<any, string>` is `false`, and if you cannot say
why in one sentence you are not finished.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Expect` is the easy one and it is doing real work: the constraint
`T extends true` is what turns a failed assertion into a compile error at the
place you wrote it, rather than a `false` sitting in a type nobody reads.

## Hint 2

The trick for `Equal` is to compare two generic function types rather than the
types themselves:

```ts
type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2)
    ? true
    : false;
```

Both sides are *deferred* conditionals — they cannot be evaluated because `T`
is unresolved — and the compiler's rule for relating two deferred conditionals
is that their check types must be identical. That is how identity leaks out of
a system that otherwise only knows assignability.

## Hint 3

Test your `Equal` against the four cases that break every home-made version
before you trust it: `any` versus `string`, `never` versus `never`, a union
against itself, and `{ a: string }` against `{ a: string; b?: number }`. If all
four behave, you have the real thing.

Left to you: `NotEqual` can be written as a fresh conditional or as a negation
of `Equal`. One of them stays correct if `Equal` ever returns `boolean` for
some exotic input; think about which.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the failure. Why is mutual assignability wrong?
`any` is assignable to `string` and `string` is assignable to `any`, so the
naive check says they are equal — and an assertion that cannot tell `any` from
your actual type is precisely the assertion you needed, because `any` creeping
into an inferred type is the regression you are trying to catch.

## Hint 2

The optional-property case is the second reason. `{ a: string }` and
`{ a: string; b?: number }` are mutually assignable, because an absent optional
property satisfies both directions. They are not the same type, and a test that
cannot tell them apart will not notice when someone makes a required field
optional.

## Hint 3

This implementation is famous, slightly cursed, and has a known caveat worth
knowing: it relies on an internal identity check that the TypeScript team has
never promised to keep. It has survived every release since 2016 and is used by
`type-fest`, `expect-type` and `tsd`, so the risk is low — but if a future
version changes it, the fix is a library upgrade rather than a rewrite of your
tests, which is a good argument for putting `Equal` in exactly one file.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — predicates for the awkward types

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Four type-level questions, each of which is a puzzle
about one of the compiler's special cases.

```ts
export type IsAny<T> = /* ... */;
export type IsNever<T> = /* ... */;
export type IsUnknown<T> = /* ... */;
export type IsUnion<T> = /* ... */;

export const TYPE_CHECKS: [
  Expect<Equal<IsAny<any>, true>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsAny<unknown>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsAny<never>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsNever<never>, true>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsNever<any>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnknown<unknown>, true>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnknown<any>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnion<string | number>, true>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnion<string>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnion<never>, false>>,
  Expect<Equal<IsUnion<boolean>, true>>,
];
```

Copy `Equal` and `Expect` in from `ex1` — a test toolkit is allowed to be one
file, and this exercise is about the four predicates.

Each result must be exactly `true` or exactly `false`, never `boolean`. That
constraint is what makes these hard: several natural-looking implementations
return `boolean` because a conditional distributed over a union and produced
both answers.

The `IsUnion<boolean>` case is deliberate: `boolean` is `true | false`
internally, so it is a union, and an implementation that says otherwise is
special-casing something it should not.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`any` is the type that is assignable both ways to everything, and the standard
detection exploits it: `0 extends (1 & T) ? true : false`. For any ordinary
`T`, `1 & T` reduces to `never` or to `1`, and `0` extends neither. For
`T = any`, the intersection is `any`, and `0 extends any` is true.

## Hint 2

`never` is the empty union, so a naked conditional over it produces `never`
rather than `false` — distribution over zero members gives zero results. The
fix is to stop distribution with tuple brackets:

```ts
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
```

That bracket trick appears three times in this exercise. Learn to reach for it
whenever a conditional over a possibly-`never` type behaves strangely.

## Hint 3

For `IsUnion`, the technique is to capture the union once, distribute over it,
and compare each member back against the whole:

```ts
type IsUnion<T, U = T> = [T] extends [never]
  ? false
  : T extends U
    ? [U] extends [T]
      ? false
      : true
    : never;
```

Left to you: work out why the default type parameter `U = T` is necessary.
Distribution rewrites `T` inside the true branch but leaves `U` alone — that is
the entire mechanism, and being able to explain it is worth more than the
snippet.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Order matters between these predicates. `IsUnknown` has to reject `any` first,
because `unknown extends any` and `any extends unknown` are both true —
so a check written only in terms of `unknown` says `any` is `unknown`. Compose:
ask `IsAny` first, and only then ask the `unknown` question.

## Hint 2

There is a general shape to all four. Each one names a property that
distinguishes the special type from every ordinary type, and expresses that
property as an assignability question the compiler will actually answer:

- `any` is the only type where `1 & T` stays `any`
- `never` is the only type that is empty, so distribution vanishes
- `unknown` is the only non-`any` type that everything extends
- a union is the only thing that survives distribution as more than one member

## Hint 3

If a check comes back as `boolean` rather than `true` or `false`, you have an
accidental distribution: the conditional ran once per union member and the
results joined. Find the naked `T extends ...` — naked meaning `T` appears
alone as the check type — and wrap it in brackets. This is the single most
common bug in hand-written type predicates.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## ex3 — assertions that run in your editor

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Type-level tables are precise and awkward to read. In
a test file you want to point at a real value and say what its type must be.

```ts
export function expectAssignable<Target>(): <Actual extends Target>(actual: Actual) => Actual;
export function expectExact<Expected>(): <Actual>(
  actual: Equal<Actual, Expected> extends true ? Actual : never,
) => void;
export function expectNever(_value: never): void;
export function expectError(run: () => unknown): unknown;
```

All four are no-ops or near-no-ops at runtime. Their whole value is in the
signatures.

- `expectAssignable<{ id: string }>()(user)` compiles when `user` has an `id`
  and whatever else, and returns the argument unchanged so it can be used in an
  expression
- `expectExact<string>()(value)` compiles only when `value`'s type is exactly
  `string` — `"a"`, `string | undefined` and `any` must all fail
- `expectNever` is the exhaustiveness assertion: it accepts `never` and nothing
  else, and at runtime it throws
  `Error("unexpected value: " + JSON.stringify(value))`
- `expectError(run)` calls `run`, returns the thrown value, and throws
  `Error("expected a throw")` if nothing was thrown

Note the two-call shape of the first two — `expectExact<string>()(value)`, not
`expectExact<string>(value)`. That is not decoration: TypeScript infers all
type arguments for a call or none of them, so supplying `Expected` explicitly
would force you to supply `Actual` too, and `Actual` is the one you want
inferred.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the bodies first — they are three lines in total — and then spend your
time on the parameter types, which is where the entire exercise lives.

## Hint 2

The curried shape works like this:

```ts
export function expectAssignable<Target>() {
  return <Actual extends Target>(actual: Actual): Actual => actual;
}
```

The outer call fixes `Target` explicitly. The inner call infers `Actual` from
the argument and checks it against the constraint. Partial type argument
inference would let you write this as one call; TypeScript still does not have
it, and this pattern is the standard workaround.

## Hint 3

`expectExact`'s parameter type is the interesting one:
`Equal<Actual, Expected> extends true ? Actual : never`. When the types match
you get the identity, and the call compiles. When they do not, the parameter
type is `never`, and nothing is assignable to `never`, so the call fails at the
argument.

Left to you: what error message that produces. It is not a good one — something
about `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'never'` — and knowing that the
readable-error version needs a branded type in the false branch is a genuinely
useful piece of library-author knowledge.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`expectAssignable` and `expectExact` are two different assertions and choosing
between them is a real decision. Assignability is what your callers actually
depend on, so it is the right check for "this API accepts what I claim".
Exactness is what regresses silently, so it is the right check for "this
inference produces exactly what I claim". Most suites need both, in different
places.

## Hint 2

`expectNever` is the runtime companion to sector 04's `assertNever`, and the
reason it also throws is the same: types are erased, so a value that the
compiler proved impossible can still arrive from `JSON.parse`, from a cast, or
from JavaScript. A no-op here would be a compile-time claim with no runtime
enforcement, and the two together are what serious code wants.

## Hint 3

`expectError` returns the thrown value rather than a boolean, and that is
deliberate: the next line in a test is almost always an assertion about the
message or the type. A helper that returns `true` forces the caller back into a
`try`/`catch`, which is what you were trying to avoid.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 — fixtures with deep overrides

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. A domain object with sixteen fields makes every test
start with thirty lines of irrelevant setup, and the relevant part — the one
field this test is about — is invisible in the middle of it.

```ts
export type DeepPartial<T> = /* ... */;

export function fixture<T extends object>(
  defaults: T,
): (overrides?: DeepPartial<T>) => T;
```

`DeepPartial<T>` makes every property optional, recursively, but leaves
functions and arrays alone as whole values.

The builder returned by `fixture`:

- deep-merges `overrides` into the defaults: nested plain objects are merged
  key by key, everything else replaces wholesale
- treats arrays as whole values — an override array replaces, it does not merge
  element by element
- treats a class instance (a `Date`, say) as a whole value: replace, never
  merge into
- ignores a property explicitly set to `undefined` in the overrides, because
  "not provided" and "provided as undefined" are the same thing in a fixture
- **never mutates** `defaults`, and returns a fresh object every call, so a
  test that mutates its fixture cannot affect the next test

Example:

```ts
const user = fixture({
  id: "u1",
  name: { first: "Ada", last: "Lovelace" },
  tags: ["admin"],
  createdAt: new Date(0),
})

user()                                  // the defaults, deeply copied
user({ name: { first: "Grace" } })      // last is still "Lovelace"
user({ tags: [] })                      // tags replaced, not merged
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc03_testing_types ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two pieces that barely interact: a recursive conditional type, and a recursive
merge function. Write the type first, get the four cases in the prompt right,
and only then write the runtime — you will find the runtime's branches mirror
the type's branches exactly.

## Hint 2

The type, with its cases in the order that matters:

```ts
export type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown
  ? T
  : T extends readonly (infer E)[]
    ? readonly DeepPartial<E>[]
    : T extends object
      ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
      : T;
```

Functions before arrays before objects before everything else, because a
function *is* an object and an array *is* an object, and a conditional takes
the first branch that matches.

## Hint 3

At runtime, "plain object" is the same question as `ex1` of the migration
sector plus one more clause: the prototype has to be `Object.prototype` or
`null`, or a `Date` will be merged into rather than replaced.

```ts
const proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(value);
const isPlain = proto === Object.prototype || proto === null;
```

Left to you: how deep the copy of the defaults goes. Copying only the top level
is a bug that hides for months and then produces a test that passes alone and
fails in a suite.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The `undefined` rule is the one people argue about, so here is the argument.
`user({ name: undefined })` almost always means "I do not care about name", not
"name must be absent". Honouring the `undefined` would produce an object that
violates its own type — `name` is required in `T` — and the type says
`DeepPartial<T>`, in which every property is optional and therefore possibly
`undefined`. Skipping is the only self-consistent choice.

## Hint 2

The freshness rule is what makes fixtures safe to share across a file. Consider
a builder that returned the same nested object every time: one test pushes to
`user().tags`, and the next test in the same file sees two tags. That failure
is order-dependent, disappears when run alone, and costs somebody an afternoon.
Deep-copy on the way out and it cannot happen.

## Hint 3

Compare with the alternative some suites use — a plain object literal spread at
each call site:

```ts
const user = { ...defaultUser, name: { ...defaultUser.name, first: "Grace" } }
```

That is fine for one level and becomes unreadable at three, and it silently
shares anything you forgot to spread. The builder is the same idea with the
nesting handled once, which is the whole reason to write one.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`MockFn<F>` is a *callable object type*: a call signature plus properties. You
build one at runtime by making a function and assigning properties to it, and
then telling the compiler what you built with a single cast — there is no way
to construct a callable object in a way the checker follows all by itself.

## Hint 2

The `-?` in `MethodKeys` is doing real work. Without it, an optional method
`hook?: () => void` has type `(() => void) | undefined`, which does not extend
`AnyFn`, and the key is filtered out. `-?` removes the optionality before the
test, and `NonNullable` handles the case where the property is explicitly
`| undefined` rather than optional.

## Hint 3

The `"then"` rule is the sort of thing you only learn by hitting it. When you
`await x`, the runtime reads `x.then` to decide whether `x` is thenable. On a
Proxy that throws for unknown properties, awaiting a mock — or returning one
from an `async` function — throws from inside the await machinery, with a stack
trace that points nowhere useful.

Left to you: whether to check `key in stubs` or `stubs[key] !== undefined`.
A stub deliberately set to `undefined` should probably count as stubbed; decide
and be consistent.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The design principle behind `mockOf` is that a missing stub should be a loud
failure. The alternative — a mock that returns `undefined` for everything —
produces test failures three layers away from the cause, usually as
"cannot read property x of undefined" inside the code under test. The error
message here names the object and the method, which is the difference between a
one-minute fix and a twenty-minute hunt.

## Hint 2

`Partial<T>` as the stub type rather than `Partial<Pick<T, MethodKeys<T>>>` is
a deliberate loosening: fakes often need to stub data properties too. But note
what `Partial<T>` still gives you — every stub is checked against the real
signature, so when `find` gains a second parameter, every mock of it stops
compiling. That is the entire reason to type a mock at all.

## Hint 3

`returns` and `throws` returning `MockFn<F>` makes them chainable, and the rule
that the most recent wins means you need one piece of state, not two booleans.
A single discriminated variable — `{ kind: "none" } | { kind: "value"; value }
| { kind: "throw"; reason }` — is the shape that cannot get into an
inconsistent state, and it is sector 04's habit showing up in a mock library.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Before you replace anything, ask the object two questions:
`Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, key)` tells you whether the property
is the object's own and what its flags were. `undefined` means it came from the
prototype, and that single fact is what `restore` branches on.

## Hint 2

The recording wrapper needs `this`, so it cannot be an arrow function:

```ts
const spy = function (this: unknown, ...args: unknown[]): unknown {
  calls.push(args);
  return original.apply(this, args);
};
```

`function` gets `this` from the call site; an arrow captures it from the
enclosing scope, which here is the module. That difference breaks any method
that touches its own state.

## Hint 3

Restoring an own property is not `target[key] = original`. That assignment goes
through setters and it silently makes the property enumerable, writable and
configurable regardless of what it was:

```ts
Object.defineProperty(target, key, descriptor);
```

Left to you: whether `restore` should also clear `calls`. There is a reasonable
argument each way; the prompt does not require it, so make a choice and be able
to defend it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason a leaked own property matters is not aesthetics. `Object.keys` on a
class instance suddenly includes a method name; `JSON.stringify` serialises a
function to nothing but changes the key set; a deep-equality assertion in an
unrelated test fails with a diff that mentions a method. All of these
reproduce only when the tests run in a particular order, which is the worst
class of test failure there is.

## Hint 2

The `calls` type is an `infer` on a generic indexed access:
`T[K] extends (...args: infer A) => unknown ? A[] : never`. `Parameters<T[K]>`
would be shorter and does not work directly, because `T[K]` is not known to be
a function type from the compiler's point of view until you have narrowed it —
`MethodKeys` guarantees it, but the constraint does not carry that proof.

## Hint 3

Modern JavaScript has a tidier way to express the restore contract:

```ts
using spy = spyOn(target, "method")   // Symbol.dispose runs restore at block end
```

That is explicit resource management, TypeScript 5.2 and up. If you add a
`[Symbol.dispose]() { this.restore() }` to your spy, every test that uses
`using` cannot forget to restore — which is exactly the failure this exercise
is about.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Map<T[K], T>` gives you storage, uniqueness and insertion order in one
object, and `Map` preserves insertion order across a `set` on an existing key —
which is precisely the "replaced item keeps its position" rule, for free.

## Hint 2

`failNext` is one pending reason and one check at the top of every method:

```ts
const check = (): void => {
  if (pending !== NONE) { const reason = pending; pending = NONE; throw reason }
};
```

Every method is `async`, so a `throw` becomes a rejection automatically —
which is why a sentinel for "nothing pending" is cleaner than `undefined`
(somebody will eventually call `failNext(undefined)`).

## Hint 3

Copying is `structuredClone` in any modern runtime, or a small recursive clone
if you want to stay dependency-free and predictable. Note what `JSON.parse(
JSON.stringify(x))` does to a `Date`, a `Map` and an `undefined` property, and
decide whether your fake should have those failure modes.

Left to you: whether `query`'s predicate sees copies or the stored objects.
There is a performance answer and a safety answer and they disagree.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The copy-on-read rule is the difference between a fake that finds bugs and a
fake that creates them. Without it, a test does
`const u = await repo.get("u1"); u.name = "x"` and silently edits the store —
so the next assertion in the same test passes for the wrong reason, and a real
database would never have behaved that way.

## Hint 2

`K extends keyof T` plus `id: T[K]` is what makes this fake typed rather than
stringly typed. `createFakeRepository<User, "id">("id")` gives `get` a
parameter of `User["id"]`, so passing a number where the id is a string is a
compile error. Compare with a fake typed as
`Record<string, unknown>` and consider which one still helps after somebody
changes the id to a branded type.

## Hint 3

`failNext` exists because error paths are the least tested part of every
codebase and the hardest to reach with a real dependency. Being able to say
"the next call fails" in one line turns "what happens if the database is down"
from an integration test into a unit test — and that class of helper is what a
fake gives you that a mocking library cannot.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`const A extends readonly Arbitrary<unknown>[]` is the piece that makes the
whole thing work. Without the `const` type parameter modifier the array literal
widens to `Arbitrary<number | string>[]` and the positions are gone before the
mapped type ever runs.

## Hint 2

A mapped type over a tuple stays a tuple, and that is what `Samples` relies on:

```ts
type Samples<A extends readonly unknown[]> = { -readonly [I in keyof A]: ... }
```

`keyof A` on a tuple gives the numeric indices plus the array methods, and
the mapped-type-over-tuple rule handles that for you — you get a tuple back
with the same length and the same positions. The `-readonly` hands the property
a mutable tuple, which spreads into the parameters cleanly.

## Hint 3

Seed advancement is a loop, not arithmetic — apply `next` the stated number of
times. That is O(runs × arbitraries) calls to a multiply-and-add, which is
nothing, and it is worth resisting the urge to find a closed form because the
specification is the loop.

Left to you: whether `sample` receives the advanced seed or advances internally.
The prompt says the former, and it matters — an arbitrary that keeps state is
not reproducible, and reproducibility is the entire value of a seed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason property tests are worth the setup is the class of bug they find.
"Reversing a list twice gives the original list" is one line and covers every
list; three examples cover three lists. The bugs it finds are the ones nobody
thought to write an example for — empty inputs, duplicates, boundary values —
which are exactly the ones that reach production.

## Hint 2

Determinism is a design requirement, not a testing convenience. A property
test that fails once a week with a random seed and cannot be reproduced is
worse than no test, because it trains the team to re-run CI until it goes
green. Real frameworks solve this by printing the seed on failure so you can
replay it; the seed parameter here is the same idea.

## Hint 3

`integer`'s modulo is a genuinely biased generator — small values are slightly
more likely when the range does not divide the modulus evenly — and a real
library goes to some trouble to avoid that. It is the right choice here because
the specification has to be exact, and it is worth knowing that you have
implemented the version whose bias is documented rather than the version whose
bias is a surprise.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two arrays: hooks, and tests. Each test entry records its body, its name, and
the hook count at registration time. `run` walks the tests, and for each one
replays the first `n` hooks into a fresh context object.

## Hint 2

The type change happens by assertion at the return, and it is the only cast in
the file:

```ts
beforeEach<E extends object>(hook: (context: C) => E | Promise<E>) {
  hooks.push(hook as (context: unknown) => unknown);
  return suite as unknown as Suite<C & E>;
}
```

You are returning the same object with a wider type parameter. That is sound
here because `C` is phantom — it appears only in parameter positions of
callbacks that you supply the value for — so no caller can hold a `Suite<C>`
that later receives a value typed wrongly.

## Hint 3

Building the context is a fold:

```ts
let context: Record<string, unknown> = {};
for (const hook of hooks.slice(0, count)) {
  context = { ...context, ...(await hook(context)) };
}
```

Left to you: whether a hook's result overwrites an earlier key or is rejected.
Overwriting is what every real runner does, and it is what the spread above
gives you — make sure that is a decision rather than an accident.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason to build this rather than read about it is that it explains a
feature you have probably used and found slightly magical. Vitest's
`test.extend`, Playwright's fixtures and Jest's typed `beforeEach` patterns all
do this: accumulate a context type through a builder chain so that the test
callback's parameter is precisely what the hooks provide. Forty lines, and the
magic is one intersection type.

## Hint 2

Think about why a test only runs the hooks registered before it. The
alternative — every test runs every hook — is what a naive implementation does,
and it produces a context at runtime that is *wider* than the type says.
That direction is harmless in practice but it means the types are describing a
different program than the one running, and the day someone adds an expensive
hook at the bottom of the file, every test above it gets slower for no visible
reason.

## Hint 3

The per-test fresh context is what makes the harness usable. Share one context
object between tests and a test that mutates `context.cart` leaks into the
next, which is the fixture-freshness problem from `ex4` in a different costume.
Build it from scratch each time; the hooks are cheap and correctness is not.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`toFixed(2)` is the formatting, and note that it returns a string with the sign
already attached for negatives — which is why the prompt gives you the sign
separately and the amounts are all positive. Read the examples again if that
seems fussy; it is the difference between `"-3.50"` and `"--3.50"`.

## Hint 2

The exhaustiveness assertion is the one from sector 04:

```ts
function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled kind: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}
```

and the call must be `return assertNever(entry)` in the `default`, not a bare
call — the `return` is what convinces the compiler the function always produces
a string.

## Hint 3

`Object.entries` over the table gives you `[key, case]` pairs in insertion
order, which for a mapped type over a string-literal union is the order you
wrote the keys in. That is what "key order of the table" means and it is
stable — object key order for non-numeric string keys is specified.

Left to you: whether `runTable` catches a throw from `describeEntry`. The
prompt does not say; decide what a test runner should do when the code under
test explodes rather than returning the wrong answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The mapped-type table is a small idea with a large payoff, and it is worth
noticing what it replaces. The usual shape is an array of cases, which compiles
happily with three of the four kinds covered — so the test suite silently stops
covering the case you just added. `{ [K in Kind]: Case<K> }` makes that
omission a compile error, at the table, with the missing key named.

## Hint 2

`Case<K>` being generic in `K` rather than taking `Entry` is doing work too:
inside `CASES.credit`, the `input.kind` must be exactly `"credit"`. Without
that, you could put a debit case under the credit key and the table would still
compile — covering the same kind twice and the other one not at all.

## Hint 3

There is a natural next step worth knowing about even though the prompt does
not ask for it: make `expected` a template literal type where possible, so that
`"+12.00"` is checked for shape as well as presence. That is sector d17's
territory, and it is the point where the table starts checking the *format* and
not only the coverage.

lessons.title: V3·TC4 — ESM, CommonJS and the dual-package hazard
lessons.summary: Two module systems, one file extension, and a package.json field with its own resolution algorithm. This sector builds the pieces: an exports-map resolver with conditions and patterns, extension rules per moduleResolution mode, the esModuleInterop default dance, a checker for the exports mistakes that ship broken types, and the dual-package hazard — one library, two copies, instanceof says no.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TC4 — ESM, CommonJS and the dual-package hazard

There is a class of bug that no amount of skill with types will save you from,
because it happens before your code runs and before the compiler sees it. The
import resolves to the wrong file. The types resolve to a different file than
the code. Two copies of the same library are loaded, so `instanceof` returns
false for an object that plainly is an instance. `import config from "./cfg"`
gives you `{ default: {...} }` in one build and `{...}` in another. Every one
of those is a module resolution problem, and every one of them has been an
afternoon of somebody's life.

The reason it is hard is historical. Node invented CommonJS in 2009 — `require`
is a function, it runs at any time, it returns a value, and `module.exports` is
just an object you can mutate. ES modules arrived in 2015 with the opposite
design — `import` is a declaration, hoisted, statically analysable, with live
bindings and an asynchronous loading phase. They are not two syntaxes for one
idea; they are two different models, and Node had to run both in the same
process without breaking a decade of packages.

The result is the system you now have to know. A `.js` file is ESM or CJS
depending on the nearest `package.json`'s `type` field. `.mjs` and `.cjs` say
so explicitly. A package can expose different entry points to `import` and
`require` through the `exports` field, which is not a path but a small
declarative resolver with conditions, patterns, and its own precedence rules.
TypeScript then layers `moduleResolution` on top, with `node10` (the old
guessing algorithm), `node16`/`nodenext` (the real Node rules, extensions
required, format determined by `type`), and `bundler` (exports and conditions,
but extensionless imports allowed because a bundler is doing the work).

The dual-package hazard is what happens when the machinery works exactly as
designed and you still lose. A library ships an ESM build and a CJS build.
Your app imports it; a dependency requires it. Both succeed. You now have two
module instances, two copies of every class, two singletons, two module-level
caches. `error instanceof LibraryError` is false. A registry that "must" be
global is two registries. There is no error message; the symptom is behaviour
that makes no sense.

This sector builds the machinery so you can reason about it. An exports
resolver with conditions and `*` patterns. The extension rules for each
resolution mode, including TypeScript's `.js`-means-`.ts` rewrite. Format
detection from extension and `type`. A codemod that adds the extensions
`nodenext` demands. The interop rules behind `esModuleInterop` and
`__esModule`. A dual-package detector. A package-manifest checker that catches
the mistakes which ship broken types to your users. And a types resolver that
walks `exports`, `typesVersions`, `types` and `typings` in the right order.

None of it requires a filesystem: every exercise takes the data as arguments,
which is the only way to make this testable and, not coincidentally, the way
the real resolvers are structured internally.

A closing orientation before you start. If you are writing an application, the
advice is short — ESM, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "nodenext"` or
`"bundler"`, and never look at a `.cjs` file again. Everything in this sector
matters most if you *publish* a package, and the sector after next is about
what you publish. If you only consume, read it anyway: the day a dependency
gets this wrong, you will be the one holding the stack trace.

## ex1 — the exports field is a resolver

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `"exports"` looks like configuration. It is an
algorithm, and this is it.

```ts
export type ExportsField =
  | string
  | null
  | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export function resolveExports(
  exports: ExportsField,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
): string | null;
```

`subpath` is `"."` or `"./something"`. Rules, in order:

- a **string** `exports` maps only `"."`; any other subpath gives `null`
- `null` anywhere means "explicitly blocked" and resolves to `null`
- an **object** whose first key starts with `"."` is a **subpath map**;
  otherwise it is a **conditions map** that applies to `"."` only
- in a subpath map: an exact key match wins; failing that, keys containing
  exactly one `*` are patterns, the pattern with the **longest prefix before
  the `*`** wins, and the captured text is substituted into the `*` in the
  target
- in a conditions map: keys are tried in **declaration order**, and the first
  key that appears in `conditions`, or is literally `"default"`, is taken —
  then resolution continues into its value
- if nothing matches at any level, the result is `null`

Examples:

```ts
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", require: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["import"])
// "./m.js"
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", default: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["require"])
// "./c.js"
resolveExports({ "./*": "./src/*.js" }, "./util", [])            // "./src/util.js"
resolveExports({ "./a/*": "./x/*", "./*": "./y/*" }, "./a/b", []) // "./x/b"
resolveExports({ ".": "./i.js" }, "./other", [])                 // null
resolveExports({ "./private/*": null }, "./private/x", [])       // null
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex1
```

## ex2 — three resolution modes, three answers

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. The same relative import resolves to different files
depending on `moduleResolution`, and knowing which is which is the difference
between a build that works and an hour of confusion.

```ts
export type Mode = "node10" | "node16-cjs" | "node16-esm";

export function resolveRelative(
  specifier: string,
  files: readonly string[],
  mode: Mode,
): string | null;
```

`files` is the set of paths that exist. `specifier` is a relative path already
joined against the importing directory — treat it as a plain string key.

- **node10** and **node16-cjs** (CommonJS resolution): try the specifier
  exactly; then with each of `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx` appended, in
  that order; then `<specifier>/index` with the same list, in the same order.
- **node16-esm**: no guessing at all. Try the specifier exactly. Then apply
  TypeScript's rewrite rule: a specifier ending `.js` may be satisfied by the
  same path with `.ts`, `.tsx` or `.d.ts`; one ending `.mjs` by `.mts` or
  `.d.mts`; one ending `.cjs` by `.cts` or `.d.cts`. Nothing else — no
  extension guessing, no directory index.

Return the first path that exists, or `null`.

Examples, with `files = ["./util.ts", "./thing/index.ts", "./data.json"]`:

- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node10")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`
- `resolveRelative("./util.js", files, "node16-esm")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-cjs")` → `"./thing/index.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex2
```

## ex3 — which module system is this file?

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Every question in this sector eventually reduces to
this one, and the answer depends on two things that are not in the file.

```ts
export type Format = "esm" | "cjs";

export function formatOf(
  path: string,
  nearestPackageType: "module" | "commonjs" | undefined,
): Format;

export function declarationFor(path: string): string;
```

`formatOf`:

- `.mjs` and `.mts` are always ESM; `.cjs` and `.cts` are always CJS —
  the extension wins and the `package.json` is irrelevant
- `.js`, `.jsx`, `.ts` and `.tsx` take their format from `nearestPackageType`:
  `"module"` gives ESM, and both `"commonjs"` and `undefined` give CJS, because
  the absence of a `type` field means CommonJS
- `.json` is CJS
- anything else throws `Error("unknown extension: " + extension)`, where the
  extension includes the dot

`declarationFor` maps a source path to the declaration file the compiler emits
for it: `.ts` → `.d.ts`, `.mts` → `.d.mts`, `.cts` → `.d.cts`,
`.tsx` → `.d.ts`. Anything else throws
`Error("no declaration output for " + path)`.

Examples:

- `formatOf("src/a.mjs", "commonjs")` → `"esm"`
- `formatOf("src/a.js", undefined)` → `"cjs"`
- `formatOf("src/a.ts", "module")` → `"esm"`
- `declarationFor("src/a.mts")` → `"src/a.d.mts"`

Watch the `.d.ts` case in `formatOf`: it ends with `.ts`, and it must be
treated as `.ts` and not as some other extension. Pick your extension carefully.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex3
```

## ex4 — the codemod nodenext makes you write

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Switching a project to `nodenext` produces one error
per relative import in the codebase: *Relative import paths need explicit file
extensions*. Nobody fixes four hundred of those by hand.

```ts
export function addExtensions(
  source: string,
  from: ".ts" | ".mts" | ".cts",
): string;
```

Rewrite every **relative** specifier in a static `import` or `export`
statement to carry the extension the emitted file will have: `.ts` → `.js`,
`.mts` → `.mjs`, `.cts` → `.cjs`.

Rules:

- only specifiers starting `./` or `../` are touched; bare specifiers and
  `node:` builtins are left alone
- a specifier that already ends in `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.json` or `.node` is
  left alone
- all of these forms must be handled: `import x from "..."`,
  `import { a } from "..."`, `import type { A } from "..."`, `import "..."`,
  `export * from "..."`, `export { a } from "..."`
- both quote styles, and the original quote character is preserved
- everything else in the file is untouched, byte for byte

Example — with `from` of `".ts"`:

```ts
import { load } from "./loader"
import type { Cfg } from '../config/types'
import "./polyfill"
export * from "./api"
import fs from "node:fs"
import { x } from "./data.json"
```

becomes the same file with `"./loader.js"`, `'../config/types.js'`,
`"./polyfill.js"` and `"./api.js"`, while the `node:fs` and `./data.json` lines
are unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex4
```

## ex5 — the interop dance

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `import x from "cjs-module"` has to mean something,
and what it means has changed twice. These are the rules every bundler and
every transpiler implements.

```ts
export function interopDefault(mod: unknown): unknown;
export function namedExports(mod: unknown): string[];
export function interopNamespace(mod: unknown): Record<string, unknown>;
```

`interopDefault(mod)` — what `import x from "..."` binds when the module was
CommonJS:

- if `mod` is an object with `__esModule === true`, the module was transpiled
  from ESM, so its real default is `mod.default` — return that, even when it is
  `undefined`
- otherwise the whole `module.exports` object *is* the default, so return `mod`
  unchanged, including when `mod` is a function, a string, or `null`

`namedExports(mod)` returns the own enumerable string keys of `mod`, excluding
`"default"` and `"__esModule"`, sorted ascending. A non-object gives `[]`.

`interopNamespace(mod)` builds what `import * as ns` should see: an object with
every named export, plus a `default` set to `interopDefault(mod)`, with
`__esModule` omitted. The result is frozen with `Object.freeze`, because a real
module namespace object is immutable.

Examples:

- `interopDefault({ __esModule: true, default: 42, extra: 1 })` → `42`
- `interopDefault({ a: 1, b: 2 })` → the same object
- `interopDefault(function f() {})` → the function
- `namedExports({ __esModule: true, default: 1, b: 2, a: 3 })` → `["a", "b"]`
- `interopNamespace({ a: 1 })` → a frozen `{ a: 1, default: { a: 1 } }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex5
```

## ex6 — find the two copies

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. The hazard has no error message, so the only way to
catch it is to look at what got loaded.

```ts
export interface Instance {
  package: string;
  format: "esm" | "cjs";
  importedBy: string;
}

export interface Hazard {
  package: string;
  importers: string[];
}

export function findDualPackages(instances: readonly Instance[]): Hazard[];

export function dangerousHazards(
  hazards: readonly Hazard[],
  stateful: readonly string[],
): string[];
```

`findDualPackages` returns one entry per package that appears with **both**
formats. `importers` is the deduplicated, ascending-sorted list of every
`importedBy` for that package across both formats. The result is sorted by
package name ascending. A package loaded in only one format is not a hazard,
however many times it appears.

`dangerousHazards` returns the names of hazardous packages that also appear in
`stateful` — the ones where two copies genuinely break something: classes used
with `instanceof`, singletons, registries, symbol keys, module-level caches.
Sorted ascending, and duplicates removed.

Example:

```ts
findDualPackages([
  { package: "zod", format: "esm", importedBy: "app" },
  { package: "zod", format: "cjs", importedBy: "legacy-plugin" },
  { package: "zod", format: "esm", importedBy: "app" },
  { package: "lodash", format: "cjs", importedBy: "app" },
])
// [{ package: "zod", importers: ["app", "legacy-plugin"] }]
```

and `dangerousHazards(that, ["zod", "react"])` → `["zod"]`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex6
```

## ex7 — the manifest mistakes that ship broken types

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Most packages with broken types are broken in one of
five ways, all of them visible in `package.json` without running anything.

```ts
export interface PackageJson {
  name: string;
  type?: "module" | "commonjs";
  main?: string;
  types?: string;
  exports?: unknown;
}

export function checkPackage(pkg: PackageJson): string[];
```

Return diagnostics, sorted ascending, with no duplicates. The five rules:

1. `exports: "types" must be the first key in <path>` — a conditions object
   containing a `"types"` key that is not its first key. `<path>` is the
   condition path from the root, joined with `/`, or `"."` at the top level.
2. `exports: no default condition in <path>` — a conditions object with at
   least one key and no `"default"` key.
3. `exports: "." is not exported` — the `exports` value is a subpath map (its
   first key starts with `"."`) and there is no `"."` key.
4. `exports: require condition resolves to ESM <target>` — a string target
   ending `.mjs` reached under a `"require"` condition; and the mirror,
   `exports: import condition resolves to CJS <target>` for a `.cjs` target
   under `"import"`.
5. `main "<main>" is not reachable through exports` — both `main` and `exports`
   are present and `main` does not appear as any string target anywhere in
   `exports`.

Anything that is not an object or a string inside `exports` is ignored rather
than crashing — a real manifest can contain anything.

Example:

```ts
checkPackage({
  name: "x",
  main: "./dist/i.cjs",
  exports: { ".": { import: "./dist/i.mjs", require: "./dist/i.cjs", types: "./dist/i.d.ts" } },
})
// [ 'exports: "types" must be the first key in .' ]
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex7
```

## ex8 — where do the types actually come from?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Four mechanisms compete to answer one question, and
they have a strict precedence.

```ts
export type ExportsField = string | null | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export interface TypesPackage {
  exports?: ExportsField;
  typesVersions?: Record<string, Record<string, string[]>>;
  types?: string;
  typings?: string;
}

export function resolveTypes(
  pkg: TypesPackage,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
  tsVersion: string,
): string | null;
```

Precedence, stopping at the first mechanism that is **present**:

1. **`exports`** — resolve it with `"types"` prepended to `conditions`. Reuse
   the `ex1` algorithm; copy it in. If `exports` is present and nothing
   resolves, the answer is `null` — you do not fall through to `types`.
2. **`typesVersions`** — its keys are version ranges, tried in declaration
   order; the first whose range matches `tsVersion` wins. Inside that block,
   keys are path patterns matched against the subpath **without** the leading
   `"./"`, with `"."` written as `"index"`. An exact key wins over a `*`
   pattern; the capture substitutes into the **first** entry of the target
   array. The result is returned with a `"./"` prefix.
3. **`types`**, then **`typings`** — used only for `subpath === "."`.
4. Otherwise `null`.

Version ranges are simple: `"*"` matches everything, `">=X.Y"` and `"<X.Y"`
compare major then minor numerically. `tsVersion` is `"X.Y"` or `"X.Y.Z"`.
Any other range string matches nothing.

Examples:

```ts
resolveTypes({ exports: { ".": { types: "./t.d.ts", default: "./i.js" } } }, ".", ["import"], "5.4")
// "./t.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=4.0": { "*": ["types/*.d.ts"] } } }, "./a", [], "5.4")
// "./types/a.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=9.0": { "*": ["new/*"] } }, types: "./i.d.ts" }, ".", [], "5.4")
// null - typesVersions is present, so types is not consulted
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex8
```

## challenge — resolve a graph, then find the hazard (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. One resolver, applied across a dependency graph,
reporting where two formats of the same package are in play.

```ts
export type ExportsField = string | null | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export interface Manifest {
  name: string;
  type?: "module" | "commonjs";
  exports?: ExportsField;
  imports?: Record<string, ExportsField>;
}

export type Format = "esm" | "cjs";

export interface Resolution {
  from: string;
  specifier: string;
  package: string;
  target: string;
  format: Format;
}

export interface Analysis {
  resolutions: Resolution[];
  hazards: string[];
  errors: string[];
}

export function analyse(
  packages: Readonly<Record<string, Manifest>>,
  edges: readonly { from: string; specifier: string }[],
): Analysis;
```

For each edge, `from` is a package name in `packages`. Its format is `"esm"`
when its `type` is `"module"` and `"cjs"` otherwise, and that decides the
conditions used: ESM importers ask for `["import", "node"]`, CJS importers for
`["require", "node"]`.

Resolution:

- a specifier starting `"#"` is looked up in the **importing** package's
  `imports`; a missing entry is the error code `ERR_PACKAGE_IMPORT_NOT_DEFINED`
- otherwise the specifier is a bare one: the package name is the first segment,
  or the first two when it starts with `"@"`, and the subpath is `"."` or
  `"./"` plus the rest
- an unknown package is `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`
- a package with no `exports` field is `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`, and so
  is a subpath that resolves to `null`
- a specifier starting `"."` or `"/"` is `ERR_UNSUPPORTED`

The resolved `format` is the **target's** format, from `ex3`'s rules: the
target's extension, falling back to the *resolved package's* `type` field.

Output:

- `resolutions` in edge order
- `errors` as `<from> -> <specifier>: <CODE>`, in edge order
- `hazards`: names of packages that appear in `resolutions` with both formats,
  sorted ascending

Honest difficulty note: none of the pieces is new — `ex1` gives you the exports
resolver, `ex3` the format rule, `ex6` the hazard grouping. The work is the
bare-specifier split, which has to handle `"@scope/pkg/sub/path"` correctly,
and remembering that the format of a resolution comes from the **target file**
and the **target package's** manifest, not the importer's.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution challenge
```

## review1 — what kind of specifier is that?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Before any resolver can do anything, it has to
classify the string. Six kinds, and the order of the checks is the whole
exercise.

```ts
export type SpecifierKind =
  | "subpath-import"
  | "builtin"
  | "data-url"
  | "absolute"
  | "relative"
  | "bare";

export function classifySpecifier(specifier: string): SpecifierKind;

export function parseBare(
  specifier: string,
): { name: string; subpath: string } | null;
```

`classifySpecifier`, checked in this order:

- starts with `"#"` → `"subpath-import"`
- starts with `"node:"`, or is exactly one of `"fs"`, `"path"`, `"http"`,
  `"url"`, `"events"`, `"crypto"`, `"util"`, `"stream"` → `"builtin"`
- starts with `"data:"` → `"data-url"`
- starts with `"/"`, or with `"file:"`, or matches a Windows drive prefix such
  as `"C:\\"` or `"C:/"` → `"absolute"`
- starts with `"./"` or `"../"`, or is exactly `"."` or `".."` → `"relative"`
- anything else → `"bare"`

`parseBare` splits a bare specifier into a package name and a subpath, and
returns `null` when the name is not a valid npm package name. For this
exercise, valid means: not empty; no uppercase letters; does not start with
`"."` or `"_"`; a scoped name is `"@scope/name"` where both halves are
non-empty and follow the same rules. The subpath is `"."` when there is
nothing after the name, and `"./"` plus the rest otherwise.

Examples:

- `classifySpecifier("node:fs")` → `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs")` →
  `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs-extra")` → `"bare"`
- `classifySpecifier("C:/tmp/x.js")` → `"absolute"`
- `parseBare("@scope/pkg/sub/deep")` →
  `{ name: "@scope/pkg", subpath: "./sub/deep" }`
- `parseBare("Lodash")` → `null`; `parseBare("./x")` → `null`

```

```

# Reading - typescript/v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution

Module resolution is the part of the toolchain that runs before your code and
before the type checker, and gets blamed for neither. These are the notes.

## Notes

**Two module systems, and the difference is not syntax.** CommonJS is
imperative: `require` is a function call that runs at any point, returns a
value, and can be conditional. ESM is declarative: imports are hoisted,
statically analysable, produce live bindings, and load in a separate
asynchronous phase before evaluation. That is why `require("esm")` was
impossible for years — the caller is synchronous and the callee needs an async
graph phase. Node 22 added `require(esm)` for graphs with no top-level await,
which softens the boundary without removing it.

**Format is decided by extension, then by the nearest `package.json`.** `.mjs`
and `.mts` are ESM; `.cjs` and `.cts` are CJS; `.js` and `.ts` follow the
nearest `type` field, and *no* field means CommonJS, forever, for
compatibility. That last rule is why shipping a CJS build from an ESM package
works: a three-line `dist/cjs/package.json` containing `{"type":"commonjs"}`
flips the format for that directory and nothing else.

**`exports` is a resolver, not a path.** Subpath keys, condition keys, `*`
patterns, `null` to block, and — the rule that catches everyone — conditions
matched in **declaration order**, first match wins. `"default"` must be last.
`"types"` must be first, because TypeScript asks for `["types", ...]` and takes
whatever matches first.

**`moduleResolution` decides which algorithm the compiler runs.** `node10` is
the old guessing algorithm: extensionless imports, directory indexes, no
`exports`. `node16`/`nodenext` are Node's real rules: explicit extensions in
ESM, format from `type`, `exports` honoured. `bundler` is `exports` and
conditions with extensionless imports allowed. Applications can use `bundler`;
libraries should be checked under `nodenext`, because that is what their users
will run.

**`.js` in a specifier means the emitted file.** TypeScript never rewrites
import specifiers on emit, so under `nodenext` you write `./util.js` and the
compiler looks through to `./util.ts`. It is not a hack; it is the consequence
of a promise the project made in 2012 and has kept.

**The dual-package hazard is emergent.** Both resolutions are correct, both
builds are valid, and the failure is that two module instances exist. Symptoms:
`instanceof` false for an obvious instance, a singleton that is two things, a
registry that is empty in one half of the app. There is no error and no line to
blame — only the loaded graph, which is why `ex6` takes instances rather than
reasoning about manifests.

## ex1 — the exports algorithm

Three mechanisms in one field, and the one that gets missed is pattern
matching, which replaced the older `"./*"`-style folder exports because they
could not express a rename. Longest-prefix wins, and the capture substitutes
into the target's `*`.

The `null` target is a genuine feature: `"./internal/*": null` is how a package
declares that a path exists and is private. Before `exports`, every file in a
published package was importable, which meant no library could refactor its own
internals without breaking someone who had reached into them.

## ex2 and ex3 — modes and formats

The candidate-list framing is the point: each resolution mode is the same
algorithm with a different list of things to try. Writing them side by side is
the fastest way to internalise why `node10` finds files that `node16-esm` does
not, and why a library that only builds under the former ships broken.

`declarationFor` exists to make one thing concrete: declaration files have a
format too. `.d.mts` and `.d.cts` were added for the same reason as `.mjs` and
`.cjs`, because a `.d.ts` cannot say whether `export =` means what CommonJS
means by it.

## ex4 — the codemod

Notice what makes a regex acceptable here: the transformation is local, the
syntax is unambiguous in the cases that matter, and the compiler checks the
result. The same reasoning would not license a regex rename of a variable.

The detail worth remembering is that `import type` needs the extension too.
The binding disappears at emit; the specifier is still resolved.

## ex5 — interop

Two different interop schemes exist and they disagree. The transpiler scheme
looks for `__esModule` and is what `esModuleInterop`, Babel, esbuild and every
bundler implement. Node's own scheme ignores `__esModule` entirely: the default
is `module.exports`, and named exports are best-effort from static analysis of
the CJS source. A package can therefore behave differently under a bundler and
under Node, which is one of the more expensive ways to learn this material.

## ex7 and ex8 — the manifest, and where types come from

The five rules in `ex7` are, near enough, what `arethetypeswrong` checks, and
the first one — `types` must come first — accounts for a startling share of
"this package has no types" reports. The precedence in `ex8` is the other half:
if `exports` is present it is the only mechanism consulted, so a perfectly good
top-level `types` field is ignored and the fix is a `"types"` condition.

## the challenge and review1

The challenge is the sector assembled: parse, resolve, determine format,
aggregate. The bug it is designed to provoke is using the importer's `type`
field to decide the target's format — the importer's manifest is the one
already in your hand, and it is the wrong one.

`review1` is the entry point of every resolver ever written, and the ordering
of its six branches is the exercise: `"fs"` is both a builtin and a
bare-specifier shape, and only the order tells them apart.

## Further reading

- [Node.js: Modules — Packages](https://nodejs.org/api/packages.html) — the normative description of `exports`, `imports`, conditions and the dual-package hazard, including the official mitigations.
- [TypeScript handbook: Modules — Reference](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/modules/reference.html) — every `moduleResolution` mode side by side, with worked examples.
- [`arethetypeswrong`](https://arethetypeswrong.github.io/) — run it against any package you publish; the failure names are the vocabulary the ecosystem uses.
- [TypeScript 4.7 release notes: ESM in Node.js](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-4-7/#esm-nodejs) — where `node16`, `.mts`, `.cts` and the `.js`-specifier rule were introduced, with the reasoning.
- [Node 22: `require(esm)`](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.12.0) — the change that makes the two systems slightly less separate, and its precise limits.
