# V3·TC4 — ESM, CommonJS and the dual-package hazard

There is a class of bug that no amount of skill with types will save you from,
because it happens before your code runs and before the compiler sees it. The
import resolves to the wrong file. The types resolve to a different file than
the code. Two copies of the same library are loaded, so `instanceof` returns
false for an object that plainly is an instance. `import config from "./cfg"`
gives you `{ default: {...} }` in one build and `{...}` in another. Every one
of those is a module resolution problem, and every one of them has been an
afternoon of somebody's life.

The reason it is hard is historical. Node invented CommonJS in 2009 — `require`
is a function, it runs at any time, it returns a value, and `module.exports` is
just an object you can mutate. ES modules arrived in 2015 with the opposite
design — `import` is a declaration, hoisted, statically analysable, with live
bindings and an asynchronous loading phase. They are not two syntaxes for one
idea; they are two different models, and Node had to run both in the same
process without breaking a decade of packages.

The result is the system you now have to know. A `.js` file is ESM or CJS
depending on the nearest `package.json`'s `type` field. `.mjs` and `.cjs` say
so explicitly. A package can expose different entry points to `import` and
`require` through the `exports` field, which is not a path but a small
declarative resolver with conditions, patterns, and its own precedence rules.
TypeScript then layers `moduleResolution` on top, with `node10` (the old
guessing algorithm), `node16`/`nodenext` (the real Node rules, extensions
required, format determined by `type`), and `bundler` (exports and conditions,
but extensionless imports allowed because a bundler is doing the work).

The dual-package hazard is what happens when the machinery works exactly as
designed and you still lose. A library ships an ESM build and a CJS build.
Your app imports it; a dependency requires it. Both succeed. You now have two
module instances, two copies of every class, two singletons, two module-level
caches. `error instanceof LibraryError` is false. A registry that "must" be
global is two registries. There is no error message; the symptom is behaviour
that makes no sense.

This sector builds the machinery so you can reason about it. An exports
resolver with conditions and `*` patterns. The extension rules for each
resolution mode, including TypeScript's `.js`-means-`.ts` rewrite. Format
detection from extension and `type`. A codemod that adds the extensions
`nodenext` demands. The interop rules behind `esModuleInterop` and
`__esModule`. A dual-package detector. A package-manifest checker that catches
the mistakes which ship broken types to your users. And a types resolver that
walks `exports`, `typesVersions`, `types` and `typings` in the right order.

None of it requires a filesystem: every exercise takes the data as arguments,
which is the only way to make this testable and, not coincidentally, the way
the real resolvers are structured internally.

A closing orientation before you start. If you are writing an application, the
advice is short — ESM, `"type": "module"`, `moduleResolution: "nodenext"` or
`"bundler"`, and never look at a `.cjs` file again. Everything in this sector
matters most if you *publish* a package, and the sector after next is about
what you publish. If you only consume, read it anyway: the day a dependency
gets this wrong, you will be the one holding the stack trace.

## ex1 — the exports field is a resolver

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `"exports"` looks like configuration. It is an
algorithm, and this is it.

```ts
export type ExportsField =
  | string
  | null
  | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export function resolveExports(
  exports: ExportsField,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
): string | null;
```

`subpath` is `"."` or `"./something"`. Rules, in order:

- a **string** `exports` maps only `"."`; any other subpath gives `null`
- `null` anywhere means "explicitly blocked" and resolves to `null`
- an **object** whose first key starts with `"."` is a **subpath map**;
  otherwise it is a **conditions map** that applies to `"."` only
- in a subpath map: an exact key match wins; failing that, keys containing
  exactly one `*` are patterns, the pattern with the **longest prefix before
  the `*`** wins, and the captured text is substituted into the `*` in the
  target
- in a conditions map: keys are tried in **declaration order**, and the first
  key that appears in `conditions`, or is literally `"default"`, is taken —
  then resolution continues into its value
- if nothing matches at any level, the result is `null`

Examples:

```ts
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", require: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["import"])
// "./m.js"
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", default: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["require"])
// "./c.js"
resolveExports({ "./*": "./src/*.js" }, "./util", [])            // "./src/util.js"
resolveExports({ "./a/*": "./x/*", "./*": "./y/*" }, "./a/b", []) // "./x/b"
resolveExports({ ".": "./i.js" }, "./other", [])                 // null
resolveExports({ "./private/*": null }, "./private/x", [])       // null
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex1
```

## ex2 — three resolution modes, three answers

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. The same relative import resolves to different files
depending on `moduleResolution`, and knowing which is which is the difference
between a build that works and an hour of confusion.

```ts
export type Mode = "node10" | "node16-cjs" | "node16-esm";

export function resolveRelative(
  specifier: string,
  files: readonly string[],
  mode: Mode,
): string | null;
```

`files` is the set of paths that exist. `specifier` is a relative path already
joined against the importing directory — treat it as a plain string key.

- **node10** and **node16-cjs** (CommonJS resolution): try the specifier
  exactly; then with each of `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx` appended, in
  that order; then `<specifier>/index` with the same list, in the same order.
- **node16-esm**: no guessing at all. Try the specifier exactly. Then apply
  TypeScript's rewrite rule: a specifier ending `.js` may be satisfied by the
  same path with `.ts`, `.tsx` or `.d.ts`; one ending `.mjs` by `.mts` or
  `.d.mts`; one ending `.cjs` by `.cts` or `.d.cts`. Nothing else — no
  extension guessing, no directory index.

Return the first path that exists, or `null`.

Examples, with `files = ["./util.ts", "./thing/index.ts", "./data.json"]`:

- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node10")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`
- `resolveRelative("./util.js", files, "node16-esm")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-cjs")` → `"./thing/index.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex2
```

## ex3 — which module system is this file?

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Every question in this sector eventually reduces to
this one, and the answer depends on two things that are not in the file.

```ts
export type Format = "esm" | "cjs";

export function formatOf(
  path: string,
  nearestPackageType: "module" | "commonjs" | undefined,
): Format;

export function declarationFor(path: string): string;
```

`formatOf`:

- `.mjs` and `.mts` are always ESM; `.cjs` and `.cts` are always CJS —
  the extension wins and the `package.json` is irrelevant
- `.js`, `.jsx`, `.ts` and `.tsx` take their format from `nearestPackageType`:
  `"module"` gives ESM, and both `"commonjs"` and `undefined` give CJS, because
  the absence of a `type` field means CommonJS
- `.json` is CJS
- anything else throws `Error("unknown extension: " + extension)`, where the
  extension includes the dot

`declarationFor` maps a source path to the declaration file the compiler emits
for it: `.ts` → `.d.ts`, `.mts` → `.d.mts`, `.cts` → `.d.cts`,
`.tsx` → `.d.ts`. Anything else throws
`Error("no declaration output for " + path)`.

Examples:

- `formatOf("src/a.mjs", "commonjs")` → `"esm"`
- `formatOf("src/a.js", undefined)` → `"cjs"`
- `formatOf("src/a.ts", "module")` → `"esm"`
- `declarationFor("src/a.mts")` → `"src/a.d.mts"`

Watch the `.d.ts` case in `formatOf`: it ends with `.ts`, and it must be
treated as `.ts` and not as some other extension. Pick your extension carefully.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex3
```

## ex4 — the codemod nodenext makes you write

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Switching a project to `nodenext` produces one error
per relative import in the codebase: *Relative import paths need explicit file
extensions*. Nobody fixes four hundred of those by hand.

```ts
export function addExtensions(
  source: string,
  from: ".ts" | ".mts" | ".cts",
): string;
```

Rewrite every **relative** specifier in a static `import` or `export`
statement to carry the extension the emitted file will have: `.ts` → `.js`,
`.mts` → `.mjs`, `.cts` → `.cjs`.

Rules:

- only specifiers starting `./` or `../` are touched; bare specifiers and
  `node:` builtins are left alone
- a specifier that already ends in `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.json` or `.node` is
  left alone
- all of these forms must be handled: `import x from "..."`,
  `import { a } from "..."`, `import type { A } from "..."`, `import "..."`,
  `export * from "..."`, `export { a } from "..."`
- both quote styles, and the original quote character is preserved
- everything else in the file is untouched, byte for byte

Example — with `from` of `".ts"`:

```ts
import { load } from "./loader"
import type { Cfg } from '../config/types'
import "./polyfill"
export * from "./api"
import fs from "node:fs"
import { x } from "./data.json"
```

becomes the same file with `"./loader.js"`, `'../config/types.js'`,
`"./polyfill.js"` and `"./api.js"`, while the `node:fs` and `./data.json` lines
are unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex4
```

## ex5 — the interop dance

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `import x from "cjs-module"` has to mean something,
and what it means has changed twice. These are the rules every bundler and
every transpiler implements.

```ts
export function interopDefault(mod: unknown): unknown;
export function namedExports(mod: unknown): string[];
export function interopNamespace(mod: unknown): Record<string, unknown>;
```

`interopDefault(mod)` — what `import x from "..."` binds when the module was
CommonJS:

- if `mod` is an object with `__esModule === true`, the module was transpiled
  from ESM, so its real default is `mod.default` — return that, even when it is
  `undefined`
- otherwise the whole `module.exports` object *is* the default, so return `mod`
  unchanged, including when `mod` is a function, a string, or `null`

`namedExports(mod)` returns the own enumerable string keys of `mod`, excluding
`"default"` and `"__esModule"`, sorted ascending. A non-object gives `[]`.

`interopNamespace(mod)` builds what `import * as ns` should see: an object with
every named export, plus a `default` set to `interopDefault(mod)`, with
`__esModule` omitted. The result is frozen with `Object.freeze`, because a real
module namespace object is immutable.

Examples:

- `interopDefault({ __esModule: true, default: 42, extra: 1 })` → `42`
- `interopDefault({ a: 1, b: 2 })` → the same object
- `interopDefault(function f() {})` → the function
- `namedExports({ __esModule: true, default: 1, b: 2, a: 3 })` → `["a", "b"]`
- `interopNamespace({ a: 1 })` → a frozen `{ a: 1, default: { a: 1 } }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex5
```

## ex6 — find the two copies

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. The hazard has no error message, so the only way to
catch it is to look at what got loaded.

```ts
export interface Instance {
  package: string;
  format: "esm" | "cjs";
  importedBy: string;
}

export interface Hazard {
  package: string;
  importers: string[];
}

export function findDualPackages(instances: readonly Instance[]): Hazard[];

export function dangerousHazards(
  hazards: readonly Hazard[],
  stateful: readonly string[],
): string[];
```

`findDualPackages` returns one entry per package that appears with **both**
formats. `importers` is the deduplicated, ascending-sorted list of every
`importedBy` for that package across both formats. The result is sorted by
package name ascending. A package loaded in only one format is not a hazard,
however many times it appears.

`dangerousHazards` returns the names of hazardous packages that also appear in
`stateful` — the ones where two copies genuinely break something: classes used
with `instanceof`, singletons, registries, symbol keys, module-level caches.
Sorted ascending, and duplicates removed.

Example:

```ts
findDualPackages([
  { package: "zod", format: "esm", importedBy: "app" },
  { package: "zod", format: "cjs", importedBy: "legacy-plugin" },
  { package: "zod", format: "esm", importedBy: "app" },
  { package: "lodash", format: "cjs", importedBy: "app" },
])
// [{ package: "zod", importers: ["app", "legacy-plugin"] }]
```

and `dangerousHazards(that, ["zod", "react"])` → `["zod"]`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex6
```

## ex7 — the manifest mistakes that ship broken types

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Most packages with broken types are broken in one of
five ways, all of them visible in `package.json` without running anything.

```ts
export interface PackageJson {
  name: string;
  type?: "module" | "commonjs";
  main?: string;
  types?: string;
  exports?: unknown;
}

export function checkPackage(pkg: PackageJson): string[];
```

Return diagnostics, sorted ascending, with no duplicates. The five rules:

1. `exports: "types" must be the first key in <path>` — a conditions object
   containing a `"types"` key that is not its first key. `<path>` is the
   condition path from the root, joined with `/`, or `"."` at the top level.
2. `exports: no default condition in <path>` — a conditions object with at
   least one key and no `"default"` key.
3. `exports: "." is not exported` — the `exports` value is a subpath map (its
   first key starts with `"."`) and there is no `"."` key.
4. `exports: require condition resolves to ESM <target>` — a string target
   ending `.mjs` reached under a `"require"` condition; and the mirror,
   `exports: import condition resolves to CJS <target>` for a `.cjs` target
   under `"import"`.
5. `main "<main>" is not reachable through exports` — both `main` and `exports`
   are present and `main` does not appear as any string target anywhere in
   `exports`.

Anything that is not an object or a string inside `exports` is ignored rather
than crashing — a real manifest can contain anything.

Example:

```ts
checkPackage({
  name: "x",
  main: "./dist/i.cjs",
  exports: { ".": { import: "./dist/i.mjs", require: "./dist/i.cjs", types: "./dist/i.d.ts" } },
})
// [ 'exports: "types" must be the first key in .' ]
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex7
```

## ex8 — where do the types actually come from?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Four mechanisms compete to answer one question, and
they have a strict precedence.

```ts
export type ExportsField = string | null | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export interface TypesPackage {
  exports?: ExportsField;
  typesVersions?: Record<string, Record<string, string[]>>;
  types?: string;
  typings?: string;
}

export function resolveTypes(
  pkg: TypesPackage,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
  tsVersion: string,
): string | null;
```

Precedence, stopping at the first mechanism that is **present**:

1. **`exports`** — resolve it with `"types"` prepended to `conditions`. Reuse
   the `ex1` algorithm; copy it in. If `exports` is present and nothing
   resolves, the answer is `null` — you do not fall through to `types`.
2. **`typesVersions`** — its keys are version ranges, tried in declaration
   order; the first whose range matches `tsVersion` wins. Inside that block,
   keys are path patterns matched against the subpath **without** the leading
   `"./"`, with `"."` written as `"index"`. An exact key wins over a `*`
   pattern; the capture substitutes into the **first** entry of the target
   array. The result is returned with a `"./"` prefix.
3. **`types`**, then **`typings`** — used only for `subpath === "."`.
4. Otherwise `null`.

Version ranges are simple: `"*"` matches everything, `">=X.Y"` and `"<X.Y"`
compare major then minor numerically. `tsVersion` is `"X.Y"` or `"X.Y.Z"`.
Any other range string matches nothing.

Examples:

```ts
resolveTypes({ exports: { ".": { types: "./t.d.ts", default: "./i.js" } } }, ".", ["import"], "5.4")
// "./t.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=4.0": { "*": ["types/*.d.ts"] } } }, "./a", [], "5.4")
// "./types/a.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=9.0": { "*": ["new/*"] } }, types: "./i.d.ts" }, ".", [], "5.4")
// null - typesVersions is present, so types is not consulted
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex8
```

## challenge — resolve a graph, then find the hazard (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. One resolver, applied across a dependency graph,
reporting where two formats of the same package are in play.

```ts
export type ExportsField = string | null | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export interface Manifest {
  name: string;
  type?: "module" | "commonjs";
  exports?: ExportsField;
  imports?: Record<string, ExportsField>;
}

export type Format = "esm" | "cjs";

export interface Resolution {
  from: string;
  specifier: string;
  package: string;
  target: string;
  format: Format;
}

export interface Analysis {
  resolutions: Resolution[];
  hazards: string[];
  errors: string[];
}

export function analyse(
  packages: Readonly<Record<string, Manifest>>,
  edges: readonly { from: string; specifier: string }[],
): Analysis;
```

For each edge, `from` is a package name in `packages`. Its format is `"esm"`
when its `type` is `"module"` and `"cjs"` otherwise, and that decides the
conditions used: ESM importers ask for `["import", "node"]`, CJS importers for
`["require", "node"]`.

Resolution:

- a specifier starting `"#"` is looked up in the **importing** package's
  `imports`; a missing entry is the error code `ERR_PACKAGE_IMPORT_NOT_DEFINED`
- otherwise the specifier is a bare one: the package name is the first segment,
  or the first two when it starts with `"@"`, and the subpath is `"."` or
  `"./"` plus the rest
- an unknown package is `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`
- a package with no `exports` field is `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED`, and so
  is a subpath that resolves to `null`
- a specifier starting `"."` or `"/"` is `ERR_UNSUPPORTED`

The resolved `format` is the **target's** format, from `ex3`'s rules: the
target's extension, falling back to the *resolved package's* `type` field.

Output:

- `resolutions` in edge order
- `errors` as `<from> -> <specifier>: <CODE>`, in edge order
- `hazards`: names of packages that appear in `resolutions` with both formats,
  sorted ascending

Honest difficulty note: none of the pieces is new — `ex1` gives you the exports
resolver, `ex3` the format rule, `ex6` the hazard grouping. The work is the
bare-specifier split, which has to handle `"@scope/pkg/sub/path"` correctly,
and remembering that the format of a resolution comes from the **target file**
and the **target package's** manifest, not the importer's.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution challenge
```

## review1 — what kind of specifier is that?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Before any resolver can do anything, it has to
classify the string. Six kinds, and the order of the checks is the whole
exercise.

```ts
export type SpecifierKind =
  | "subpath-import"
  | "builtin"
  | "data-url"
  | "absolute"
  | "relative"
  | "bare";

export function classifySpecifier(specifier: string): SpecifierKind;

export function parseBare(
  specifier: string,
): { name: string; subpath: string } | null;
```

`classifySpecifier`, checked in this order:

- starts with `"#"` → `"subpath-import"`
- starts with `"node:"`, or is exactly one of `"fs"`, `"path"`, `"http"`,
  `"url"`, `"events"`, `"crypto"`, `"util"`, `"stream"` → `"builtin"`
- starts with `"data:"` → `"data-url"`
- starts with `"/"`, or with `"file:"`, or matches a Windows drive prefix such
  as `"C:\\"` or `"C:/"` → `"absolute"`
- starts with `"./"` or `"../"`, or is exactly `"."` or `".."` → `"relative"`
- anything else → `"bare"`

`parseBare` splits a bare specifier into a package name and a subpath, and
returns `null` when the name is not a valid npm package name. For this
exercise, valid means: not empty; no uppercase letters; does not start with
`"."` or `"_"`; a scoped name is `"@scope/name"` where both halves are
non-empty and follow the same rules. The subpath is `"."` when there is
nothing after the name, and `"./"` plus the rest otherwise.

Examples:

- `classifySpecifier("node:fs")` → `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs")` →
  `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs-extra")` → `"bare"`
- `classifySpecifier("C:/tmp/x.js")` → `"absolute"`
- `parseBare("@scope/pkg/sub/deep")` →
  `{ name: "@scope/pkg", subpath: "./sub/deep" }`
- `parseBare("Lodash")` → `null`; `parseBare("./x")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution review1
```

## Concepts, in the order you will need them

### The decision table you actually need

| you are writing | `type` | `module` | `moduleResolution` |
|---|---|---|---|
| an app that gets bundled | `module` | `esnext` | `bundler` |
| a Node app or CLI | `module` | `nodenext` | `nodenext` |
| a library, ESM only | `module` | `nodenext` | `nodenext` |
| a library, dual | `module` | `nodenext` | `nodenext`, plus a CJS build |

The one row worth arguing about is the last. Dual publishing doubles your build
matrix, doubles your test matrix, and creates the hazard in the first place.
Publish ESM-only if your consumers can take it, which in 2025 most can.

### The exports map, annotated

```jsonc
{
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",   // FIRST, always
      "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
      "require": "./dist/index.cjs",
      "default": "./dist/index.mjs"    // LAST, always
    },
    "./plugin/*": {
      "types": "./dist/plugin/*.d.ts",
      "default": "./dist/plugin/*.mjs"
    },
    "./package.json": "./package.json", // tooling asks for this
    "./internal/*": null                 // explicitly blocked
  }
}
```

Four things in that snippet are conventions rather than requirements, and all
four are load-bearing: `types` first, `default` last, exporting
`./package.json` because build tools read it, and blocking internals so you can
refactor them.

### Why `.d.ts` is not enough

A declaration file describes a module, and a module has a format. Under
`nodenext`, `import x from "pkg"` type-checks against the `.d.ts` reached
through the `"types"` condition of the `"import"` branch — which may be a
different file than the one `require` reaches. If a package ships one `.d.ts`
for both, one of the two is wrong: either `export =` is described as a default
export, or the named exports do not exist in CJS. This is the types half of the
dual-package hazard, and it is what `.d.mts` and `.d.cts` exist to fix.

## Worked example — reading a resolution failure

```
error TS2307: Cannot find module 'chalk' or its corresponding type declarations.
  There are types at './node_modules/chalk/dist/index.d.ts', but this result
  could not be resolved under your current 'moduleResolution' setting.
```

That second sentence is the whole diagnosis, and TypeScript added it precisely
because everybody misread the first. The types exist. Your `moduleResolution`
is `node10`, which ignores `exports`; the package exposes its types only
through an `exports` map. The fix is on your side — switch to `bundler` or
`nodenext` — and no amount of `paths` or `typeRoots` will do anything useful.

The mirror failure:

```
error TS1479: The current file is a CommonJS module whose imports will produce
  'require' calls; however, the referenced file is an ECMAScript module.
```

Here your file is CJS — because there is no `"type": "module"` in the nearest
`package.json` — and you imported an ESM-only package. The fix is to make your
file ESM, or to use a dynamic `import()`, which is allowed from CJS and returns
a promise.

## Common mistakes

**`types` after `import` in the exports map.** First match wins; TypeScript
asks for `types` first but the resolver takes the first key *it* matches, which
is `import`. Your package appears untyped.

**No `default` condition.** A consumer with an unusual condition set — a
runtime you have never heard of, a bundler with `--conditions` — resolves
nothing at all.

**`main` and `exports` pointing at different builds.** Old tooling gets one
copy, new tooling gets another, in the same program.

**Extensionless relative imports under `nodenext`.** They compile under
`bundler` and fail in Node. Libraries must be checked under `nodenext` for
exactly this reason.

**Assuming `import x from "cjs"` gives named exports.** Node's static analysis
of CJS is best-effort; a module whose exports are computed gives you a default
and nothing else.

**Mutating an imported namespace.** Works under transpiled interop, throws
against real ESM.

**Shipping `.d.ts` for both builds.** One of the two descriptions is wrong.

## The interview answer

"What is the dual-package hazard?" — a package that ships both an ESM and a CJS
build can end up loaded twice in one program, because one importer resolved the
`import` condition and another resolved `require`. Both resolutions are
correct. The result is two module instances: two copies of every class, so
`instanceof` fails; two module-level caches; two singletons. There is no error
message.

Then the fixes, in order of preference: publish ESM only; or make the package
stateless so two copies are harmless; or have the CJS build be a thin wrapper
that `import()`s the ESM one; or, at the application level, alias the package
so one build wins.

If they want more, the adjacent material is why `exports` conditions are
order-sensitive, why `types` must come first, and why `.d.mts`/`.d.cts` exist.

## Check yourself

1. What decides whether `index.js` is ESM or CJS, and what does a missing
   `type` field mean?
2. In an `exports` conditions object, why must `default` be last?
3. Why must `types` be first, and what does a user see when it is not?
4. What does a `null` target in an exports map mean, and what problem did it
   solve?
5. Under `nodenext`, why do you write `./util.js` when the file is `util.ts`?
6. Name three things `node10` resolution does that `nodenext` does not.
7. What does `__esModule` mean, and which interop scheme ignores it?
8. Why can two correct resolutions produce two copies of one library?
9. Give three symptoms of the dual-package hazard.
10. What is the three-line `package.json` trick for shipping a CJS build?
11. Why do `.d.mts` and `.d.cts` exist?
12. What is the `"#internal"` imports field for, and which package's manifest
    resolves it?
13. Which mechanisms provide types, and in what precedence order?
14. Why is `moduleResolution: "bundler"` wrong for a published library?
15. What does error TS1479 mean and what are the two fixes?

# Long read — how the ecosystem ended up with two of everything

## The fifteen-year overlap

CommonJS was not designed by a committee; it was designed by Node in 2009,
borrowing a proposal that was meant for a different problem. It is startlingly
simple: `require` is an ordinary function that reads a file, wraps it in a
function, runs it, and returns whatever the wrapper assigned to `module.exports`.
Everything about that is dynamic. You can `require` conditionally, in a loop,
from a variable, at any time. You can mutate another module's exports after the
fact. Circular dependencies work — badly, with partially-populated objects, but
they work.

ES modules were designed by a committee, for the web, with a different set of
requirements. Imports must be statically analysable so that a browser can fetch
the graph before evaluating anything. Bindings are live, so a `let` exported
from one module is observed changing by its importers. The graph is loaded
asynchronously, then linked, then evaluated in a defined order. Circularity is
handled by the linker rather than by luck.

Those two designs cannot be merged, and the ten years since have been about
making them coexist. Node's answer had three parts: a file's format is
determined out-of-band (extension or `type`); ESM can import CJS (with the
whole `module.exports` as the default); and CJS could not, for a long time,
require ESM at all, because a synchronous call cannot await an asynchronous
graph. Node 22 relaxed that last one for graphs without top-level await, using
a synchronous evaluation path — a genuinely significant change that will take
years to be safe to rely on.

## Why `exports` had to be invented

Before `exports`, a package's public API was "every file in it". `require("lodash/fp/curry")`
worked because the file existed. That is a terrible contract for a maintainer:
every internal file is a public API, every refactor is a breaking change, and
nobody can tell which is which.

`exports` closed that. When present, it is the *only* way into the package;
paths not listed are not reachable, and `null` says so explicitly. That single
change is the largest improvement to package encapsulation in the history of
npm, and it is why the field also acquired conditions — once you are declaring
entry points explicitly, declaring *different* entry points for different
environments costs nothing extra.

The condition mechanism is more general than people use it for. `node`,
`browser`, `import`, `require`, `default` are the well-known ones; `development`
and `production` are supported by bundlers; anything else can be passed with
`--conditions`, which is how you can ship a debug build that is only reachable
when someone asks for it. The rule that makes it all work — first matching key
in declaration order — is also the rule that makes it fragile, because JSON
object key order is invisible in a code review that only reads the keys.

## The types problem, which is worse

Runtime resolution has one answer per specifier. Type resolution has to produce
an answer that *matches* it — the declaration file that describes the file that
will actually load. Once a package can serve different files to `import` and
`require`, its types must be able to do the same, and a single `types` field at
the top of `package.json` cannot express that.

Hence the `"types"` condition, which must be first because conditions are
ordered. Hence `.d.mts` and `.d.cts`, because a declaration file has a format.
Hence `arethetypeswrong`, which exists because getting this right by hand is
genuinely difficult and the failures are silent — your users get `any`, or a
default import that does not exist at runtime, and they blame their own
configuration.

The failure that best illustrates the whole problem is "masquerading as CJS".
A package ships `dist/index.mjs` and `dist/index.d.ts`. The `.d.ts` has no
format marker, so under the nearest `package.json` with no `type` field it is
CommonJS. TypeScript therefore describes an ESM file with CJS semantics:
`export default` in the declaration means `module.exports.default`, and a
consumer's `import x from` binds the wrong thing. Everything compiles. Nothing
works. The fix is one extension change.

## Performance, briefly

Resolution is not free, and in a large monorepo it is measurable. Every
specifier is a series of filesystem probes — Node walks up directories looking
for `node_modules`, TypeScript tries a candidate list per specifier, and both
cache aggressively but must invalidate on file changes.

Two practical consequences. First, `node10` resolution is the slowest, because
its candidate list is longest — five extensions plus five index candidates per
specifier, versus one or four for `node16-esm`. Second, deep dependency trees
cost more than wide ones, because the directory walk is per level. Neither is
usually your bottleneck, but if `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` reports a large
"Program time" with modest "Check time", resolution and I/O are where it went.

## When not to care about any of this

If you are writing an application that is bundled and deployed as one artifact,
most of this sector is background. Set `"type": "module"`, use `bundler`
resolution, import whatever you like, and let the bundler flatten it. The
hazard can still bite you through your dependencies, but the fix is an alias in
one config file, and you will have exactly one build to check.

The material becomes essential the moment you publish. A package is consumed by
people whose configuration you do not control, on runtimes you have not tested,
through resolvers you have never read. The manifest is your entire contract
with them, and it is the one thing you cannot fix in a patch release without
someone's build breaking.

The other case where it matters is a monorepo, because a monorepo is a
publishing exercise with the registry removed. Workspace packages resolve
through the same `exports` field, get the same conditions, and produce the same
hazard when one package is built as ESM and another consumes it through a CJS
test runner. The next sector is about that world specifically — project
references, build order, and why the answer is usually "build the dependency
properly rather than reaching into its source".
