exercises.prompt:
## ex1 — the exports field is a resolver

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `"exports"` looks like configuration. It is an
algorithm, and this is it.

```ts
export type ExportsField =
  | string
  | null
  | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export function resolveExports(
  exports: ExportsField,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
): string | null;
```

`subpath` is `"."` or `"./something"`. Rules, in order:

- a **string** `exports` maps only `"."`; any other subpath gives `null`
- `null` anywhere means "explicitly blocked" and resolves to `null`
- an **object** whose first key starts with `"."` is a **subpath map**;
  otherwise it is a **conditions map** that applies to `"."` only
- in a subpath map: an exact key match wins; failing that, keys containing
  exactly one `*` are patterns, the pattern with the **longest prefix before
  the `*`** wins, and the captured text is substituted into the `*` in the
  target
- in a conditions map: keys are tried in **declaration order**, and the first
  key that appears in `conditions`, or is literally `"default"`, is taken —
  then resolution continues into its value
- if nothing matches at any level, the result is `null`

Examples:

```ts
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", require: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["import"])
// "./m.js"
resolveExports({ ".": { import: "./m.js", default: "./c.js" } }, ".", ["require"])
// "./c.js"
resolveExports({ "./*": "./src/*.js" }, "./util", [])            // "./src/util.js"
resolveExports({ "./a/*": "./x/*", "./*": "./y/*" }, "./a/b", []) // "./x/b"
resolveExports({ ".": "./i.js" }, "./other", [])                 // null
resolveExports({ "./private/*": null }, "./private/x", [])       // null
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two mutually recursive ideas, and separating them is most of the work: one
function picks a target for a subpath, and another resolves a value that may be
a string, a `null`, or a nested conditions object. The second is where the
recursion lives, because conditions nest arbitrarily deep.

## Hint 2

Telling a subpath map from a conditions map is one look at the first key:

```ts
const keys = Object.keys(exports);
const isSubpathMap = keys.length > 0 && keys[0]!.startsWith(".");
```

That is exactly what Node does, and it is why a map mixing `"."` and `"import"`
keys is an error in real life — there is no sensible answer, so the
specification forbids it rather than guessing.

## Hint 3

Pattern matching is a prefix and a suffix around the single `*`:

```ts
const star = key.indexOf("*");
const prefix = key.slice(0, star);
const suffix = key.slice(star + 1);
if (subpath.startsWith(prefix) && subpath.endsWith(suffix)) {
  const captured = subpath.slice(prefix.length, subpath.length - suffix.length);
}
```

Left to you: what happens when two patterns both match and have prefixes of the
same length. The prompt gives you a rule for the common case; decide what your
tie-break is and make it deterministic.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Declaration order for conditions is the rule people find surprising, and it is
worth sitting with. `{ "require": "./c.js", "import": "./m.js" }` and
`{ "import": "./m.js", "require": "./c.js" }` are the *same* map to a human and
different to the resolver — the first key that matches wins, so if a condition
you support appears early, the later ones are unreachable. It is why `"default"`
must be last: put it first and nothing after it is ever consulted.

## Hint 2

Conditions are a set the *resolver* brings, not the package. Node passes
`["node", "import"]` or `["node", "require"]` plus anything from
`--conditions`; a bundler passes `["browser", "import"]`; TypeScript passes
`["types", ...]`. The package declares what it has; the environment declares
what it wants. Getting that direction right is what makes the design make
sense.

## Hint 3

The blocking `null` is a real feature, not an edge case. `"./internal/*": null`
is how a package says "these files exist and are not yours", and it is the
mechanism that made `exports` a genuine encapsulation boundary — before it,
every file in a package was importable, and libraries could not refactor their
internals without breaking someone.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — three resolution modes, three answers

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. The same relative import resolves to different files
depending on `moduleResolution`, and knowing which is which is the difference
between a build that works and an hour of confusion.

```ts
export type Mode = "node10" | "node16-cjs" | "node16-esm";

export function resolveRelative(
  specifier: string,
  files: readonly string[],
  mode: Mode,
): string | null;
```

`files` is the set of paths that exist. `specifier` is a relative path already
joined against the importing directory — treat it as a plain string key.

- **node10** and **node16-cjs** (CommonJS resolution): try the specifier
  exactly; then with each of `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx` appended, in
  that order; then `<specifier>/index` with the same list, in the same order.
- **node16-esm**: no guessing at all. Try the specifier exactly. Then apply
  TypeScript's rewrite rule: a specifier ending `.js` may be satisfied by the
  same path with `.ts`, `.tsx` or `.d.ts`; one ending `.mjs` by `.mts` or
  `.d.mts`; one ending `.cjs` by `.cts` or `.d.cts`. Nothing else — no
  extension guessing, no directory index.

Return the first path that exists, or `null`.

Examples, with `files = ["./util.ts", "./thing/index.ts", "./data.json"]`:

- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node10")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./util", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`
- `resolveRelative("./util.js", files, "node16-esm")` → `"./util.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-cjs")` → `"./thing/index.ts"`
- `resolveRelative("./thing", files, "node16-esm")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build a list of candidate paths in priority order and then find the first that
exists. Every mode is the same three lines with a different candidate list,
which is a good sign you have understood the shape rather than the special
cases.

## Hint 2

For the ESM rewrite, strip the output extension and try the source ones:

```ts
const REWRITES: Record<string, string[]> = {
  ".js": [".ts", ".tsx", ".d.ts"],
  ".mjs": [".mts", ".d.mts"],
  ".cjs": [".cts", ".d.cts"],
};
```

Note the direction. You write `./util.js` in the source and TypeScript finds
`./util.ts` — the specifier names the *output* file, because that is what will
exist at runtime, and the compiler does not rewrite it on the way out.

## Hint 3

A `Set` for the file list makes the lookups honest, and it also makes the
ordering of your candidates the only thing that determines the answer — which
is exactly what you want to be reasoning about.

Left to you: whether `.json` should be in the CommonJS candidate list. Node
resolves it; TypeScript only does with `resolveJsonModule`. The prompt does not
include it — decide what you would do in a real tool and why.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The `.js`-means-`.ts` rule is the design decision people find hardest to
accept, and the reasoning is worth knowing. TypeScript decided very early that
it would not rewrite import specifiers during emit — what you write is what is
emitted. Under Node's ESM rules the emitted file must have an extension, and
the emitted file is `.js`. So the source must say `.js`, and the compiler looks
through it to the `.ts`. It is not TypeScript being awkward; it is the only
option that leaves the emit honest.

## Hint 2

`node10` is the resolution mode that made bundlers necessary and made
publishing hard. It guesses extensions, it walks up directories looking in
`node_modules`, it ignores `exports` entirely. Everything about it is
convenient and nothing about it matches what Node does today, which is why a
package whose types resolve under `node10` and nowhere else is a package that
appears to work until a user switches to `nodenext`.

## Hint 3

There is a fourth mode this exercise omits: `bundler`. It reads `exports` and
conditions like `node16` but permits extensionless relative imports, because
the bundler resolves them. It is the right choice for application code that
will be bundled and the wrong choice for a library, because the output will not
run in Node unaided.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## ex3 — which module system is this file?

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Every question in this sector eventually reduces to
this one, and the answer depends on two things that are not in the file.

```ts
export type Format = "esm" | "cjs";

export function formatOf(
  path: string,
  nearestPackageType: "module" | "commonjs" | undefined,
): Format;

export function declarationFor(path: string): string;
```

`formatOf`:

- `.mjs` and `.mts` are always ESM; `.cjs` and `.cts` are always CJS —
  the extension wins and the `package.json` is irrelevant
- `.js`, `.jsx`, `.ts` and `.tsx` take their format from `nearestPackageType`:
  `"module"` gives ESM, and both `"commonjs"` and `undefined` give CJS, because
  the absence of a `type` field means CommonJS
- `.json` is CJS
- anything else throws `Error("unknown extension: " + extension)`, where the
  extension includes the dot

`declarationFor` maps a source path to the declaration file the compiler emits
for it: `.ts` → `.d.ts`, `.mts` → `.d.mts`, `.cts` → `.d.cts`,
`.tsx` → `.d.ts`. Anything else throws
`Error("no declaration output for " + path)`.

Examples:

- `formatOf("src/a.mjs", "commonjs")` → `"esm"`
- `formatOf("src/a.js", undefined)` → `"cjs"`
- `formatOf("src/a.ts", "module")` → `"esm"`
- `declarationFor("src/a.mts")` → `"src/a.d.mts"`

Watch the `.d.ts` case in `formatOf`: it ends with `.ts`, and it must be
treated as `.ts` and not as some other extension. Pick your extension carefully.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"The extension" is ambiguous for `a.d.ts` and that ambiguity is the exercise.
Taking everything after the *last* dot gives `.ts`, which is the answer you
want here. Taking everything after the first dot gives `.d.ts`, which is what
you want in `declarationFor`. Two different questions, two different splits.

## Hint 2

A lookup table beats a chain of `if`s and documents itself:

```ts
const ALWAYS: Record<string, Format> = {
  ".mjs": "esm", ".mts": "esm", ".cjs": "cjs", ".cts": "cjs", ".json": "cjs",
};
const FROM_TYPE = new Set([".js", ".jsx", ".ts", ".tsx"]);
```

Then the whole function is two lookups and a throw.

## Hint 3

For `declarationFor`, the mapping is on the source extension and the output
keeps the middle `.d.`:

```ts
"src/a.mts" -> "src/a" + ".d.mts"
```

Left to you: what `declarationFor("src/a.d.ts")` should do. It is already a
declaration; the prompt's rules make it throw or produce nonsense depending on
how you slice. Decide, and make the behaviour deliberate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The rule that a missing `type` field means CommonJS is the compatibility
decision the whole ecosystem rests on. Every package published before 2019 has
no `type` field, and all of them must keep working. It also means "ESM by
default" can never happen without a breaking change to Node itself, which is
why `.mjs` exists and will not go away.

## Hint 2

"Nearest `package.json`" is doing quiet work in the parameter name. Node walks
up from the file until it finds one — not the project root's, not the nearest
`node_modules` boundary. This is why a `dist/cjs/package.json` containing only
`{ "type": "commonjs" }` is the standard trick for shipping a CJS build from a
package whose root says `"type": "module"`. Three lines of JSON in a build
directory, and it is the single most useful thing in this sector for people who
publish packages.

## Hint 3

The `.d.mts` and `.d.cts` extensions exist for exactly the same reason as
`.mjs` and `.cjs`: a declaration file has a format too. A `.d.ts` describing an
ESM module and a `.d.ts` describing a CJS module differ in what `export =` and
default imports mean, and before those extensions existed there was no way to
say which you had.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 — the codemod nodenext makes you write

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Switching a project to `nodenext` produces one error
per relative import in the codebase: *Relative import paths need explicit file
extensions*. Nobody fixes four hundred of those by hand.

```ts
export function addExtensions(
  source: string,
  from: ".ts" | ".mts" | ".cts",
): string;
```

Rewrite every **relative** specifier in a static `import` or `export`
statement to carry the extension the emitted file will have: `.ts` → `.js`,
`.mts` → `.mjs`, `.cts` → `.cjs`.

Rules:

- only specifiers starting `./` or `../` are touched; bare specifiers and
  `node:` builtins are left alone
- a specifier that already ends in `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.json` or `.node` is
  left alone
- all of these forms must be handled: `import x from "..."`,
  `import { a } from "..."`, `import type { A } from "..."`, `import "..."`,
  `export * from "..."`, `export { a } from "..."`
- both quote styles, and the original quote character is preserved
- everything else in the file is untouched, byte for byte

Example — with `from` of `".ts"`:

```ts
import { load } from "./loader"
import type { Cfg } from '../config/types'
import "./polyfill"
export * from "./api"
import fs from "node:fs"
import { x } from "./data.json"
```

becomes the same file with `"./loader.js"`, `'../config/types.js'`,
`"./polyfill.js"` and `"./api.js"`, while the `node:fs` and `./data.json` lines
are unchanged.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One regular expression with three capture groups — the keyword part, the quote,
and the specifier — plus a replace callback that decides whether to change
anything. Trying to parse the statement forms separately gives you six regexes
that overlap.

## Hint 2

The pattern that covers every listed form:

```ts
/(\bfrom\s*|\bimport\s*)(["'])((?:\.\.?\/)[^"']*)\2/g
```

`from` handles `import ... from` and `export ... from`; a bare `import`
followed directly by a string handles the side-effect form. The back-reference
`\2` is what forces the closing quote to match the opening one.

## Hint 3

The replace callback should return the original match unchanged when the
specifier already has an extension — that is how you get "untouched, byte for
byte" without any special casing:

```ts
source.replace(PATTERN, (match, lead, quote, spec) =>
  hasExtension(spec) ? match : `${lead}${quote}${spec}${output}${quote}`)
```

Left to you: what to do about `./styles.css`, which is a relative specifier
with an extension that is not in the skip list. There is a defensible answer
either way, and a real codemod has a flag for it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A regex codemod on source code is the wrong tool in general and the right tool
here, and knowing why is the point. It is right because the transformation is
local, syntactically unambiguous in the cases that matter, and reviewable in a
diff. It would be wrong for anything that needs scope information — renaming a
variable, say — where you need a real parser and the AST.

## Hint 2

The failure mode you are accepting: a string in your code that looks like an
import specifier. `const sql = "select * from './x'"` will not match this
pattern because of the `from\s*` plus quote structure, but a sufficiently
strange file could. The mitigation is not a cleverer regex — it is that you run
this once, read the diff, and the compiler checks the result.

## Hint 3

`import type { A } from "./x"` needs the extension too, which surprises people
who reason that the import disappears at emit. Under `verbatimModuleSyntax` it
does disappear — but the specifier is still resolved by the compiler, and the
resolution rules do not care that the binding is type-only.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — the interop dance

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `import x from "cjs-module"` has to mean something,
and what it means has changed twice. These are the rules every bundler and
every transpiler implements.

```ts
export function interopDefault(mod: unknown): unknown;
export function namedExports(mod: unknown): string[];
export function interopNamespace(mod: unknown): Record<string, unknown>;
```

`interopDefault(mod)` — what `import x from "..."` binds when the module was
CommonJS:

- if `mod` is an object with `__esModule === true`, the module was transpiled
  from ESM, so its real default is `mod.default` — return that, even when it is
  `undefined`
- otherwise the whole `module.exports` object *is* the default, so return `mod`
  unchanged, including when `mod` is a function, a string, or `null`

`namedExports(mod)` returns the own enumerable string keys of `mod`, excluding
`"default"` and `"__esModule"`, sorted ascending. A non-object gives `[]`.

`interopNamespace(mod)` builds what `import * as ns` should see: an object with
every named export, plus a `default` set to `interopDefault(mod)`, with
`__esModule` omitted. The result is frozen with `Object.freeze`, because a real
module namespace object is immutable.

Examples:

- `interopDefault({ __esModule: true, default: 42, extra: 1 })` → `42`
- `interopDefault({ a: 1, b: 2 })` → the same object
- `interopDefault(function f() {})` → the function
- `namedExports({ __esModule: true, default: 1, b: 2, a: 3 })` → `["a", "b"]`
- `interopNamespace({ a: 1 })` → a frozen `{ a: 1, default: { a: 1 } }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`__esModule` is a marker that transpilers add to the output of an ES module
compiled to CommonJS. Its presence means "this object is a fake namespace, the
real default is inside", and its absence means "this is a genuine CommonJS
module, the export object is the default". Two cases, and everything follows.

## Hint 2

Be careful with the non-object cases. `module.exports = function () {}` is
extremely common — the entire `express` API is a function — and
`typeof fn === "function"`, not `"object"`. Your check for the `__esModule`
marker has to tolerate a function, because a function can carry properties.

## Hint 3

For `namedExports`, `Object.keys` already gives own enumerable string keys, so
the work is filtering two names and sorting. Sorting matters for
determinism, and determinism matters because this output ends up in generated
code.

Left to you: what `interopNamespace(null)` should do. A namespace with only a
`default` of `null` is one defensible answer; throwing is another. The prompt
does not decide it for you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The historical detail that explains everything: TypeScript's original emit did
*not* do this. `import x from "cjs"` compiled to `const x = require("cjs")` and
then `x.default`, which was `undefined` for real CommonJS modules — hence the
famous `import * as express from "express"` workaround, which was wrong
according to the ESM specification but worked. `esModuleInterop` added the
runtime helper that makes the correct syntax work, and `allowSyntheticDefaultImports`
does the same thing for type checking only.

## Hint 2

Node's own interop is *not* this. When real ESM imports a real CommonJS module,
Node gives you `module.exports` as the default and — since it can now
statically analyse simple CJS files — a best-effort set of named exports. It
does not look at `__esModule` at all. So a package can behave one way under a
bundler and another under Node, which is a genuine source of "works in dev,
breaks in production".

## Hint 3

The freezing in `interopNamespace` is not decoration. A real module namespace
object is sealed, its properties are non-writable from outside, and
`ns.default = x` throws in strict mode. Code that mutates an imported namespace
works under a naive interop shim and fails against real ESM, and the frozen
object is what makes that failure show up in a test rather than in production.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Group by package name, and for each group collect two things: the set of
formats and the set of importers. A package is a hazard when its format set has
two members. `Map<string, { formats: Set<...>; importers: Set<string> }>` is
the whole data structure.

## Hint 2

Sets give you the deduplication for free, and `[...set].sort()` gives you the
determinism. Do not be tempted to sort as you insert; the sort at the end is
one line and cannot get out of step with the insertion path.

## Hint 3

`dangerousHazards` is a set intersection, and the argument order matters for
the output: the prompt asks for hazardous packages that are also stateful, so
iterate the hazards and filter by membership in `stateful`.

Left to you: whether a package appearing with the same format from two
different importers deserves any mention at all. It is not a hazard — but it is
worth knowing whether you would want the tool to say so.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason this is worth detecting rather than reasoning about is that nothing
in the system is wrong. Each import resolved correctly. Each copy is a valid
build of the library. The failure is emergent: `instanceof` compares prototype
identity, and two module instances have two prototypes. There is no line of
code to blame, which is why the only practical defence is a tool that looks at
the loaded graph.

## Hint 2

The `stateful` list is the judgement call that turns a report into a priority.
Two copies of a pure formatting library cost you bundle size and nothing else.
Two copies of a library with a global registry — a validation library whose
error classes you check, an ORM with a connection pool, anything with
`Symbol.for` — cost you an outage. The tool cannot know which is which; a
human maintains the list.

## Hint 3

The three standard fixes, in ascending order of effort: mark the package as
external and let one copy win via a bundler alias; publish only ESM, so there
is no second build to load; or make the package stateless so two copies do not
matter. The third is the only one that scales, and it is why the good advice
for library authors is to keep module-level state to zero.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 — the manifest mistakes that ship broken types

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Most packages with broken types are broken in one of
five ways, all of them visible in `package.json` without running anything.

```ts
export interface PackageJson {
  name: string;
  type?: "module" | "commonjs";
  main?: string;
  types?: string;
  exports?: unknown;
}

export function checkPackage(pkg: PackageJson): string[];
```

Return diagnostics, sorted ascending, with no duplicates. The five rules:

1. `exports: "types" must be the first key in <path>` — a conditions object
   containing a `"types"` key that is not its first key. `<path>` is the
   condition path from the root, joined with `/`, or `"."` at the top level.
2. `exports: no default condition in <path>` — a conditions object with at
   least one key and no `"default"` key.
3. `exports: "." is not exported` — the `exports` value is a subpath map (its
   first key starts with `"."`) and there is no `"."` key.
4. `exports: require condition resolves to ESM <target>` — a string target
   ending `.mjs` reached under a `"require"` condition; and the mirror,
   `exports: import condition resolves to CJS <target>` for a `.cjs` target
   under `"import"`.
5. `main "<main>" is not reachable through exports` — both `main` and `exports`
   are present and `main` does not appear as any string target anywhere in
   `exports`.

Anything that is not an object or a string inside `exports` is ignored rather
than crashing — a real manifest can contain anything.

Example:

```ts
checkPackage({
  name: "x",
  main: "./dist/i.cjs",
  exports: { ".": { import: "./dist/i.mjs", require: "./dist/i.cjs", types: "./dist/i.d.ts" } },
})
// [ 'exports: "types" must be the first key in .' ]
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One recursive walk collects everything. Carry two things down: the path so far,
and the set of conditions you are currently inside. Every rule is either a
check on an object as you enter it, or a check on a string when you reach one.

## Hint 2

The condition set is what makes rule 4 possible:

```ts
function walk(node: unknown, path: string, conditions: string[]): void {
  if (typeof node === "string") {
    if (conditions.includes("require") && node.endsWith(".mjs")) { /* ... */ }
    return;
  }
  // ...object: for each key, recurse with the key appended
}
```

Note that a target under `{ "node": { "require": "./x.mjs" } }` is still under
`require` — the set accumulates on the way down rather than being replaced.

## Hint 3

Rule 5 needs every string target anywhere in the tree, which the same walk can
collect into a set as it goes. Compare with `main` exactly as written: a real
tool would normalise `./dist/i.cjs` and `dist/i.cjs`, and deciding whether to
do that is a judgement about how forgiving you want to be.

Left to you: what counts as a "conditions object" versus a subpath map at
depths below the root. The prompt gives you the first-key rule; apply it
consistently and the recursion stays honest.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Rule 1 is the one that breaks the most real packages, and the reason is the
declaration-order rule from `ex1`. Conditions are tried in order and the first
match wins — so if `"import"` comes before `"types"`, TypeScript, which asks
for `["types", "import", ...]`, matches `"import"` first and gets the
JavaScript file. Your users see "could not find a declaration file", the
maintainer sees a `types` key sitting right there, and the fix is to move one
line.

## Hint 2

Rule 4 is what `arethetypeswrong` calls masquerading. A `require` condition
that hands back an ESM file means `require()` of that package throws
`ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` at runtime — or, worse, works in a bundler and fails in Node.
The mirror case, an `import` condition serving CJS, usually works but gives
your users the interop behaviour of `ex5` rather than real named exports.

## Hint 3

Rule 5 catches a subtler thing: two entry points that disagree. `main` is what
`node10` resolution and old bundlers use; `exports` is what everything modern
uses. If they point at different builds, half your users get one and half get
the other — and that is the dual-package hazard originating inside a single
package.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 — where do the types actually come from?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. Four mechanisms compete to answer one question, and
they have a strict precedence.

```ts
export type ExportsField = string | null | { [key: string]: ExportsField };

export interface TypesPackage {
  exports?: ExportsField;
  typesVersions?: Record<string, Record<string, string[]>>;
  types?: string;
  typings?: string;
}

export function resolveTypes(
  pkg: TypesPackage,
  subpath: string,
  conditions: readonly string[],
  tsVersion: string,
): string | null;
```

Precedence, stopping at the first mechanism that is **present**:

1. **`exports`** — resolve it with `"types"` prepended to `conditions`. Reuse
   the `ex1` algorithm; copy it in. If `exports` is present and nothing
   resolves, the answer is `null` — you do not fall through to `types`.
2. **`typesVersions`** — its keys are version ranges, tried in declaration
   order; the first whose range matches `tsVersion` wins. Inside that block,
   keys are path patterns matched against the subpath **without** the leading
   `"./"`, with `"."` written as `"index"`. An exact key wins over a `*`
   pattern; the capture substitutes into the **first** entry of the target
   array. The result is returned with a `"./"` prefix.
3. **`types`**, then **`typings`** — used only for `subpath === "."`.
4. Otherwise `null`.

Version ranges are simple: `"*"` matches everything, `">=X.Y"` and `"<X.Y"`
compare major then minor numerically. `tsVersion` is `"X.Y"` or `"X.Y.Z"`.
Any other range string matches nothing.

Examples:

```ts
resolveTypes({ exports: { ".": { types: "./t.d.ts", default: "./i.js" } } }, ".", ["import"], "5.4")
// "./t.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=4.0": { "*": ["types/*.d.ts"] } } }, "./a", [], "5.4")
// "./types/a.d.ts"
resolveTypes({ typesVersions: { ">=9.0": { "*": ["new/*"] } }, types: "./i.d.ts" }, ".", [], "5.4")
// null - typesVersions is present, so types is not consulted
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Present, not successful" is the rule that makes this exercise. Each mechanism
either handles the question or ends it. Writing it as a chain of `??` gives you
fall-through, which is wrong, and produces a resolver far more forgiving than
the real one.

## Hint 2

The range check is small enough to write inline:

```ts
const parse = (v: string) => { const [ma = "0", mi = "0"] = v.split("."); return [Number(ma), Number(mi)] as const };
const compare = (a: readonly [number, number], b: readonly [number, number]) =>
  a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1];
```

Then `">=4.0"` is `compare(version, parse("4.0")) >= 0`, and anything not
starting `>=` or `<` or equal to `*` matches nothing.

## Hint 3

The `typesVersions` subpath convention is genuinely odd and worth reading
twice: `"."` is written as `"index"` and other subpaths drop the `"./"`. So
`"./a"` matches the pattern `"*"` with a capture of `"a"`, and `"."` matches it
with a capture of `"index"`.

Left to you: what happens when the target array has more than one entry. The
real algorithm tries each in turn against the filesystem; you have no
filesystem, so the prompt says take the first — but know that the array is
there for a reason.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`typesVersions` exists to solve one problem: a package that wants to ship
different declaration files to different TypeScript versions, because a type
feature it uses does not exist in older compilers. It predates `exports` and is
largely superseded by it — but `@types` packages and anything supporting a wide
compiler range still use it, so a resolver has to know it.

## Hint 2

The precedence order is the part to memorise, because it explains almost every
"my types are not found" report. If `exports` exists, it is the only mechanism
that matters, and a missing `"types"` condition means no types at all — no
matter how correct the top-level `types` field looks. That surprises people
every time, and it is exactly rule 1 of the previous exercise seen from the
other side.

## Hint 3

Note what is *not* in this list: `@types/<name>` from DefinitelyTyped, which
the compiler consults when a package provides no types of its own, and the
`typeRoots` setting that controls where it looks. Those are a fallback outside
the package, and they are why a package with a broken `exports` map can still
appear to work for users who happen to have an old `@types` package installed.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the specifier parser first and test it in your head on four inputs:
`"lodash"`, `"lodash/fp"`, `"@scope/pkg"`, `"@scope/pkg/sub/deep"`. The scoped
case is the only interesting one, and the rule is that a leading `"@"` means
the name is two segments rather than one.

## Hint 2

```ts
function splitBare(specifier: string): { name: string; subpath: string } {
  const parts = specifier.split("/");
  const take = specifier.startsWith("@") ? 2 : 1;
  const name = parts.slice(0, take).join("/");
  const rest = parts.slice(take).join("/");
  return { name, subpath: rest === "" ? "." : `./${rest}` };
}
```

Note that this happily produces a name of `"@scope"` for a malformed
specifier. Real resolvers reject that; decide whether yours needs to.

## Hint 3

Format of the target is two lookups: the extension table from `ex3`, and, if
the extension is a neutral one, the *resolved* package's `type`. The bug to
avoid is using the importer's `type` — which is easy to do by accident,
because the importer's manifest is the one already in your hand.

Left to you: whether a resolution error should also suppress the edge from the
hazard analysis. It must — an edge that did not resolve loaded nothing — but
check that your code actually does it rather than assuming.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason this analysis works on a graph rather than a package is that the
hazard is a property of the *graph*. A perfectly correct package with both an
ESM and a CJS build is not broken; it becomes a problem only when two different
importers in one program reach for different conditions. That is why no
package-level checker can find it and why this exercise takes edges.

## Hint 2

`imports` — the `"#internal"` mechanism — is the least known part of the
specification and worth a moment. It is a private, package-scoped alias map
with the same conditions machinery as `exports`, and its main use is
substituting a browser implementation for a Node one without a bundler alias.
Because it is resolved against the *importing* package, two packages can use
the same `#db` specifier and get different files, which is exactly right.

## Hint 3

Think about what the output is for. A list of resolutions is a debugging aid; a
list of hazards is a decision. The most useful real version of this tool prints
the importer chain for each side of a hazard, because "zod is loaded twice" is
not actionable and "zod is ESM from your app and CJS from legacy-plugin" tells
you which dependency to pin, alias, or replace.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## review1 — what kind of specifier is that?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Before any resolver can do anything, it has to
classify the string. Six kinds, and the order of the checks is the whole
exercise.

```ts
export type SpecifierKind =
  | "subpath-import"
  | "builtin"
  | "data-url"
  | "absolute"
  | "relative"
  | "bare";

export function classifySpecifier(specifier: string): SpecifierKind;

export function parseBare(
  specifier: string,
): { name: string; subpath: string } | null;
```

`classifySpecifier`, checked in this order:

- starts with `"#"` → `"subpath-import"`
- starts with `"node:"`, or is exactly one of `"fs"`, `"path"`, `"http"`,
  `"url"`, `"events"`, `"crypto"`, `"util"`, `"stream"` → `"builtin"`
- starts with `"data:"` → `"data-url"`
- starts with `"/"`, or with `"file:"`, or matches a Windows drive prefix such
  as `"C:\\"` or `"C:/"` → `"absolute"`
- starts with `"./"` or `"../"`, or is exactly `"."` or `".."` → `"relative"`
- anything else → `"bare"`

`parseBare` splits a bare specifier into a package name and a subpath, and
returns `null` when the name is not a valid npm package name. For this
exercise, valid means: not empty; no uppercase letters; does not start with
`"."` or `"_"`; a scoped name is `"@scope/name"` where both halves are
non-empty and follow the same rules. The subpath is `"."` when there is
nothing after the name, and `"./"` plus the rest otherwise.

Examples:

- `classifySpecifier("node:fs")` → `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs")` →
  `"builtin"`; `classifySpecifier("fs-extra")` → `"bare"`
- `classifySpecifier("C:/tmp/x.js")` → `"absolute"`
- `parseBare("@scope/pkg/sub/deep")` →
  `{ name: "@scope/pkg", subpath: "./sub/deep" }`
- `parseBare("Lodash")` → `null`; `parseBare("./x")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc04_esm_cjs_resolution review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The order in the prompt is not arbitrary, and one case proves it: `"fs"` is a
builtin and also looks exactly like a bare specifier. Check builtins before
bare, or every Node builtin becomes a package lookup.

## Hint 2

The Windows drive test is a small regular expression and it is worth writing
rather than guessing: `/^[A-Za-z]:[\\/]/`. Both separators appear in the wild,
and a single letter is the only valid drive form.

## Hint 3

For `parseBare`, validate the *name*, not the whole specifier, and validate
each half of a scoped name with the same predicate. Writing one
`isValidSegment` helper and calling it once or twice is shorter and more
obviously correct than one large regex.

Left to you: whether `"."` alone should classify as relative or as bare. The
prompt tells you; make sure your `startsWith("./")` check does not silently
disagree with it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The uppercase rule is real npm history: package names were once
case-insensitive and are now lowercase-only, with old names grandfathered in.
A resolver that accepts `"Lodash"` will find nothing on a case-sensitive
filesystem and everything on macOS, which is the classic "works on my machine"
generator.

## Hint 2

The `"node:"` prefix is worth understanding rather than memorising. It was
added so that a builtin can be named unambiguously — without it, a package
called `fs` on npm would shadow the builtin, and `node:fs` cannot be shadowed
by anything. It is also the only way to import some newer builtins, such as
`node:test`, at all.

## Hint 3

This function is the entry point of every module resolver ever written, and the
six-way split is the same everywhere: Node's, esbuild's, Vite's, TypeScript's.
If you can write it from memory and explain why each branch precedes the next,
you can read any of their resolvers, because they all start here.

lessons.title: V3·TC5 — Project references, monorepos and build speed
lessons.summary: A monorepo is a build-graph problem wearing a directory structure. This sector builds the machinery tsc --build actually runs: topological order with cycle reporting, reverse reachability for "what does this change affect", the up-to-date check against .tsbuildinfo, composite configuration rules, path mapping, critical paths, a parallel scheduler, and the source-versus-declaration redirect that makes editors fast.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TC5 — Project references, monorepos and build speed

At some size a single `tsconfig.json` stops working. Not because the compiler
refuses — it will happily check four hundred thousand lines — but because every
edit costs a full check of everything, the editor takes eleven seconds to
respond, and there is no way to say "the API package may not import from the
web app". One program, one graph, no boundaries, no incrementality.

Project references are TypeScript's answer, and they are best understood as
turning your repository into a build graph. Each project is a `tsconfig.json`
with `composite: true`, which means it emits declaration files and a
`.tsbuildinfo` manifest. A project that depends on another lists it in
`references`. `tsc --build` then does what `make` does: work out the order,
work out what is stale, and rebuild only that.

Three things fall out of that design, and all three are the reason to bother.

**Incrementality.** A project whose inputs have not changed and whose
references have not been rebuilt is skipped entirely — not re-checked, skipped.
On a repository of thirty packages, a change to a leaf touches one project; a
change to the shared types package touches everything downstream and nothing
upstream. That difference is the whole game, and the up-to-date check that
decides it is `ex3`.

**Boundaries.** A project can only see what it references. That is a real
architectural constraint enforced by the compiler rather than by a lint rule
people disable, and it is often worth adopting for that reason alone. It also
means the reference list must actually match the import graph, which is what
`ex4` checks — a missing reference is a build that fails mysteriously, and an
unused one is a false dependency that serialises your build for no reason.

**Parallelism.** Once the work is a graph, independent projects can build at
the same time. But only up to a point: the critical path through the graph is a
hard floor on wall-clock time no matter how many cores you have. `ex6` computes
that floor and `ex7` schedules against it, and together they explain why adding
workers stops helping — and why the cheapest build speedup is usually to break
a long chain rather than to buy a bigger machine.

There is a fourth thing, and it is the one that makes references usable day to
day: **the source redirect**. Naively, a project that references another sees
its `.d.ts` files — so nothing works until you build. TypeScript's language
service instead redirects to the *source* files of referenced projects, so
go-to-definition lands in real code and edits are visible immediately, with no
build. That behaviour is on by default and switched off by
`disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect`, and knowing it exists explains most
of the difference between how references behave in your editor and in CI.
`ex8` is that decision, written out.

The exercises are models, not wrappers. `buildOrder` is the topological sort
`tsc --build` runs; `statusOf` is its up-to-date check; `planBuild` in the
challenge puts both together with a scheduler and produces the plan the real
tool prints with `--dry`. Building the model is the fastest way to understand
what the tool is doing, and — the honest reason — the fastest way to work out
why your build did something unexpected at half past six on a Friday.

One note on scope. This sector is about the graph, not about your package
manager. Workspaces, hoisting, `pnpm` symlinks and lockfiles are a real and
adjacent problem, and they interact with the previous sector's resolution
rules. Here, projects are nodes and references are edges, and everything takes
its data as arguments.

## ex1 — build order, and the cycle that stops it

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The first thing `tsc --build` does with your graph.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export type BuildOrder =
  | { ok: true; order: string[] }
  | { ok: false; cycle: string[] };

export function buildOrder(projects: readonly Project[]): BuildOrder;
```

Rules:

- dependencies come before the projects that reference them
- ties are broken by path, ascending, so the output is deterministic across
  machines
- a reference to a project that is not in the list throws
  `Error('unknown reference: <ref> from <path>')`
- a cycle returns `{ ok: false, cycle }`, where `cycle` starts and ends with the
  same project and lists the path between them, taking the
  alphabetically-first entry point into the cycle

Examples:

```ts
buildOrder([
  { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
  { path: "core", references: [] },
])
// { ok: true, order: ["core", "ui", "app"] }

buildOrder([
  { path: "a", references: ["b"] },
  { path: "b", references: ["a"] },
])
// { ok: false, cycle: ["a", "b", "a"] }
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex1
```

## ex2 — what does this change touch?

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Build order answers "in what sequence". This answers
the question CI actually asks: given these changed files, what has to be
rebuilt and retested?

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export function affected(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  changed: readonly string[],
): string[];
```

Rules:

- the result includes every changed project that exists in the graph, plus
  every project that depends on one of them, directly or transitively
- dependencies are *not* affected: changing `app` does not affect `core`
- a changed path that is not a project in the list is ignored
- the result is sorted ascending, with no duplicates
- cycles in the graph must not cause an infinite loop

Example:

```ts
const graph = [
  { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
  { path: "core", references: [] },
  { path: "tools", references: [] },
]

affected(graph, ["core"])          // ["app", "core", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["ui"])            // ["app", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["app"])           // ["app"]
affected(graph, ["nonexistent"])   // []
affected(graph, [])                // []
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex2
```

## ex3 — the up-to-date check

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. This is the function that makes `tsc --build` fast, and
knowing its exact order is how you diagnose a build that rebuilds everything
every time.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface BuildInfo {
  outputs: readonly string[];
  builtAt: number;
}

export interface Snapshot {
  fileTimes: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  buildInfos: Readonly<Record<string, BuildInfo>>;
}

export type Status =
  | "missing-buildinfo"
  | "missing-output"
  | "stale-input"
  | "stale-reference"
  | "up-to-date";

export function statusOf(
  project: Project,
  inputs: readonly string[],
  snapshot: Snapshot,
): Status;
```

Checks, in **this order**, returning the first that applies:

1. no `BuildInfo` for this project → `"missing-buildinfo"`
2. any output listed in the build info absent from `fileTimes` →
   `"missing-output"`
3. any input's time **greater than** `builtAt` → `"stale-input"`. An input
   absent from `fileTimes` also counts as stale — it was deleted, and the
   output no longer corresponds to reality.
4. any referenced project with no build info, or with a `builtAt` **greater
   than** this project's → `"stale-reference"`
5. otherwise → `"up-to-date"`

Note the strict comparisons. A file written in the same millisecond as the
build is *not* stale, which is deliberate — the alternative rebuilds forever on
filesystems with coarse timestamps.

Examples, with `snapshot.fileTimes = { "a.ts": 10, "out/a.js": 20 }` and
`buildInfos = { app: { outputs: ["out/a.js"], builtAt: 20 } }`:

- `statusOf({ path: "app", references: [] }, ["a.ts"], snapshot)` → `"up-to-date"`
- with `a.ts` at time `30` → `"stale-input"`
- with an extra output `"out/b.js"` that is not in `fileTimes` →
  `"missing-output"`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex3
```

## ex4 — the configuration rules references impose

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Project references only work if several unrelated
settings agree, and the compiler's error messages for each are individually
clear and collectively confusing.

```ts
export interface ProjectConfig {
  path: string;
  composite?: boolean;
  rootDir?: string;
  outDir?: string;
  files: readonly string[];
  references: readonly string[];
  imports: readonly string[];   // project paths this one actually imports from
}

export function validateProjects(projects: readonly ProjectConfig[]): string[];
```

Return diagnostics, sorted ascending, no duplicates:

- `<path>: referenced project <other> must set composite: true` — for each
  reference whose target does not have `composite: true`
- `<path>: missing reference to <other>` — it imports from a project it does
  not reference
- `<path>: unused reference to <other>` — it references a project it never
  imports from
- `<path>: outDir is required on a composite project` — `composite` is true and
  `outDir` is absent
- `<path>: file "<file>" is outside rootDir "<root>"` — `rootDir` is set and a
  file does not start with it

A reference or import naming a project that is not in the list is ignored by
the first three rules — a missing project is a different problem, and reporting
it five times is not helpful.

Example:

```ts
validateProjects([
  { path: "app", composite: true, outDir: "app/dist", files: [],
    references: ["core"], imports: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "core", outDir: "core/dist", files: [], references: [], imports: [] },
  { path: "ui", composite: true, outDir: "ui/dist", files: [], references: [], imports: [] },
])
// [
//   "app: missing reference to ui",
//   "app: referenced project core must set composite: true",
// ]
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex4
```

## ex5 — path mapping, exactly

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `paths` is the setting everyone uses and nobody reads
the rules for, which is why "why is it resolving to the wrong file" is a weekly
question in every monorepo.

```ts
export function resolvePaths(
  specifier: string,
  paths: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>,
  baseUrl: string,
  exists: (path: string) => boolean,
): string | null;
```

The algorithm:

1. An **exact** key — one with no `*` — that equals the specifier wins outright,
   ahead of every pattern.
2. Otherwise, among keys containing exactly one `*`, the one with the **longest
   prefix before the `*`** wins. Only that key's substitutions are tried; there
   is no falling through to a shorter match.
3. For the winning key, each substitution in its array is tried **in order**.
   The `*` in the substitution is replaced by the text the specifier's `*`
   captured; an exact key's substitutions are used as they are.
4. Each candidate is joined onto `baseUrl` — `baseUrl`, a `/`, then the
   candidate — unless `baseUrl` is `""`, in which case the candidate is used as
   it is. A trailing slash on `baseUrl` is not doubled.
5. The first candidate for which `exists` returns true is the answer. If none
   exists, or nothing matched, the answer is `null`.

Examples, with `baseUrl` of `"."` and every candidate existing:

```ts
resolvePaths("@app/core", { "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"] }, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/index.ts"

resolvePaths("@app/core/util", {
  "@app/core/*": ["packages/core/src/*.ts"],
  "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"],
}, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/util.ts"   - longer prefix wins
```

and with an `exists` that only accepts the second entry:

```ts
resolvePaths("x", { x: ["a.ts", "b.ts"] }, "", exists)   // "b.ts"
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex5
```

## ex6 — the floor no number of cores can beat

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Before you buy a bigger CI machine, find out whether
parallelism can help at all.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface CriticalPath {
  length: number;
  path: string[];
}

export function criticalPath(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  durations: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
): CriticalPath;
```

The critical path is the longest chain of dependencies, weighted by build
duration. Its total is the minimum possible wall-clock time for the whole build
with unlimited workers.

Rules:

- `path` runs from the deepest dependency to the final project, in build order
- a missing duration is `0`
- ties are broken by taking the lexicographically smaller `path` array,
  compared element by element
- a graph with a cycle throws `Error("cycle detected")`
- an empty graph gives `{ length: 0, path: [] }`

Example:

```ts
criticalPath(
  [
    { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
    { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
    { path: "core", references: [] },
    { path: "tools", references: [] },
  ],
  { app: 5, ui: 3, core: 10, tools: 100 },
)
// { length: 18, path: ["core", "ui", "app"] }
```

Note what that example shows: `tools` takes a hundred seconds and is not on the
critical path, because nothing waits for it. With two workers this build takes
a hundred seconds; with unlimited workers it takes eighteen; and no amount of
hardware gets it below eighteen.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex6
```

## ex7 — scheduling the graph across workers

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Now put a real number of workers on it and find out
what the build actually costs.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface Assignment {
  project: string;
  worker: number;
  start: number;
  end: number;
}

export interface Schedule {
  makespan: number;
  assignments: Assignment[];
}

export function planParallelBuild(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  durations: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
  workers: number,
): Schedule;
```

The simulation, which is ordinary list scheduling:

- time starts at `0`
- at each step, a project is **ready** when it has not started and every
  reference it names has finished at or before the current time
- ready projects are started in ascending path order, on the free worker with
  the lowest index, until either no worker is free or nothing is ready
- when nothing more can start, time advances to the earliest `end` among
  running projects
- a missing duration is `0` — such a project still occupies a worker, starting
  and ending at the same instant
- `assignments` is sorted by `start` ascending, then by `worker` ascending
- `makespan` is the largest `end`, or `0` for an empty graph
- `workers` below `1` throws `RangeError("workers must be at least 1")`
- a reference to an unknown project is ignored

Example — the graph from `ex6` with `{ app: 5, ui: 3, core: 10, tools: 100 }`
and two workers: `core` and `tools` start at `0` on workers `0` and `1`; `ui`
starts at `10` on worker `0`; `app` starts at `13`; makespan is `100`, because
`tools` is still running.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex7
```

## ex8 — source or declaration?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. When project `app` reads a type from project `core`,
which file does the compiler actually read? The answer is different in your
editor and in CI, and this is the setting that decides it.

```ts
export interface RefProject {
  rootDir: string;
  outDir: string;
  sources: readonly string[];
  declarationMap: boolean;
  built: boolean;
}

export interface Resolved {
  file: string;
  kind: "source" | "declaration";
  goToDefinition: string;
}

export function outputFor(project: RefProject, source: string): string | null;

export function sourceOfTruth(
  project: RefProject,
  source: string,
  options: { redirect: boolean },
): Resolved | null;
```

`outputFor` computes the declaration file a source emits: strip `rootDir` from
the front, prepend `outDir`, and change the extension — `.ts` and `.tsx` become
`.d.ts`, `.mts` becomes `.d.mts`, `.cts` becomes `.d.cts`. Returns `null` if
the source is not in `sources`, is not under `rootDir`, or has any other
extension.

`sourceOfTruth`:

- `redirect: true` — the default, and what the editor does: the compiler reads
  the **source** file. `kind` is `"source"`, `file` and `goToDefinition` are
  both the source path, and it works whether or not the project has been built.
- `redirect: false` — what `disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect` gives you:
  the compiler reads the emitted declaration. If the project is not `built`,
  return `null`. Otherwise `kind` is `"declaration"`, `file` is the `.d.ts`
  path, and `goToDefinition` is the **source** when `declarationMap` is true and
  the `.d.ts` otherwise.
- a source `outputFor` cannot map returns `null` in every case.

Example:

```ts
const core = {
  rootDir: "packages/core/src",
  outDir: "packages/core/dist",
  sources: ["packages/core/src/money.ts"],
  declarationMap: true,
  built: true,
}

outputFor(core, "packages/core/src/money.ts")   // "packages/core/dist/money.d.ts"
sourceOfTruth(core, "packages/core/src/money.ts", { redirect: false })
// { file: "packages/core/dist/money.d.ts", kind: "declaration",
//   goToDefinition: "packages/core/src/money.ts" }
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex8
```

## challenge — tsc --build --dry (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Order, staleness, propagation and scheduling, in
one function that prints what the build is about to do.

```ts
export interface BuildProject {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
  inputs: readonly string[];
  outputs: readonly string[];
  duration: number;
}

export interface World {
  fileTimes: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  builtAt: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}

export interface BuildPlan {
  order: string[];
  rebuilt: string[];
  skipped: string[];
  makespan: number;
  lines: string[];
}

export function planBuild(
  projects: readonly BuildProject[],
  world: World,
  workers: number,
): BuildPlan;
```

Walk the projects in topological order — dependencies first, ties by path
ascending — and decide each one:

A project **rebuilds** when any of these holds:

- it has no entry in `world.builtAt`
- one of its `outputs` is missing from `world.fileTimes`
- one of its `inputs` is missing from `world.fileTimes`, or has a time greater
  than its `builtAt`
- any project it references is itself being rebuilt — this is the propagation,
  and it is why the order matters
- any project it references has a `builtAt` greater than its own

Otherwise it is **skipped**.

Then schedule the rebuilt projects across `workers` with the list-scheduling
rule from `ex7`: ready in ascending path order, lowest free worker, clock
advances to the next completion. References to skipped projects impose no wait.

Output:

- `order` is the full topological order
- `rebuilt` and `skipped` are in that same order
- `lines` is `BUILD <path>` or `SKIP <path>` for each project in order,
  followed by one final `MAKESPAN <n>`
- a cycle throws `Error("cycle detected: " + cycle.join(" -> "))` with the cycle
  in the `ex1` format
- `workers` below `1` throws `RangeError("workers must be at least 1")`

Honest difficulty note: every piece exists in an earlier exercise. The two
things that catch people are the **propagation** — a project rebuilds because
its reference is being rebuilt in this same run, not because of any timestamp —
and the fact that the scheduler must only consider dependencies among the
rebuilt set, because a skipped project is already finished at time zero.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references challenge
```

## review1 — why did it rebuild?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. The same rules from the other side: not "what will
happen" but "what just happened, and why".

```ts
export type Cause =
  | "no-buildinfo"
  | "output-missing"
  | "config-changed"
  | "input-changed"
  | "reference-newer"
  | "none";

export interface Evidence {
  hasBuildInfo: boolean;
  missingOutputs: readonly string[];
  newestInput: number;
  builtAt: number;
  newestReference: number;
  configChangedAt: number;
}

export function diagnose(evidence: Evidence): { cause: Cause; explanation: string };
```

Precedence, first match wins, with the exact explanation for each:

1. `hasBuildInfo` is false → `"no-buildinfo"`, explained as
   `no .tsbuildinfo: this project has never been built here`
2. `missingOutputs` is non-empty → `"output-missing"`, explained as
   `output missing: <first entry after sorting ascending>`
3. `configChangedAt > builtAt` → `"config-changed"`, explained as
   `tsconfig changed at <configChangedAt>, after the last build at <builtAt>`
4. `newestInput > builtAt` → `"input-changed"`, explained as
   `input newer than build: <newestInput> > <builtAt>`
5. `newestReference > builtAt` → `"reference-newer"`, explained as
   `a referenced project was rebuilt at <newestReference>`
6. otherwise → `"none"`, explained as `up to date`

Example:

```ts
diagnose({
  hasBuildInfo: true,
  missingOutputs: [],
  newestInput: 40,
  builtAt: 20,
  newestReference: 50,
  configChangedAt: 5,
})
// { cause: "input-changed", explanation: "input newer than build: 40 > 20" }
```

Note that both the input and the reference are newer in that example, and the
answer names only the first. A diagnosis reports the reason it found, in the
order the build checks them — which is exactly the order that lets someone act
on it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references review1
```

# Reading - typescript/v3tc05_project_references

A monorepo is a build graph. Project references are how TypeScript is told
about it, and every behaviour that surprises you follows from the graph. These
are the notes.

## Notes

**`composite: true` is a package of settings, not a flag.** It forces
`declaration: true`, because dependents read `.d.ts` files. It turns on
`incremental`, so a `.tsbuildinfo` is written. It requires the input file set
to be knowable without scanning, which is why `files` or `include` becomes
mandatory. And it makes `rootDir` meaningful, because the output layout must be
predictable for the redirect to work.

**`tsc --build` is `make`.** Topological order, up-to-date check, rebuild what
is stale, propagate. Every question about its behaviour is answerable from
those four steps, and every one of them is an exercise in this sector. The
practical consequence is that `tsc -p` and `tsc --build` are different programs
with different jobs: the first checks one project, the second orchestrates
many.

**Staleness propagates through the graph, not through time.** A project
rebuilds because a project it references was rebuilt in the same run, or
because that project's build info is newer. This is why a change to a shared
types package rebuilds almost everything and a change to a leaf app rebuilds
one project. Real `tsc` softens this by comparing the emitted `.d.ts` with the
previous one: identical output does not propagate, which is why a body-only
change is cheap and a signature change is not.

**The critical path bounds the build.** No number of workers gets you below the
longest weighted dependency chain. If your makespan is near the critical path,
buy nothing and restructure; if it is far above, add workers. Computing both —
`ex6` and `ex7` — turns "the build is slow" into a decision.

**References must match imports, in both directions.** A missing reference
gives you a build that fails in CI and works in the editor, because the editor
resolved the source and the build had not emitted the declaration yet. An
unused reference gives you a false edge that serialises two projects and can
drag a whole subtree onto the critical path.

**The source redirect explains the editor.** By default, the language service
reads the *sources* of referenced projects rather than their declarations, so
you see edits immediately and go-to-definition lands in real code with no
build. `disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect` turns that off, which is
sometimes right for CI and almost never right for an editor.

**`paths` is not a module system.** It affects type resolution and nothing
else; the emitted JavaScript keeps the specifier verbatim, and something at
runtime has to make it resolve. In a repository with real workspace packages
and `exports` fields, `paths` is usually a second mechanism to keep in sync
with the first.

## ex1 to ex3 — the core loop

Three functions and you have the essential behaviour of `--build`. The
colour-marking depth-first search is worth having in your fingers, because the
cycle report is what makes the error usable and Kahn's algorithm cannot produce
it. `affected` is the reverse-reachability closure that every monorepo tool
implements. `statusOf` is the up-to-date check, and its ordering — build info,
outputs, inputs, references — is the order you should recite when diagnosing a
build that rebuilds too much.

The strict `>` in the timestamp comparisons is a real bug class. With `>=`, a
file written in the same clock tick as the build info looks permanently newer,
and the project rebuilds every time. On a filesystem with one-second timestamp
resolution that is not a corner case.

## ex4 to ex5 — configuration

The five rules in `ex4` map onto five compiler errors that arrive separately
and confusingly. Checking them together, in one place, is the sort of small
tool that pays for itself in a week on a repository with twenty packages.

`ex5`'s resolution rule that catches people is that only the best-matching
key's substitutions are tried. There is no fallback to a shorter pattern, so a
mapping that matches but whose target does not exist produces `null` rather
than trying the next key.

## ex6 to ex7 — the parallelism story

The critical path is Amdahl's law made concrete: the serial fraction of a build
is its longest chain. List scheduling is the greedy heuristic every real tool
uses, because optimal DAG scheduling is NP-hard, and the usual improvement is
to prioritise by remaining critical path rather than alphabetically.

The zero-duration case in `ex7` is the one that hangs a naive loop, and it is
worth having hit it once: a project that starts and finishes at the same
instant must still be removed from the running set, which means the clock
advance has to handle "the next event is now".

## ex8, the challenge and review1

The redirect decision in `ex8` explains most of the difference between how
references feel in an editor and in CI. `declarationMap` is the cheap addition
that makes go-to-definition and cross-project rename work.

The challenge is the sector assembled, and its trap is propagation: a project
rebuilds because a reference is being rebuilt *in this run*, which is a fact
about the plan rather than about any timestamp. `review1` inverts it into a
diagnosis, which is the shape a real support tool takes — expensive evidence
gathered by the caller, policy as a pure function.

## Further reading

- [TypeScript handbook: Project References](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/project-references.html) — `composite`, `--build`, and the constraints, from the source.
- [tsconfig reference: `disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect) — the setting behind `ex8`, and why you might turn it off.
- [TypeScript 3.0 release notes: project references](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-3-0/) — the original design discussion, including what problem `--build` was meant to solve.
- [Turborepo: task graphs and caching](https://turborepo.com/docs/core-concepts/package-and-task-graph) — the same graph model with content hashing instead of timestamps, which is the upgrade path from this sector.
- [Amdahl's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law) — why the critical path is a floor, stated generally.

# V3·TC5 — Project references, monorepos and build speed

At some size a single `tsconfig.json` stops working. Not because the compiler
refuses — it will happily check four hundred thousand lines — but because every
edit costs a full check of everything, the editor takes eleven seconds to
respond, and there is no way to say "the API package may not import from the
web app". One program, one graph, no boundaries, no incrementality.

Project references are TypeScript's answer, and they are best understood as
turning your repository into a build graph. Each project is a `tsconfig.json`
with `composite: true`, which means it emits declaration files and a
`.tsbuildinfo` manifest. A project that depends on another lists it in
`references`. `tsc --build` then does what `make` does: work out the order,
work out what is stale, and rebuild only that.

Three things fall out of that design, and all three are the reason to bother.

**Incrementality.** A project whose inputs have not changed and whose
references have not been rebuilt is skipped entirely — not re-checked, skipped.
On a repository of thirty packages, a change to a leaf touches one project; a
change to the shared types package touches everything downstream and nothing
upstream. That difference is the whole game, and the up-to-date check that
decides it is `ex3`.

**Boundaries.** A project can only see what it references. That is a real
architectural constraint enforced by the compiler rather than by a lint rule
people disable, and it is often worth adopting for that reason alone. It also
means the reference list must actually match the import graph, which is what
`ex4` checks — a missing reference is a build that fails mysteriously, and an
unused one is a false dependency that serialises your build for no reason.

**Parallelism.** Once the work is a graph, independent projects can build at
the same time. But only up to a point: the critical path through the graph is a
hard floor on wall-clock time no matter how many cores you have. `ex6` computes
that floor and `ex7` schedules against it, and together they explain why adding
workers stops helping — and why the cheapest build speedup is usually to break
a long chain rather than to buy a bigger machine.

There is a fourth thing, and it is the one that makes references usable day to
day: **the source redirect**. Naively, a project that references another sees
its `.d.ts` files — so nothing works until you build. TypeScript's language
service instead redirects to the *source* files of referenced projects, so
go-to-definition lands in real code and edits are visible immediately, with no
build. That behaviour is on by default and switched off by
`disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect`, and knowing it exists explains most
of the difference between how references behave in your editor and in CI.
`ex8` is that decision, written out.

The exercises are models, not wrappers. `buildOrder` is the topological sort
`tsc --build` runs; `statusOf` is its up-to-date check; `planBuild` in the
challenge puts both together with a scheduler and produces the plan the real
tool prints with `--dry`. Building the model is the fastest way to understand
what the tool is doing, and — the honest reason — the fastest way to work out
why your build did something unexpected at half past six on a Friday.

One note on scope. This sector is about the graph, not about your package
manager. Workspaces, hoisting, `pnpm` symlinks and lockfiles are a real and
adjacent problem, and they interact with the previous sector's resolution
rules. Here, projects are nodes and references are edges, and everything takes
its data as arguments.

## ex1 — build order, and the cycle that stops it

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. The first thing `tsc --build` does with your graph.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export type BuildOrder =
  | { ok: true; order: string[] }
  | { ok: false; cycle: string[] };

export function buildOrder(projects: readonly Project[]): BuildOrder;
```

Rules:

- dependencies come before the projects that reference them
- ties are broken by path, ascending, so the output is deterministic across
  machines
- a reference to a project that is not in the list throws
  `Error('unknown reference: <ref> from <path>')`
- a cycle returns `{ ok: false, cycle }`, where `cycle` starts and ends with the
  same project and lists the path between them, taking the
  alphabetically-first entry point into the cycle

Examples:

```ts
buildOrder([
  { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
  { path: "core", references: [] },
])
// { ok: true, order: ["core", "ui", "app"] }

buildOrder([
  { path: "a", references: ["b"] },
  { path: "b", references: ["a"] },
])
// { ok: false, cycle: ["a", "b", "a"] }
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex1
```

## ex2 — what does this change touch?

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Build order answers "in what sequence". This answers
the question CI actually asks: given these changed files, what has to be
rebuilt and retested?

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export function affected(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  changed: readonly string[],
): string[];
```

Rules:

- the result includes every changed project that exists in the graph, plus
  every project that depends on one of them, directly or transitively
- dependencies are *not* affected: changing `app` does not affect `core`
- a changed path that is not a project in the list is ignored
- the result is sorted ascending, with no duplicates
- cycles in the graph must not cause an infinite loop

Example:

```ts
const graph = [
  { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
  { path: "core", references: [] },
  { path: "tools", references: [] },
]

affected(graph, ["core"])          // ["app", "core", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["ui"])            // ["app", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["app"])           // ["app"]
affected(graph, ["nonexistent"])   // []
affected(graph, [])                // []
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex2
```

## ex3 — the up-to-date check

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. This is the function that makes `tsc --build` fast, and
knowing its exact order is how you diagnose a build that rebuilds everything
every time.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface BuildInfo {
  outputs: readonly string[];
  builtAt: number;
}

export interface Snapshot {
  fileTimes: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  buildInfos: Readonly<Record<string, BuildInfo>>;
}

export type Status =
  | "missing-buildinfo"
  | "missing-output"
  | "stale-input"
  | "stale-reference"
  | "up-to-date";

export function statusOf(
  project: Project,
  inputs: readonly string[],
  snapshot: Snapshot,
): Status;
```

Checks, in **this order**, returning the first that applies:

1. no `BuildInfo` for this project → `"missing-buildinfo"`
2. any output listed in the build info absent from `fileTimes` →
   `"missing-output"`
3. any input's time **greater than** `builtAt` → `"stale-input"`. An input
   absent from `fileTimes` also counts as stale — it was deleted, and the
   output no longer corresponds to reality.
4. any referenced project with no build info, or with a `builtAt` **greater
   than** this project's → `"stale-reference"`
5. otherwise → `"up-to-date"`

Note the strict comparisons. A file written in the same millisecond as the
build is *not* stale, which is deliberate — the alternative rebuilds forever on
filesystems with coarse timestamps.

Examples, with `snapshot.fileTimes = { "a.ts": 10, "out/a.js": 20 }` and
`buildInfos = { app: { outputs: ["out/a.js"], builtAt: 20 } }`:

- `statusOf({ path: "app", references: [] }, ["a.ts"], snapshot)` → `"up-to-date"`
- with `a.ts` at time `30` → `"stale-input"`
- with an extra output `"out/b.js"` that is not in `fileTimes` →
  `"missing-output"`

## ex4 — the configuration rules references impose

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Project references only work if several unrelated
settings agree, and the compiler's error messages for each are individually
clear and collectively confusing.

```ts
export interface ProjectConfig {
  path: string;
  composite?: boolean;
  rootDir?: string;
  outDir?: string;
  files: readonly string[];
  references: readonly string[];
  imports: readonly string[];   // project paths this one actually imports from
}

export function validateProjects(projects: readonly ProjectConfig[]): string[];
```

Return diagnostics, sorted ascending, no duplicates:

- `<path>: referenced project <other> must set composite: true` — for each
  reference whose target does not have `composite: true`
- `<path>: missing reference to <other>` — it imports from a project it does
  not reference
- `<path>: unused reference to <other>` — it references a project it never
  imports from
- `<path>: outDir is required on a composite project` — `composite` is true and
  `outDir` is absent
- `<path>: file "<file>" is outside rootDir "<root>"` — `rootDir` is set and a
  file does not start with it

A reference or import naming a project that is not in the list is ignored by
the first three rules — a missing project is a different problem, and reporting
it five times is not helpful.

Example:

```ts
validateProjects([
  { path: "app", composite: true, outDir: "app/dist", files: [],
    references: ["core"], imports: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "core", outDir: "core/dist", files: [], references: [], imports: [] },
  { path: "ui", composite: true, outDir: "ui/dist", files: [], references: [], imports: [] },
])
// [
//   "app: missing reference to ui",
//   "app: referenced project core must set composite: true",
// ]
```

## ex5 — path mapping, exactly

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `paths` is the setting everyone uses and nobody reads
the rules for, which is why "why is it resolving to the wrong file" is a weekly
question in every monorepo.

```ts
export function resolvePaths(
  specifier: string,
  paths: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>,
  baseUrl: string,
  exists: (path: string) => boolean,
): string | null;
```

The algorithm:

1. An **exact** key — one with no `*` — that equals the specifier wins outright,
   ahead of every pattern.
2. Otherwise, among keys containing exactly one `*`, the one with the **longest
   prefix before the `*`** wins. Only that key's substitutions are tried; there
   is no falling through to a shorter match.
3. For the winning key, each substitution in its array is tried **in order**.
   The `*` in the substitution is replaced by the text the specifier's `*`
   captured; an exact key's substitutions are used as they are.
4. Each candidate is joined onto `baseUrl` — `baseUrl`, a `/`, then the
   candidate — unless `baseUrl` is `""`, in which case the candidate is used as
   it is. A trailing slash on `baseUrl` is not doubled.
5. The first candidate for which `exists` returns true is the answer. If none
   exists, or nothing matched, the answer is `null`.

Examples, with `baseUrl` of `"."` and every candidate existing:

```ts
resolvePaths("@app/core", { "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"] }, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/index.ts"

resolvePaths("@app/core/util", {
  "@app/core/*": ["packages/core/src/*.ts"],
  "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"],
}, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/util.ts"   - longer prefix wins
```

and with an `exists` that only accepts the second entry:

```ts
resolvePaths("x", { x: ["a.ts", "b.ts"] }, "", exists)   // "b.ts"
```

## ex6 — the floor no number of cores can beat

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Before you buy a bigger CI machine, find out whether
parallelism can help at all.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface CriticalPath {
  length: number;
  path: string[];
}

export function criticalPath(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  durations: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
): CriticalPath;
```

The critical path is the longest chain of dependencies, weighted by build
duration. Its total is the minimum possible wall-clock time for the whole build
with unlimited workers.

Rules:

- `path` runs from the deepest dependency to the final project, in build order
- a missing duration is `0`
- ties are broken by taking the lexicographically smaller `path` array,
  compared element by element
- a graph with a cycle throws `Error("cycle detected")`
- an empty graph gives `{ length: 0, path: [] }`

Example:

```ts
criticalPath(
  [
    { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
    { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
    { path: "core", references: [] },
    { path: "tools", references: [] },
  ],
  { app: 5, ui: 3, core: 10, tools: 100 },
)
// { length: 18, path: ["core", "ui", "app"] }
```

Note what that example shows: `tools` takes a hundred seconds and is not on the
critical path, because nothing waits for it. With two workers this build takes
a hundred seconds; with unlimited workers it takes eighteen; and no amount of
hardware gets it below eighteen.

