
## ex7 — scheduling the graph across workers

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Now put a real number of workers on it and find out
what the build actually costs.

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export interface Assignment {
  project: string;
  worker: number;
  start: number;
  end: number;
}

export interface Schedule {
  makespan: number;
  assignments: Assignment[];
}

export function planParallelBuild(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  durations: Readonly<Record<string, number>>,
  workers: number,
): Schedule;
```

The simulation, which is ordinary list scheduling:

- time starts at `0`
- at each step, a project is **ready** when it has not started and every
  reference it names has finished at or before the current time
- ready projects are started in ascending path order, on the free worker with
  the lowest index, until either no worker is free or nothing is ready
- when nothing more can start, time advances to the earliest `end` among
  running projects
- a missing duration is `0` — such a project still occupies a worker, starting
  and ending at the same instant
- `assignments` is sorted by `start` ascending, then by `worker` ascending
- `makespan` is the largest `end`, or `0` for an empty graph
- `workers` below `1` throws `RangeError("workers must be at least 1")`
- a reference to an unknown project is ignored

Example — the graph from `ex6` with `{ app: 5, ui: 3, core: 10, tools: 100 }`
and two workers: `core` and `tools` start at `0` on workers `0` and `1`; `ui`
starts at `10` on worker `0`; `app` starts at `13`; makespan is `100`, because
`tools` is still running.

## ex8 — source or declaration?

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. When project `app` reads a type from project `core`,
which file does the compiler actually read? The answer is different in your
editor and in CI, and this is the setting that decides it.

```ts
export interface RefProject {
  rootDir: string;
  outDir: string;
  sources: readonly string[];
  declarationMap: boolean;
  built: boolean;
}

export interface Resolved {
  file: string;
  kind: "source" | "declaration";
  goToDefinition: string;
}

export function outputFor(project: RefProject, source: string): string | null;

export function sourceOfTruth(
  project: RefProject,
  source: string,
  options: { redirect: boolean },
): Resolved | null;
```

`outputFor` computes the declaration file a source emits: strip `rootDir` from
the front, prepend `outDir`, and change the extension — `.ts` and `.tsx` become
`.d.ts`, `.mts` becomes `.d.mts`, `.cts` becomes `.d.cts`. Returns `null` if
the source is not in `sources`, is not under `rootDir`, or has any other
extension.

`sourceOfTruth`:

- `redirect: true` — the default, and what the editor does: the compiler reads
  the **source** file. `kind` is `"source"`, `file` and `goToDefinition` are
  both the source path, and it works whether or not the project has been built.
- `redirect: false` — what `disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect` gives you:
  the compiler reads the emitted declaration. If the project is not `built`,
  return `null`. Otherwise `kind` is `"declaration"`, `file` is the `.d.ts`
  path, and `goToDefinition` is the **source** when `declarationMap` is true and
  the `.d.ts` otherwise.
- a source `outputFor` cannot map returns `null` in every case.

Example:

```ts
const core = {
  rootDir: "packages/core/src",
  outDir: "packages/core/dist",
  sources: ["packages/core/src/money.ts"],
  declarationMap: true,
  built: true,
}

outputFor(core, "packages/core/src/money.ts")   // "packages/core/dist/money.d.ts"
sourceOfTruth(core, "packages/core/src/money.ts", { redirect: false })
// { file: "packages/core/dist/money.d.ts", kind: "declaration",
//   goToDefinition: "packages/core/src/money.ts" }
```
```

```

## challenge — tsc --build --dry (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Order, staleness, propagation and scheduling, in
one function that prints what the build is about to do.

```ts
export interface BuildProject {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
  inputs: readonly string[];
  outputs: readonly string[];
  duration: number;
}

export interface World {
  fileTimes: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
  builtAt: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}

export interface BuildPlan {
  order: string[];
  rebuilt: string[];
  skipped: string[];
  makespan: number;
  lines: string[];
}

export function planBuild(
  projects: readonly BuildProject[],
  world: World,
  workers: number,
): BuildPlan;
```

Walk the projects in topological order — dependencies first, ties by path
ascending — and decide each one:

A project **rebuilds** when any of these holds:

- it has no entry in `world.builtAt`
- one of its `outputs` is missing from `world.fileTimes`
- one of its `inputs` is missing from `world.fileTimes`, or has a time greater
  than its `builtAt`
- any project it references is itself being rebuilt — this is the propagation,
  and it is why the order matters
- any project it references has a `builtAt` greater than its own

Otherwise it is **skipped**.

Then schedule the rebuilt projects across `workers` with the list-scheduling
rule from `ex7`: ready in ascending path order, lowest free worker, clock
advances to the next completion. References to skipped projects impose no wait.

Output:

- `order` is the full topological order
- `rebuilt` and `skipped` are in that same order
- `lines` is `BUILD <path>` or `SKIP <path>` for each project in order,
  followed by one final `MAKESPAN <n>`
- a cycle throws `Error("cycle detected: " + cycle.join(" -> "))` with the cycle
  in the `ex1` format
- `workers` below `1` throws `RangeError("workers must be at least 1")`

Honest difficulty note: every piece exists in an earlier exercise. The two
things that catch people are the **propagation** — a project rebuilds because
its reference is being rebuilt in this same run, not because of any timestamp —
and the fact that the scheduler must only consider dependencies among the
rebuilt set, because a skipped project is already finished at time zero.

## review1 — why did it rebuild?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. The same rules from the other side: not "what will
happen" but "what just happened, and why".

```ts
export type Cause =
  | "no-buildinfo"
  | "output-missing"
  | "config-changed"
  | "input-changed"
  | "reference-newer"
  | "none";

export interface Evidence {
  hasBuildInfo: boolean;
  missingOutputs: readonly string[];
  newestInput: number;
  builtAt: number;
  newestReference: number;
  configChangedAt: number;
}

export function diagnose(evidence: Evidence): { cause: Cause; explanation: string };
```

Precedence, first match wins, with the exact explanation for each:

1. `hasBuildInfo` is false → `"no-buildinfo"`, explained as
   `no .tsbuildinfo: this project has never been built here`
2. `missingOutputs` is non-empty → `"output-missing"`, explained as
   `output missing: <first entry after sorting ascending>`
3. `configChangedAt > builtAt` → `"config-changed"`, explained as
   `tsconfig changed at <configChangedAt>, after the last build at <builtAt>`
4. `newestInput > builtAt` → `"input-changed"`, explained as
   `input newer than build: <newestInput> > <builtAt>`
5. `newestReference > builtAt` → `"reference-newer"`, explained as
   `a referenced project was rebuilt at <newestReference>`
6. otherwise → `"none"`, explained as `up to date`

Example:

```ts
diagnose({
  hasBuildInfo: true,
  missingOutputs: [],
  newestInput: 40,
  builtAt: 20,
  newestReference: 50,
  configChangedAt: 5,
})
// { cause: "input-changed", explanation: "input newer than build: 40 > 20" }
```

Note that both the input and the reference are newer in that example, and the
answer names only the first. A diagnosis reports the reason it found, in the
order the build checks them — which is exactly the order that lets someone act
on it.

## Concepts, in the order you will need them

### A minimal reference setup

```jsonc
// tsconfig.base.json - settings, no files
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "composite": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "declarationMap": true,
    "incremental": true,
    "strict": true
  }
}
```

```jsonc
// packages/core/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" },
  "include": ["src/**/*"]
}
```

```jsonc
// packages/app/tsconfig.json
{
  "extends": "../../tsconfig.base.json",
  "compilerOptions": { "rootDir": "src", "outDir": "dist" },
  "include": ["src/**/*"],
  "references": [{ "path": "../core" }]
}
```

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json at the root - a solution file: references only, no files
{ "files": [], "references": [{ "path": "packages/core" }, { "path": "packages/app" }] }
```

That last file is the one people miss. A root config with `"files": []` and
nothing but references is how you get `tsc --build` at the repository root to
mean "everything", and it is also what editors use to discover the graph.

### The commands worth knowing

```
tsc --build                    # build everything stale, in order
tsc --build --dry              # print the plan; do nothing
tsc --build --verbose          # say why each project was or was not built
tsc --build --force            # ignore up-to-date checks
tsc --build --clean            # delete outputs and build info
tsc --build --watch            # incremental rebuilds on change
```

`--dry --verbose` together are the diagnostic pair. They answer the only
question you ever have, which is why something rebuilt.

## Worked example — diagnosing a slow monorepo

Symptom: a one-line change in `packages/app` takes ninety seconds.

```
$ tsc --build --dry --verbose
Project 'packages/types' is up to date
Project 'packages/core' is out of date because output 'dist/index.js' does not exist
Project 'packages/ui' is out of date because its dependency 'packages/core' was rebuilt
...
```

`core` rebuilt because an output is missing, not because anything changed —
somebody deleted `dist` and left `.tsbuildinfo` behind, or a `.gitignore`
change removed it in CI. Everything downstream then rebuilt by propagation.
The fix is `--clean` followed by one full build, not a faster machine.

A second, more interesting version:

```
Project 'packages/core' is out of date because oldest output is older than newest input
```

Here a file genuinely changed. Now the question is whether the ninety seconds
is the critical path or a worker shortage, which is `ex6` against `ex7`: if
`criticalPath` says eighty-five seconds, no amount of parallelism will help and
the answer is to split `core` — usually by pulling the pure type declarations
into a `types` package that changes rarely.

## Common mistakes

**A shared package that changes constantly.** Everything downstream rebuilds
every time. Split the stable types from the volatile implementation.

**Test projects on the dependency chain.** Nothing should reference a test
project. One spurious edge can add its whole subtree to the critical path.

**`paths` instead of real workspace packages.** Type resolution works, runtime
resolution does not, and you now maintain two mechanisms that must agree.

**Deleting `dist` without deleting `.tsbuildinfo`.** The build believes it is
up to date and the next step fails on a missing file.

**Forgetting `declarationMap`.** Go-to-definition lands in generated
declarations, cross-project rename does not work, and everybody blames the
editor.

**A missing reference for an import.** Works in the editor via the source
redirect; fails in CI because the declaration had not been emitted yet.

**One giant project because references seemed complicated.** Every edit costs a
full check, and there are no boundaries to enforce.

## The interview answer

"How do you keep a large TypeScript monorepo fast?" — start with the model:
it is a build graph, and `tsc --build` is `make` for it. Each package is a
composite project that emits declarations and a build info file; references
declare the edges; the build computes a topological order, checks staleness
against inputs, outputs and references, rebuilds what is stale, and propagates.

Then the levers, in the order you would pull them. Make sure references match
imports exactly, because missing ones break CI and unused ones serialise the
build. Compute the critical path: if the wall-clock time is near it, adding
workers is pointless and the fix is to break the chain — usually by extracting
a stable types package that rarely changes. Turn on `declarationMap` so the
editor stays usable. And know that `tsc` skips propagation when a rebuilt
project's declarations are byte-identical, which is why signature changes cost
so much more than body changes.

## Check yourself

1. What does `composite: true` imply, and why does each implication follow?
2. Why are cycles forbidden between projects but legal between files?
3. Name the four staleness checks in order, and say why the order matters.
4. Why is the timestamp comparison `>` and not `>=`?
5. What is the affected set of a change, in graph terms?
6. Why does changing a leaf package cost more than changing an app?
7. What does an unused reference cost you?
8. What happens in CI when a reference is missing but the import resolves?
9. What is the critical path, and what does it bound?
10. When does adding build workers stop helping?
11. What does the source-of-project-reference redirect do, and why does the
    editor want it?
12. What does `declarationMap` buy you?
13. Why does `paths` not fix runtime resolution?
14. Given `"@app/core/*"` and `"@app/*"`, which mapping is used, and is there a
    fallback?
15. Why does `tsc` compare emitted declarations byte for byte?
lessons.fullReading:
# Long read — why the build graph is the architecture

## One program does not scale, and the reason is not speed

The first argument for project references is compile time, and it is the least
interesting one. The better argument is that a single program has no
boundaries. Every file can import every other file. The rule that the payments
package must not depend on the admin UI exists in a document, or in a lint
rule, or in somebody's head — and each of those is a rule that gets broken on a
deadline and discovered six months later when the admin UI has to be deployed
to satisfy a payments release.

A project boundary is different in kind. `app` cannot import from `internal`
because the compiler has not been told they are connected; the import does not
resolve, and it does not resolve on the first attempt, in the editor, before
the commit. That is architecture enforced by the mechanism you already run,
which is the only kind that survives.

The cost is that you now have a graph to maintain, and graphs have properties
that flat structures do not: cycles, critical paths, propagation. This sector
is those properties.

## What is actually in a .tsbuildinfo

The file is JSON, and it is worth opening one once. It contains the list of
input files with their content hashes, the emit signatures of the outputs, the
resolved compiler options, and — for `incremental` builds within a project —
the dependency graph between files, so that changing one file can re-check only
the files affected by it.

Two of those deserve attention. The **content hashes** mean that touching a
file without changing it does not trigger work, which is a real improvement
over pure timestamps and the reason `git checkout` of an identical file is
cheap. The **emit signatures** are the mechanism behind the sector's most
useful piece of trivia: after rebuilding a project, `tsc` compares the newly
generated declaration output against the previous signature, and if nothing
changed, dependents keep their up-to-date status. Change a function body and
the `.d.ts` is identical and nothing propagates. Change its return type and
everything downstream rebuilds.

That asymmetry is worth designing around. A package whose *public types* are
stable is cheap to depend on even if its implementation changes daily. A
package whose types churn is expensive for everyone downstream. Splitting a
volatile package into a stable type surface and a volatile implementation is
frequently the single highest-value change available in a slow monorepo, and it
is invisible if you think of the build as "compiling files".

## The editor is a different program

The language service does not run `tsc --build`. It opens the project
containing the file you are editing, follows references, and — because of the
source redirect — reads the *sources* of referenced projects rather than their
declarations. That means it type-checks more code than the build does, sees
your unbuilt edits immediately, and gives go-to-definition that lands in real
implementations.

It also means the editor can be slower than the build, and can report errors
the build does not, and can be up to date when the build is stale. Every one of
those is a support question somewhere, and all of them are explained by the
single fact that the two programs read different files.

The redirect has a scaling limit. On a repository with hundreds of projects,
following references into sources means loading a large fraction of the
repository into the editor's program. That is when
`disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect` starts to look attractive — at the
cost of requiring a build before your edits are visible across a boundary,
which is a trade most teams are not willing to make until they have to.

## The other tools, and what they add

`tsc --build` is a correct, single-machine, timestamp-and-hash-based build
system. The monorepo tools layered on top — Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, Rush — add
three things it does not have.

**Content-addressed caching across machines.** If this exact input set has been
built before, anywhere, download the output instead of computing it. That turns
a cold CI build from minutes into seconds and is the single largest win
available, and it requires hermetic inputs — the tool must know every file that
affects the output, which is a stronger claim than "these are my source files".

**Task graphs beyond compilation.** Real builds also lint, test, bundle and
publish, and those have their own dependency structure — `test` depends on
`build` of the same package and `build` of its dependencies. `tsc` models one
task type; the others model many.

**Distribution.** Running the graph across many machines, which is only useful
once caching and hermeticity are solved.

None of that replaces understanding the graph. All three are the same
topological order, the same staleness question, and the same critical path with
better inputs — which is why the exercises here transfer directly.

## Performance notes, concretely

Three settings matter more than the rest.

`skipLibCheck: true` stops the compiler type-checking every `.d.ts` in
`node_modules`. On a typical application this is worth a large fraction of the
check time, and the cost is that a genuinely broken declaration file in a
dependency is not reported — which you would not have fixed anyway.

`incremental` and a persistent `.tsbuildinfo` location. In CI, that file must
be cached between runs or every build is a cold build, and the most common
cause of "our CI ignores incremental builds" is that the file lives in a
directory that is not preserved.

`isolatedDeclarations`, from TypeScript 5.5, changes the shape of the problem
rather than tuning it. It requires explicit types on everything exported, which
means declaration files can be generated from a single file without type
checking — so `.d.ts` emit becomes parallelisable and can be done by a
non-TypeScript tool. In a large repository that turns the declaration-emit part
of the critical path into something a fast tool can do in parallel. The cost is
annotations on your public API, which is a discipline the next sector argues
for on its own merits.

## When not to use project references

A single package with one build output does not need them. The setup cost is
real — a base config, a config per project, a solution file, `rootDir`
discipline — and a project with no internal boundaries gains nothing but
ceremony.

They are also a poor fit when the "packages" are not really separable: if every
change touches four of them, the graph is telling you the boundary is wrong,
and the references will only make each change more expensive. The graph is a
model of your architecture, and a bad architecture with a build graph on top is
a bad architecture that now takes longer to build.

And if you are already using a bundler-based dev server with its own
incremental transpilation, references buy you type-check parallelism and
enforced boundaries but not faster dev feedback — the bundler was never running
`tsc` in the first place. Know which of the three benefits you are buying, and
whether you needed it.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason cycles are forbidden rather than merely discouraged: a composite
project emits declaration files that its dependents consume, so building `a`
requires `b`'s output and building `b` requires `a`'s. There is no order that
works. Contrast with plain imports inside a single project, where circularity
is legal — the compiler sees all the files at once and resolves types across
the cycle without difficulty.

## Hint 2

The cycle output is a user interface decision, and it matters more than it
looks. `["a", "b", "a"]` tells someone exactly which two edges to look at. "A
cycle was detected in the project graph" sends them to draw the whole graph on
paper. Every good build tool prints the cycle; several popular ones do not, and
their users write scripts like this one.

## Hint 3

Deterministic order pays off in a place you might not expect: build logs. When
the order is stable, two CI runs produce diffable output, and "which project
started behaving differently" is a text comparison. When it is not, every log
looks different and nobody can tell whether anything changed.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## ex2 — what does this change touch?

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Build order answers "in what sequence". This answers
the question CI actually asks: given these changed files, what has to be
rebuilt and retested?

```ts
export interface Project {
  path: string;
  references: readonly string[];
}

export function affected(
  projects: readonly Project[],
  changed: readonly string[],
): string[];
```

Rules:

- the result includes every changed project that exists in the graph, plus
  every project that depends on one of them, directly or transitively
- dependencies are *not* affected: changing `app` does not affect `core`
- a changed path that is not a project in the list is ignored
- the result is sorted ascending, with no duplicates
- cycles in the graph must not cause an infinite loop

Example:

```ts
const graph = [
  { path: "app", references: ["core", "ui"] },
  { path: "ui", references: ["core"] },
  { path: "core", references: [] },
  { path: "tools", references: [] },
]

affected(graph, ["core"])          // ["app", "core", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["ui"])            // ["app", "ui"]
affected(graph, ["app"])           // ["app"]
affected(graph, ["nonexistent"])   // []
affected(graph, [])                // []
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The edges point the wrong way for this question. `references` says "I depend on
them"; you need "who depends on me". Build the reverse index once, then the
rest is an ordinary graph traversal.

## Hint 2

```ts
const dependents = new Map<string, string[]>();
for (const project of projects) {
  for (const reference of project.references) {
    dependents.set(reference, [...(dependents.get(reference) ?? []), project.path]);
  }
}
```

From there it is breadth- or depth-first from the changed set, with a `Set` of
visited nodes — which is also what makes the cycle rule free rather than a
special case.

## Hint 3

Seed the traversal only with changed paths that exist in the graph. Seeding
with unknown paths is harmless for the traversal and wrong for the output,
because the prompt says an unknown path contributes nothing — including itself.

Left to you: breadth-first or depth-first. The result is a set either way, so
this is purely about which is easier to read; pick one and do not mix them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This function is the reason monorepo tooling exists. Nx, Turborepo, Bazel and
`tsc --build` are all, at their core, this traversal plus a cache. Being able
to say "the affected set is the reverse-reachability closure of the changed
set" in an interview is worth more than naming three tools, because it is the
idea all three implement.

## Hint 2

The asymmetry is worth stating explicitly, because people get it backwards
under pressure. Changing a **leaf** — a shared types package — affects almost
everything, because everything depends on it. Changing an **entry point**
affects almost nothing. That is exactly inverted from where the code feels
important, and it is why the shared package is the one that needs the tests.

## Hint 3

Real implementations refine this in one important way: they map changed *files*
to projects first, and a change to a file that is not an input of any project —
a README, a CI config — affects nothing. Getting that mapping wrong in the
conservative direction (assume everything) makes the tool useless; getting it
wrong in the other direction ships a broken build.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write it as five early returns in the stated order and resist the urge to
compute everything up front. The order is the specification, and a version that
gathers all the evidence and then decides will get the precedence wrong the
first time you change it.

## Hint 2

The deleted-input case is easy to miss because it looks like it should be a
separate status:

```ts
for (const input of inputs) {
  const time = snapshot.fileTimes[input];
  if (time === undefined || time > info.builtAt) return "stale-input";
}
```

One condition, two situations — modified and deleted — and both mean the same
thing: the output no longer reflects the inputs.

## Hint 3

For the reference check, look up each referenced project's build info rather
than recursing. Staleness propagates through the *build*, not through this
function: `tsc --build` walks the graph in order, so by the time it asks about
`app`, it has already rebuilt `core` and updated `core`'s timestamp.

Left to you: whether a reference that is missing from `buildInfos` entirely
should be `"stale-reference"` or an error. The prompt chooses; understand why
the other choice would make the first build of a fresh checkout fail.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The strict `>` rather than `>=` is worth understanding rather than copying.
File modification times have limited resolution — one second on some
filesystems, and even a millisecond is coarse compared to how fast a small
project builds. With `>=`, a file written in the same tick as the build info
looks newer forever, and the project rebuilds on every invocation. That exact
bug has shipped in several build tools.

## Hint 2

Timestamps are a terrible way to decide this and everyone uses them anyway.
Content hashes are correct — a file touched but unchanged should not trigger a
rebuild, and a clock that jumps backwards should not make everything look
fresh — and they cost a read of every input. Bazel hashes. `tsc` uses
timestamps plus, since the `.tsbuildinfo` format gained file version hashes,
a content check for the "did the output actually change" question. Knowing
which trade-off a tool made tells you what will go wrong with it.

## Hint 3

`missing-output` is the check that catches the most common real situation: a
developer deleted `dist/` and left `.tsbuildinfo` in place. Without it, the
build info says everything is up to date, nothing rebuilds, and the next step
fails on a missing file with an error that names neither the project nor the
cause.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five independent rules over one list. Write five small loops rather than one
clever pass — the diagnostics are collected into a set and sorted at the end,
so nothing depends on the order you generate them in.

## Hint 2

The missing/unused pair is a symmetric difference and reads best as two set
operations:

```ts
const referenced = new Set(project.references);
const imported = new Set(project.imports);
for (const target of imported) if (!referenced.has(target)) { /* missing */ }
for (const target of referenced) if (!imported.has(target)) { /* unused */ }
```

Filter both by "is a known project" before comparing, or a typo in a reference
produces two diagnostics that contradict each other.

## Hint 3

The `rootDir` check is a `startsWith`, and it is worth thinking about the
trailing separator: `rootDir` of `"src"` and a file of `"srcextra/a.ts"` would
pass a naive prefix test. The prompt does not require you to handle it — decide
whether you would, in a tool people rely on.

Left to you: whether a project with no `files` and a `rootDir` is worth
reporting. It cannot violate the rule; whether the absence itself is
suspicious is a policy question, not a correctness one.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`composite: true` is not a flag, it is a package of them. It forces
`declaration: true` — a referenced project must emit `.d.ts` files or its
dependents have nothing to read — it defaults `incremental` on so a
`.tsbuildinfo` is written, and it requires every input file to be listed or
matched by `include`, because `--build` needs to know the input set without
scanning. Each of those has a separate error message and they arrive one at a
time.

## Hint 2

The unused-reference rule sounds like tidiness and is really about speed. A
reference is an edge in the build graph, so an unnecessary one serialises two
projects that could have built in parallel — and on a long chain, a single
spurious edge can add its whole subtree to the critical path. `ex6` makes that
concrete.

## Hint 3

The missing-reference rule is the one that produces the most baffling failure
in practice. The import resolves — because `node_modules` or `paths` found the
source — the types are correct, the editor is happy, and `tsc --build` fails
because it built the projects in an order that had not yet produced the
`.d.ts`. The symptom is an error that appears only in CI and only sometimes.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## ex5 — path mapping, exactly

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. `paths` is the setting everyone uses and nobody reads
the rules for, which is why "why is it resolving to the wrong file" is a weekly
question in every monorepo.

```ts
export function resolvePaths(
  specifier: string,
  paths: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>,
  baseUrl: string,
  exists: (path: string) => boolean,
): string | null;
```

The algorithm:

1. An **exact** key — one with no `*` — that equals the specifier wins outright,
   ahead of every pattern.
2. Otherwise, among keys containing exactly one `*`, the one with the **longest
   prefix before the `*`** wins. Only that key's substitutions are tried; there
   is no falling through to a shorter match.
3. For the winning key, each substitution in its array is tried **in order**.
   The `*` in the substitution is replaced by the text the specifier's `*`
   captured; an exact key's substitutions are used as they are.
4. Each candidate is joined onto `baseUrl` — `baseUrl`, a `/`, then the
   candidate — unless `baseUrl` is `""`, in which case the candidate is used as
   it is. A trailing slash on `baseUrl` is not doubled.
5. The first candidate for which `exists` returns true is the answer. If none
   exists, or nothing matched, the answer is `null`.

Examples, with `baseUrl` of `"."` and every candidate existing:

```ts
resolvePaths("@app/core", { "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"] }, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/index.ts"

resolvePaths("@app/core/util", {
  "@app/core/*": ["packages/core/src/*.ts"],
  "@app/*": ["packages/*/src/index.ts"],
}, ".", exists)
// "./packages/core/src/util.ts"   - longer prefix wins
```

and with an `exists` that only accepts the second entry:

```ts
resolvePaths("x", { x: ["a.ts", "b.ts"] }, "", exists)   // "b.ts"
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three phases: choose the key, expand it into candidates, pick the first that
exists. Keeping them separate is what makes rule 2 — no falling through to a
shorter match — easy to honour, because the choice is already made before you
touch `exists`.

## Hint 2

Matching a pattern key against the specifier is the same prefix/suffix split as
the exports patterns in the previous sector:

```ts
const star = key.indexOf("*");
const prefix = key.slice(0, star);
const suffix = key.slice(star + 1);
if (specifier.startsWith(prefix) && specifier.endsWith(suffix) &&
    specifier.length >= prefix.length + suffix.length) {
  const captured = specifier.slice(prefix.length, specifier.length - suffix.length);
}
```

## Hint 3

The `baseUrl` join has two cases and one trap:

```ts
const join = (base: string, rest: string) =>
  base === "" ? rest : `${base.replace(/\/$/, "")}/${rest}`;
```

Left to you: whether an absolute-looking candidate should skip the join. Real
TypeScript treats `paths` entries as relative to `baseUrl` and does not
special-case them, which is worth knowing because it surprises people who write
absolute paths there.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Rule 2 — only the best key's substitutions are tried — is the one that produces
the "wrong file" reports. Given `"@app/core/*"` and `"@app/*"`, a specifier
matching both uses only the first, and if that first mapping's target does not
exist, the answer is `null` rather than the second mapping's file. People
expect a fallback and there is none.

## Hint 2

`paths` does not affect the emitted JavaScript. The compiler rewrites nothing;
`import "@app/core"` is emitted verbatim, and something at runtime — a bundler,
a `tsconfig-paths` loader, a `package.json` `imports` field, a workspace
symlink — has to make that specifier resolve. A monorepo that works under `tsc`
and fails under `node dist/index.js` has almost always hit exactly this.

## Hint 3

Which is why, in a repository that already uses project references, `paths` is
usually the wrong tool. Workspace packages with real `exports` fields resolve
identically at type-check time and at runtime, with no second mechanism to keep
in sync. The place `paths` still earns its keep is a single project's internal
aliases — `"~/*": ["src/*"]` — where nothing crosses a package boundary.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason to compute this rather than measure it: measurement tells you how
long the build took, and the critical path tells you what to *change*. A build
taking four minutes with a two-minute critical path can be halved by adding
workers. A build taking four minutes with a four-minute critical path cannot be
improved by any hardware, and the fix is structural — split the project on the
chain, or remove an unnecessary reference.

## Hint 2

This is Amdahl's law with the serial fraction made concrete. The chain is the
serial part; everything else is the parallel part; and the speedup available
from more workers is bounded by the ratio. It is also why the "unused
reference" rule in `ex4` matters: a spurious edge can add an entire subtree to
the chain, and the tool that finds it is the one you already wrote.

## Hint 3

In a real repository the durations are not uniform, and the largest single win
is usually a *test* project rather than a compile. If the chain runs
`types -> core -> core-tests -> app`, then `core-tests` is on the critical path
only because something declared a dependency on it — and nothing should depend
on a test project. That is a one-line fix worth minutes per build.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two collections and a clock. `running` holds `{ project, worker, end }`;
`finished` holds the time each project completed. The loop is: start everything
you can, then jump the clock to the next completion, then repeat until nothing
is left.

## Hint 2

"The free worker with the lowest index" needs a set of busy workers, not a
count:

```ts
const busy = new Set(running.map((r) => r.worker));
const free = [];
for (let w = 0; w < workers; w += 1) if (!busy.has(w)) free.push(w);
```

A count is enough for the makespan and wrong for the assignments, and the
prompt asks for the assignments.

## Hint 3

Zero-duration projects are the case that can hang your loop. A project that
starts and ends at the same instant is still in `running` for one iteration, so
the clock advance must handle "the earliest end is now" without moving time
forwards — otherwise you either loop forever or skip ahead.

Left to you: whether to advance the clock to the minimum end, or to the minimum
end strictly greater than now. One of those terminates for zero-duration
projects and one does not; work out which before you run it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

List scheduling is a heuristic, not an optimum. Optimal scheduling of a DAG
across identical workers is NP-hard, so every real build tool uses a greedy
rule and accepts being a bit worse than perfect. The classic improvement is to
prioritise by remaining critical path rather than alphabetically — start the
project with the longest chain behind it first — and it is usually worth a
noticeable percentage.

## Hint 2

Compare the makespan this returns with `ex6`'s critical path and you have a
diagnosis. If the makespan is close to the critical path, you are worker-bound
in name only and buying cores will not help. If it is far above, you have
enough parallelism in the graph and not enough workers, and the fix is a
setting rather than a refactor.

## Hint 3

The alphabetical tie-break is deliberately naive and it makes the schedule
reproducible, which for a teaching model is worth more than a few percent. In
production, reproducibility still matters — a scheduler whose output varies run
to run makes build timings incomparable, and you lose the ability to say
whether a change made things worse.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`outputFor` is three independent validations followed by two string
operations, and doing the validations first keeps the string work simple —
by the time you are slicing, you already know the prefix is there.

## Hint 2

The extension table is small enough to write out, and mapping it explicitly
avoids a subtle bug where `.d.ts` inputs would map to `.d.d.ts`:

```ts
const DECLARATION: Record<string, string> = {
  ".ts": ".d.ts", ".tsx": ".d.ts", ".mts": ".d.mts", ".cts": ".d.cts",
};
```

Check that a source already ending `.d.ts` produces `null` rather than
nonsense, because `sources` really can contain one.

## Hint 3

`sourceOfTruth` is a decision table with three inputs — `redirect`, `built`,
`declarationMap` — and five outcomes. Write the table out on paper before you
write the `if`s; you will find one row that is `null` and one that is a
surprise.

Left to you: whether `redirect: true` should care about `built` at all. The
prompt says it does not, which is the whole reason the feature exists — decide
whether you would ever want it to.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The redirect is the feature that makes project references bearable. Without it,
editing `core` and switching to `app` shows you stale types until you run a
build, every time, and go-to-definition lands in a generated `.d.ts` with no
implementation. With it, the editor behaves as though the whole repository were
one program while the build still behaves as a graph. That is a genuinely
clever piece of engineering hiding behind a long setting name.

## Hint 2

Which is also why the setting to turn it off exists. With the redirect on, the
compiler reads sources of referenced projects, which means it *checks* more
files and gets slower — and it can report errors in a project you did not ask
to build. In a very large repository, turning it off in CI while leaving it on
for editors gives you the fast path in both places.

## Hint 3

`declarationMap` is the third piece and it is the cheapest win in this sector.
It emits `.d.ts.map` files alongside declarations, so tools reading a
declaration can find the original source: go-to-definition works, rename works
across project boundaries, and the debugger has something to show. It costs a
little emit time and a few files, and almost every monorepo should have it on.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do it in three passes and the whole thing stays readable: order, then decide,
then schedule. Trying to decide during the topological walk works — the order
guarantees dependencies are decided first — but interleaving the scheduler into
that loop does not.

## Hint 2

Propagation needs a set that grows as you walk:

```ts
const rebuilding = new Set<string>();
for (const path of order) {
  if (shouldRebuild(path, rebuilding)) rebuilding.add(path);
}
```

Because `order` is topological, every reference of `path` has already been
decided by the time you look at it — which is the entire reason `tsc --build`
computes the order first.

## Hint 3

For the scheduler, filter the graph down to the rebuilt set before you start:
a project's effective references are its references intersected with
`rebuilding`. Everything else finished before this build began.

Left to you: what `MAKESPAN` should be when nothing rebuilds. Zero is the
obvious answer and it is worth checking that your reduce produces it rather
than `-Infinity`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Run this in your head on the case that surprises everyone: you touch one file
in the deepest shared package, and twenty-nine of thirty projects rebuild. That
is not a bug in the tool — it is the propagation rule doing exactly what it
must, because every one of those projects consumed a declaration file that may
now be different. The mitigation is not a faster build; it is a smaller shared
package.

## Hint 2

Real `tsc --build` has one refinement this model omits and it is worth knowing
about. After rebuilding a project, it compares the newly emitted `.d.ts`
against the old one, and if they are byte-identical it does *not* propagate —
dependents keep their up-to-date status. That single optimisation is why
changing a function body in a shared package is cheap and changing its
signature is expensive.

## Hint 3

`--dry` exists because this decision is the thing people need to inspect. When
a build does something unexpected, the question is never "what did the compiler
emit" — it is "why did you rebuild that". A plan you can print, diff and
explain is a better debugging tool than any amount of verbose logging.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## review1 — why did it rebuild?

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. The same rules from the other side: not "what will
happen" but "what just happened, and why".

```ts
export type Cause =
  | "no-buildinfo"
  | "output-missing"
  | "config-changed"
  | "input-changed"
  | "reference-newer"
  | "none";

export interface Evidence {
  hasBuildInfo: boolean;
  missingOutputs: readonly string[];
  newestInput: number;
  builtAt: number;
  newestReference: number;
  configChangedAt: number;
}

export function diagnose(evidence: Evidence): { cause: Cause; explanation: string };
```

Precedence, first match wins, with the exact explanation for each:

1. `hasBuildInfo` is false → `"no-buildinfo"`, explained as
   `no .tsbuildinfo: this project has never been built here`
2. `missingOutputs` is non-empty → `"output-missing"`, explained as
   `output missing: <first entry after sorting ascending>`
3. `configChangedAt > builtAt` → `"config-changed"`, explained as
   `tsconfig changed at <configChangedAt>, after the last build at <builtAt>`
4. `newestInput > builtAt` → `"input-changed"`, explained as
   `input newer than build: <newestInput> > <builtAt>`
5. `newestReference > builtAt` → `"reference-newer"`, explained as
   `a referenced project was rebuilt at <newestReference>`
6. otherwise → `"none"`, explained as `up to date`

Example:

```ts
diagnose({
  hasBuildInfo: true,
  missingOutputs: [],
  newestInput: 40,
  builtAt: 20,
  newestReference: 50,
  configChangedAt: 5,
})
// { cause: "input-changed", explanation: "input newer than build: 40 > 20" }
```

Note that both the input and the reference are newer in that example, and the
answer names only the first. A diagnosis reports the reason it found, in the
order the build checks them — which is exactly the order that lets someone act
on it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc05_project_references review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Six early returns in the stated order. There is a temptation to build a list of
all applicable causes and pick the highest priority; that is more code and it
makes the precedence implicit rather than written down.

## Hint 2

The strings are asserted exactly, so build them from the evidence rather than
retyping the numbers:

```ts
return {
  cause: "input-changed",
  explanation: `input newer than build: ${evidence.newestInput} > ${evidence.builtAt}`,
};
```

Check the sort on `missingOutputs` — the prompt says the *first after sorting*,
not the first as given.

## Hint 3

`>` and not `>=` throughout, matching `ex3`. A build info written in the same
tick as its inputs is up to date, and getting that comparison wrong here
produces a diagnosis that always blames something.

Left to you: whether `diagnose` should ever return more than one cause. It
should not, by this specification — but think about what a real tool would want
when three things changed at once, and why "the first one" is still the right
answer to print.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The value of a function like this is that it turns a support question into a
lookup. "Why is my build slow" becomes "which of six causes fired", and five of
the six have an obvious fix: delete the stale directory, commit the config,
touch nothing, rebuild the dependency. The sixth — `none` — means the build was
not the problem and you should look elsewhere.

## Hint 2

`config-changed` sits above `input-changed` for a reason worth knowing. A
`tsconfig.json` change can alter every output in the project — a different
`target`, a new `strict` flag — so it invalidates everything regardless of file
times. Real `tsc` hashes the resolved options into the `.tsbuildinfo` for
exactly this, which is more robust than a timestamp because it ignores a
formatting-only edit.

## Hint 3

Notice that `newestInput` and `newestReference` are pre-computed numbers rather
than lists. That is a deliberate interface choice: the expensive part —
statting hundreds of files — happens in the caller, and the policy stays a pure
function you can test with six lines of literal data. Every diagnostic tool
worth having is shaped like this.

lessons.title: V3·TC6 — Why tsc is slow, and what to do about it
lessons.summary: tsc is slow for a small number of reasons, and none of them is "TypeScript is slow". Union cross-products, recursive types that are not tail-recursive, barrel files that pull three hundred modules into a program, lib checking you did not need, and a relation cache doing quadratic work. This sector models each, then builds the triage report that tells you which one you have.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·TC6 — Why tsc is slow, and what to do about it

Everyone has an opinion about TypeScript's compile time and almost nobody has
a measurement. The opinions are unhelpful because the causes are specific: a
build is slow for one of about six reasons, they have different fixes, and
guessing costs you a day. This sector is about telling them apart.

Start with the shape of the work. `tsc` does four things in order. It
**parses** every file in the program into a syntax tree. It **binds**, walking
those trees to build symbol tables and scopes. It **checks**, which is where
types are computed, relations are decided and errors are produced. Then it
**emits**, which for most projects is fast and for projects with declaration
output is not. `--extendedDiagnostics` gives you the split, and the split is
the diagnosis: parse-heavy means the program has too many files, check-heavy
means the types are expensive, emit-heavy means declarations.

The most common cause is the first one, and it is almost always **program
size**. A file gets into the program because something imported it, directly or
transitively, and the number of files is the dominant term in parse and bind
time. Barrel files — `index.ts` re-exporting forty modules — are the classic
multiplier: importing one symbol from a barrel pulls the whole barrel's graph
into the program, and a barrel of barrels does it exponentially. `ex4` and `ex5`
model that, and the fix is nearly always mechanical.

The second cause is **type instantiations**, and it is where the interesting
engineering is. A generic type is instantiated each time it is applied, a
conditional type is evaluated per branch, and a recursive conditional type can
run a thousand times per use. The compiler has hard limits — an instantiation
depth cap, a recursion limit, and a cap of 100,000 members on a union produced
by template literal types — and hitting them produces either a slow build or
the error *Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite*.
`ex1` and `ex2` are the two shapes: combinatorial explosion, and recursion that
is not written tail-first.

The third is **unions and the relation cache**. Deciding whether `A` is
assignable to `B` when both are unions is, in the worst case, a comparison per
pair of members. The compiler caches every relation it decides, and that cache
is why the second check of the same pair is free — and why a codebase with
thousands of distinct structurally-identical anonymous types blows out the
cache and pays full price repeatedly. `ex3` and `ex8` are those two ideas: the
quadratic cost, and the cache with its coinductive cycle assumption that makes
recursive types decidable at all.

The fourth is **things you asked for and did not need**. `skipLibCheck` off
means every `.d.ts` in `node_modules` is fully checked. A `lib` setting wider
than the code needs pulls in declaration files by the thousand line. An
`incremental` build whose `.tsbuildinfo` is not cached in CI is a cold build
every time. `ex7` and the challenge cover these, and they are usually the
cheapest wins available.

The exercises are models with exact specifications, because the point is to
understand the mechanism rather than to benchmark anything. Model the union
cross-product and you will never write the template literal type that produces
four million members. Model the relation cache and you will understand why
`interface` and `type` differ in cost. Model the diagnostics parser and you
will actually read the output next time instead of scrolling past it.

A caveat worth stating up front: measure before you optimise, and measure the
right thing. `--extendedDiagnostics` for the split, `--generateTrace` for a
per-type profile you can open in a trace viewer, and `--listFiles` when you
suspect the program is bigger than you think. Everything else is folklore, and
this sector is partly about being able to tell the folklore from the mechanism.

## ex1 — the cross-product that ate the build

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Template literal types multiply, and multiplication
gets large faster than people expect.

```ts
export function crossProductSize(sizes: readonly number[]): number;

export type Budget =
  | { ok: true; size: number }
  | { ok: false; size: number; limit: number };

export function checkTemplateUnion(
  parts: readonly number[],
  limit: number,
): Budget;
```

`crossProductSize` multiplies the sizes together:

- an empty list is `1` — one combination, the empty one
- any zero makes the whole product `0`
- if the running product would exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, return
  `Infinity` rather than a number you cannot trust
- a negative or non-integer size throws
  `RangeError("sizes must be non-negative integers")`

`checkTemplateUnion` is the budget check: compute the size, and report `ok`
when it is less than or equal to `limit`.

Examples:

- `crossProductSize([])` → `1`
- `crossProductSize([2, 3, 4])` → `24`
- `crossProductSize([1000, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000])` → `Infinity`
- `checkTemplateUnion([26, 26, 26], 100000)` → `{ ok: true, size: 17576 }`
- `checkTemplateUnion([26, 26, 26, 26], 100000)` →
  `{ ok: false, size: 456976, limit: 100000 }`

The number `100000` is not arbitrary: it is the size at which TypeScript
refuses to build a union from a template literal type, with the error
*Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent*.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex1
```

## ex2 — recursion that does not blow the stack

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. A recursive conditional type has a budget, and how you
write the recursion decides whether you get fifty iterations or a thousand.

```ts
export type Equal<A, B> =
  (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

export type Split<
  S extends string,
  D extends string,
  Acc extends string[] = [],
> = /* ... */;

export function splitRuntime(source: string, delimiter: string): string[];

export const TYPE_CHECKS: [
  Expect<Equal<Split<"a,b,c", ",">, ["a", "b", "c"]>>,
  Expect<Equal<Split<"a", ",">, ["a"]>>,
  Expect<Equal<Split<"", ",">, [""]>>,
  Expect<Equal<Split<"a,,b", ",">, ["a", "", "b"]>>,
  Expect<Equal<Split<"a-b", ",">, ["a-b"]>>,
];
```

`Split` must be written **tail-recursively**: the accumulator is a type
parameter, and the recursive call is the entire content of the branch, not
wrapped in a tuple spread. Written that way TypeScript applies its
tail-recursion optimisation for conditional types and allows about a thousand
iterations; written the natural way — `[Head, ...Split<Rest, D>]` — the
recursion is not in tail position and you get roughly fifty before *Type
instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite*.

`splitRuntime` is the value-level equivalent and must agree with the type on
every case above, including the empty string, which splits to `[""]`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex2
```

## ex3 — why big unions are quadratic

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Two functions: one that reduces a union to its
canonical members, and one that counts what deciding a relation between two
unions actually costs.

```ts
export function normalizeUnion(members: readonly string[]): string[];
export function unionRelationCost(
  source: readonly string[],
  target: readonly string[],
): number;
```

`normalizeUnion` applies the compiler's absorption rules to a list of type
names and returns the result sorted ascending:

- duplicates collapse
- `"any"` present anywhere → the whole union is `["any"]`
- otherwise `"unknown"` present → the whole union is `["unknown"]`
- `"never"` is dropped, because it contributes no values — unless the union
  would then be empty, in which case the answer is `["never"]`
- an empty input is `["never"]`

`unionRelationCost` models the comparison count for "is every member of
`source` assignable to some member of `target`". For each member of `source`,
the checker scans `target` in order until it finds an identical member:

- if the member is found at index `i` (0-based), that costs `i + 1` comparisons
- if it is not found, the scan costs `target.length` comparisons and the
  relation fails — but you still count the work, and you still process the
  remaining members
- an empty `source` costs `0`

Examples:

- `normalizeUnion(["string", "never", "string"])` → `["string"]`
- `normalizeUnion(["never"])` → `["never"]`
- `normalizeUnion(["unknown", "string"])` → `["unknown"]`
- `unionRelationCost(["a", "b"], ["a", "b", "c"])` → `3` — one plus two
- `unionRelationCost(["c"], ["a", "b"])` → `2` — not found, full scan
- `unionRelationCost(["a", "b", "c"], ["c", "b", "a"])` → `6`

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex3
```

## ex4 — barrels, and what they drag in

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The most common cause of a large program is one
`index.ts` that re-exports everything, imported for one symbol.

```ts
export interface Module {
  path: string;
  imports: readonly string[];
  reexports: readonly string[];
}

export function isBarrel(module: Module): boolean;
export function fanOut(modules: readonly Module[], entry: string): number;
```

`isBarrel` is true when a module has at least two `reexports` and no `imports`
of its own — it contributes nothing but re-exports, which is precisely what
makes it a pass-through the compiler still has to load.

`fanOut` counts the distinct modules reachable from `entry`, following both
`imports` and `reexports`, **not** counting `entry` itself:

- a path that is not a module in the list is ignored entirely — it contributes
  nothing and is not counted
- cycles are safe
- an `entry` that is not in the list gives `0`

Example:

```ts
const modules = [
  { path: "index.ts", imports: [], reexports: ["a.ts", "b.ts"] },
  { path: "a.ts", imports: ["shared.ts"], reexports: [] },
  { path: "b.ts", imports: ["shared.ts", "heavy.ts"], reexports: [] },
  { path: "shared.ts", imports: [], reexports: [] },
  { path: "heavy.ts", imports: [], reexports: [] },
  { path: "unrelated.ts", imports: [], reexports: [] },
]

isBarrel(modules[0])          // true
isBarrel(modules[1])          // false
fanOut(modules, "index.ts")   // 4
fanOut(modules, "a.ts")       // 1
```

Four versus one is the whole lesson: importing one name from the barrel costs
you four modules, importing it directly costs one.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex4
```

## ex5 — what `import type` actually prunes

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`. Two graphs live in the same source files: the one the
type checker walks, and the one the bundler walks. Measuring the difference is
how you find out whether `import type` is worth the trouble.

```ts
export interface File {
  path: string;
  valueImports: readonly string[];
  typeImports: readonly string[];
}

export function programSize(
  files: readonly File[],
  entry: string,
  includeTypeOnly: boolean,
): number;

export function typeOnlyWeight(files: readonly File[], entry: string): number;
```

`programSize` counts the files reachable from `entry`, **including** `entry`:

- with `includeTypeOnly` true, follow both `valueImports` and `typeImports` —
  this is the type-checking program
- with it false, follow only `valueImports` — this is what survives to the
  emitted output
- unknown paths are ignored and not counted
- an `entry` that is not in the list gives `0`
- cycles are safe

`typeOnlyWeight` is the difference: how many files exist only because of
type-only imports.

Example:

```ts
const files = [
  { path: "app.ts", valueImports: ["service.ts"], typeImports: ["models.ts"] },
  { path: "service.ts", valueImports: [], typeImports: ["models.ts"] },
  { path: "models.ts", valueImports: [], typeImports: ["vendor.ts"] },
  { path: "vendor.ts", valueImports: [], typeImports: [] },
]

programSize(files, "app.ts", true)    // 4
programSize(files, "app.ts", false)   // 2
typeOnlyWeight(files, "app.ts")       // 2
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex5
```

## ex6 — read the diagnostics, then the trace

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. Two parsers for the two things the compiler will tell
you about itself.

```ts
export function parseDiagnostics(text: string): Record<string, number>;

export interface TraceEvent {
  name: string;
  dur: number;
}

export interface Hotspot {
  name: string;
  total: number;
  count: number;
}

export function hotspots(
  events: readonly TraceEvent[],
  top: number,
): Hotspot[];
```

`parseDiagnostics` reads `tsc --extendedDiagnostics` output. Each interesting
line is a label, a colon, whitespace, and a value:

- the key is the label, lowercased, with every non-alphanumeric character
  removed and each word after the first capitalised — `"Check time"` becomes
  `"checkTime"`, `"Memory used"` becomes `"memoryUsed"`, `"Files"` becomes
  `"files"`
- the value is the leading number of the remainder, with commas removed and any
  trailing unit (`s`, `K`, `ms`) ignored — `"1.23s"` is `1.23`, `"1,234"` is
  `1234`, `"98304K"` is `98304`
- a line with no colon, or whose value has no leading number, is skipped

`hotspots` groups trace events by `name`, sums `dur`, counts occurrences, sorts
by `total` descending and then `name` ascending, and returns at most `top`
entries. A `top` of zero or less gives `[]`.

Example:

```ts
parseDiagnostics(`Files:              1,234
Lines of TypeScript: 200000
Check time:         4.51s
Memory used:        98304K
something without a colon`)
// { files: 1234, linesOfTypeScript: 200000, checkTime: 4.51, memoryUsed: 98304 }

hotspots(
  [
    { name: "checkExpression", dur: 100 },
    { name: "checkVariableDeclaration", dur: 300 },
    { name: "checkExpression", dur: 250 },
  ],
  2,
)
// [ { name: "checkExpression", total: 350, count: 2 },
//   { name: "checkVariableDeclaration", total: 300, count: 1 } ]
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex6
```

## ex7 — which lib files are you loading?

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`. Every declaration file in `lib` is parsed and bound
before your code is even looked at, and most projects load more than they need.

```ts
export function resolveLibFiles(
  target: string,
  lib: readonly string[] | undefined,
): string[];
```

The version chain, newest first:

```
esnext, es2023, es2022, es2021, es2020, es2019, es2018, es2017, es2016, es2015, es5
```

Including a version lib includes **every lower version in the chain**. So
`"es2020"` yields `lib.es2020.d.ts` down to `lib.es5.d.ts`.

Rules:

- when `lib` is `undefined`, the result is the chain from `target` downwards,
  plus `lib.dom.d.ts` and `lib.scripthost.d.ts` — the historical default
- when `lib` is provided, `target` is **ignored entirely**; every entry is
  expanded and unioned
- `"dom"` adds `lib.dom.d.ts`; `"dom.iterable"` adds `lib.dom.iterable.d.ts`
  **and** `lib.dom.d.ts`; `"webworker"` adds `lib.webworker.d.ts`
- `lib.dom.d.ts` and `lib.webworker.d.ts` together throw
  `Error("lib.dom.d.ts and lib.webworker.d.ts conflict")`
- an unknown target or lib name throws `Error("unknown lib: " + name)`
- the result is sorted ascending, with no duplicates

Examples:

- `resolveLibFiles("es2016", undefined)` →
  `["lib.dom.d.ts", "lib.es2015.d.ts", "lib.es2016.d.ts", "lib.es5.d.ts", "lib.scripthost.d.ts"]`
- `resolveLibFiles("es5", ["es2020"])` → the eight ES chain files and nothing
  else — no DOM
- `resolveLibFiles("es5", ["es2020", "dom", "webworker"])` throws

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex7
```

## ex8 — the relation cache, and why recursion terminates

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. The heart of the checker is one question asked
millions of times: is this assignable to that? Build the machine that answers
it, with the two tricks that make it fast and finite.

```ts
export interface TypeNode {
  name: string;
  members: Readonly<Record<string, string>>;
}

export interface Checker {
  isAssignable(source: string, target: string): boolean;
  readonly comparisons: number;
}

export function createChecker(types: Readonly<Record<string, TypeNode>>): Checker;
```

The rules:

- `"any"` is assignable to everything and everything is assignable to `"any"`
- `"never"` is assignable to everything
- everything is assignable to `"unknown"`
- the primitives `"string"`, `"number"` and `"boolean"` are assignable only to
  themselves, plus the cases above
- otherwise both names must be in `types`, and `source` is assignable to
  `target` when, for **every** member of `target`, `source` has a member of the
  same name whose type is assignable to it. Extra members on `source` are fine
  — that is structural typing.
- an unknown type name that is not one of the special names throws
  `Error("unknown type: " + name)`

Two mechanisms you must implement:

- **memoisation** — a result cache keyed by the pair, so asking the same
  question twice is free
- **the coinductive assumption** — when a pair is already *in progress*, assume
  `true` and carry on. Without it, two mutually recursive types make the
  checker loop forever; with it, `A` and `B` that reference each other are
  correctly related.

`comparisons` counts the calls that actually did work: not cache hits, and not
in-progress assumptions.

Example:

```ts
const checker = createChecker({
  Node: { name: "Node", members: { value: "string", next: "Node" } },
  Link: { name: "Link", members: { value: "string", next: "Link" } },
})
checker.isAssignable("Node", "Link")   // true - and it terminates
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance ex8
```

## challenge — the triage report (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. You have the numbers. Now turn them into a
ranked list of things to do.

```ts
export interface Report {
  files: number;
  instantiations: number;
  checkTime: number;
  programTime: number;
  totalTime: number;
  libCheckEnabled: boolean;
  incremental: boolean;
  barrels: readonly { path: string; fanOut: number }[];
  slowTypes: readonly { name: string; total: number }[];
}

export type Severity = "high" | "medium" | "low";

export interface Finding {
  code: string;
  severity: Severity;
  message: string;
}

export function triage(report: Report): { findings: Finding[]; headline: string };
```

The rules, each producing zero or more findings:

- `skip-lib-check` / high — when `libCheckEnabled` is true and `files > 2000`:
  `skipLibCheck is off and the program has <files> files`
- `no-incremental` / high — when `incremental` is false:
  `incremental is off; every build is a cold build`
- `instantiation-blowup` / high — when `instantiations > 1000000`:
  `<instantiations> type instantiations; look for a recursive type`
- `io-bound` / medium — when `programTime > checkTime`:
  `program time <programTime>s exceeds check time <checkTime>s`
- `barrel` / medium — one per barrel whose `fanOut > 50`, in ascending path
  order: `barrel <path> pulls in <fanOut> modules`
- `slow-type` / low — one per entry of `slowTypes` whose `total >= 500`, in
  descending `total` order then ascending name:
  `<name> cost <total>ms of check time`
- `unaccounted` / low — when
  `totalTime - checkTime - programTime > totalTime * 0.3`:
  `<n>s is neither program nor check time`, where `<n>` is that difference
  rounded to one decimal place

`findings` is sorted by severity (`high`, then `medium`, then `low`), then by
`code` ascending, and within a code by the order the rule produced them.

`headline` is `check-bound: <checkTime>s checking` when
`checkTime >= programTime`, and `program-bound: <programTime>s building the
program` otherwise.

Example:

```ts
triage({
  files: 5000, instantiations: 200000, checkTime: 2, programTime: 6,
  totalTime: 9, libCheckEnabled: true, incremental: true,
  barrels: [{ path: "src/index.ts", fanOut: 300 }], slowTypes: [],
})
// findings: skip-lib-check (high), barrel (medium), io-bound (medium),
//           unaccounted (low)
// headline: "program-bound: 6s building the program"
```

Honest difficulty note: the rules are easy and the ordering is where the marks
are. Sorting by severity requires a rank, not a string comparison — `"high"`,
`"low"`, `"medium"` is alphabetical order and it is not the order you want.

```
uv run dojo test typescript v3tc06_typecheck_performance challenge
```

## review1 — pick the fix

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. The sector from the other end: a symptom arrives,
and you have to name the one thing to change.

```ts
export type Symptom =
  | "editor-slow-large-repo"
  | "cold-ci-build"
  | "one-file-slow"
  | "dts-emit-slow"
  | "watch-rebuilds-everything";

export interface Context {
  hasProjectReferences: boolean;
  incrementalCached: boolean;
  skipLibCheck: boolean;
  usesBarrels: boolean;
}

export function recommend(
  symptom: Symptom,
  context: Context,
): { fix: string; because: string };
```

The decision table, checked in this order per symptom:

- `editor-slow-large-repo` — if `usesBarrels`, fix
  `import from modules, not barrels` because
  `a barrel loads its whole graph for one symbol`; else if not
  `hasProjectReferences`, fix `split into referenced projects` because
  `one program means every edit rechecks everything`; else fix
  `set disableSourceOfProjectReferenceRedirect` because
  `the editor is reading sources of every referenced project`
- `cold-ci-build` — if not `incrementalCached`, fix `cache .tsbuildinfo in CI`
  because `without it every CI build is a first build`; else if not
  `skipLibCheck`, fix `turn on skipLibCheck` because
  `node_modules declarations are being fully checked`; else fix
  `use a build cache keyed by input hashes` because
  `the remaining work is genuine and should be reused across machines`
- `one-file-slow` — always fix `run tsc --generateTrace and read the hotspots`
  because `a single slow file is almost always one expensive type`
- `dts-emit-slow` — always fix `annotate exported signatures, then consider
  isolatedDeclarations` because
  `inferred public types must be computed before they can be written out`
- `watch-rebuilds-everything` — if `usesBarrels`, fix
  `import from modules, not barrels` because
  `a barrel makes every file a dependent of every other`; else fix
  `check that outputs are not inside the input glob` because
  `emitting into a watched directory retriggers the watcher`

Example:

```ts
recommend("cold-ci-build", {
  hasProjectReferences: true, incrementalCached: true,
  skipLibCheck: false, usesBarrels: false,
})
// { fix: "turn on skipLibCheck",
//   because: "node_modules declarations are being fully checked" }
```


# Reading - typescript/v3tc06_typecheck_performance

Six causes, four phases, three commands. These are the notes.

## Notes

**The four phases, and what each is sensitive to.** Parse scales with the
number and size of files. Bind scales with declarations and scopes. Check
scales with types, relations and instantiations. Emit is usually cheap unless
you are producing declarations, in which case it scales with how much of your
public API is inferred rather than annotated. `--extendedDiagnostics` prints
all four, and the split is the diagnosis.

**Program size is the most common cause and the easiest to fix.** Every file in
the program is parsed and bound before anything is checked. Barrel files
multiply the program because importing one name from a barrel loads its entire
re-export graph — the compiler cannot know which export you meant until it has
bound all of them, and tree-shaking happens far too late to help. `--listFiles`
tells you what is actually in there, and the number usually surprises people.

**Instantiations are the second cause and the more interesting one.** Generic
application, conditional evaluation and mapped-type expansion each produce
instantiations, and recursive conditional types produce many. TypeScript 4.5
added a tail-call optimisation for conditional types whose recursive reference
*is* the branch, raising the effective limit from about fifty to about a
thousand — which makes the accumulator style in `ex2` the difference between a
type that works and one that errors.

**Unions are quadratic in the worst case, and the relation cache is what saves
you.** Relating two unions can require a comparison per pair of members. The
compiler caches every decided relation, so the same pair is free thereafter,
which is why one enormous union is rarely the problem and thousands of slightly
different anonymous types often are.

**The coinductive assumption is what makes recursive types decidable.** When
the checker is already deciding a pair and is asked about it again, it assumes
they are related. Without it, `interface Node { next: Node }` against a
structurally identical type would recurse forever. `ex8` is that algorithm,
and building it once removes most of the mystery from the checker's behaviour.

**Some causes are settings.** `skipLibCheck` off means every `.d.ts` in
`node_modules` is type-checked; on a normal application this is often the
single largest available saving. A `lib` wider than you need loads thousands of
lines before your code is read, and setting `lib` *replaces* the default rather
than extending it. An `incremental` build whose `.tsbuildinfo` is not cached in
CI is a cold build with extra steps.

## ex1 to ex3 — the type-level costs

`crossProductSize` is the arithmetic hiding inside a template literal type, and
seeing it written out is how you stop writing the six-character hex colour
type. The compiler's limit is 100,000 union members; the interesting fix is
usually to stop enumerating and validate at runtime instead.

The tail-recursion rule in `ex2` is mechanical and worth memorising: the
recursive reference must be the entire branch. `[Head, ...Recurse<Rest>]` is
not tail position; `Recurse<Rest, [...Acc, Head]>` is.

`unionRelationCost` makes the quadratic behaviour concrete, and the striking
part is that member *order* changes the cost by a factor of the union size for
an identical type.

## ex4 to ex5 — the program graph

`fanOut` on a barrel is the number people should see before they add another
`index.ts`. `typeOnlyWeight` corrects a common misconception in the other
direction: `import type` does *not* reduce the type-checking program, because
the checker still needs those declarations. It prunes the emitted import, which
matters for bundles, cycles and side effects.

## ex6 to ex7 — measurement and configuration

Parsing the diagnostics is the step that turns numbers into a regression test:
compare two runs, fail the pull request that adds three seconds. The three
numbers to watch are file count, instantiations, and the ratio of check time to
total time.

`resolveLibFiles` encodes the rule people get wrong twice: including a version
lib includes everything below it, and specifying `lib` at all replaces the
default entirely — which is why `"lib": ["dom"]` produces a program with no
`Array`.

## ex8, the challenge and review1

The checker model is the sector's core idea, and it explains the
`interface`-versus-`type` performance advice properly: an interface has a
stable identity so its relations are cached and reused, while a large anonymous
type produced per use is a cache miss per use.

The challenge and the review are the same knowledge in the two shapes a tool
takes — measurements to ranked findings, and symptom to single action. Both
matter, and the second is what somebody actually asks you for.

## Further reading

- [TypeScript wiki: Performance](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Performance) — the official checklist, including `skipLibCheck`, `incremental`, and how to read a trace.
- [`--generateTrace`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Performance-Tracing) — producing and reading a per-type profile, with the trace viewer instructions.
- [TypeScript 4.5: tail recursion elimination on conditional types](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-4-5/#tail-recursion-elimination-on-conditional-types) — the exact rule `ex2` depends on.
- [TypeScript 5.5: isolated declarations](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-5-5/#isolated-declarations) — why annotating exports makes declaration emit parallelisable.
- [`checkTypeRelatedTo` in the compiler source](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/main/src/compiler/checker.ts) — the relation cache and the `Ternary.Maybe` assumption, in the original.

# V3·TC6 — Why tsc is slow, and what to do about it

Everyone has an opinion about TypeScript's compile time and almost nobody has
a measurement. The opinions are unhelpful because the causes are specific: a
build is slow for one of about six reasons, they have different fixes, and
guessing costs you a day. This sector is about telling them apart.

Start with the shape of the work. `tsc` does four things in order. It
**parses** every file in the program into a syntax tree. It **binds**, walking
those trees to build symbol tables and scopes. It **checks**, which is where
types are computed, relations are decided and errors are produced. Then it
**emits**, which for most projects is fast and for projects with declaration
output is not. `--extendedDiagnostics` gives you the split, and the split is
the diagnosis: parse-heavy means the program has too many files, check-heavy
means the types are expensive, emit-heavy means declarations.

The most common cause is the first one, and it is almost always **program
size**. A file gets into the program because something imported it, directly or
transitively, and the number of files is the dominant term in parse and bind
time. Barrel files — `index.ts` re-exporting forty modules — are the classic
multiplier: importing one symbol from a barrel pulls the whole barrel's graph
into the program, and a barrel of barrels does it exponentially. `ex4` and `ex5`
model that, and the fix is nearly always mechanical.

The second cause is **type instantiations**, and it is where the interesting
engineering is. A generic type is instantiated each time it is applied, a
conditional type is evaluated per branch, and a recursive conditional type can
run a thousand times per use. The compiler has hard limits — an instantiation
depth cap, a recursion limit, and a cap of 100,000 members on a union produced
by template literal types — and hitting them produces either a slow build or
the error *Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite*.
`ex1` and `ex2` are the two shapes: combinatorial explosion, and recursion that
is not written tail-first.

The third is **unions and the relation cache**. Deciding whether `A` is
assignable to `B` when both are unions is, in the worst case, a comparison per
pair of members. The compiler caches every relation it decides, and that cache
is why the second check of the same pair is free — and why a codebase with
thousands of distinct structurally-identical anonymous types blows out the
cache and pays full price repeatedly. `ex3` and `ex8` are those two ideas: the
quadratic cost, and the cache with its coinductive cycle assumption that makes
recursive types decidable at all.

The fourth is **things you asked for and did not need**. `skipLibCheck` off
means every `.d.ts` in `node_modules` is fully checked. A `lib` setting wider
than the code needs pulls in declaration files by the thousand line. An
`incremental` build whose `.tsbuildinfo` is not cached in CI is a cold build
every time. `ex7` and the challenge cover these, and they are usually the
cheapest wins available.

The exercises are models with exact specifications, because the point is to
understand the mechanism rather than to benchmark anything. Model the union
cross-product and you will never write the template literal type that produces
four million members. Model the relation cache and you will understand why
`interface` and `type` differ in cost. Model the diagnostics parser and you
will actually read the output next time instead of scrolling past it.

A caveat worth stating up front: measure before you optimise, and measure the
right thing. `--extendedDiagnostics` for the split, `--generateTrace` for a
per-type profile you can open in a trace viewer, and `--listFiles` when you
suspect the program is bigger than you think. Everything else is folklore, and
this sector is partly about being able to tell the folklore from the mechanism.

## ex1 — the cross-product that ate the build
