exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The wrapper must be a `function`, not an arrow, so that `this` comes from the
call site. Then `fn.apply(this, args)` forwards both. That is the same lesson
as the spy exercise in the testing sector, and it is worth having twice.

## Hint 2

`name` and `length` are non-writable but **configurable**, so an assignment
silently fails and `defineProperty` works:

```ts
Object.defineProperty(wrapper, "name", { value: fn.name, configurable: true });
Object.defineProperty(wrapper, "length", { value: fn.length, configurable: true });
```

Try the assignment version first and watch it do nothing in strict mode — it is
a good five seconds of education.

## Hint 3

For the property version, capture the value from the descriptor *before* you
redefine, and remember that a descriptor may be an accessor rather than a data
property. The prompt's simplification is that you may treat the original value
as `descriptor.value`; note to yourself what you would do about a getter.

Left to you: whether the returned function should be typed by a cast or by
building it with the right signature. The signature is generic in `F`, so a
cast is unavoidable — write the comment that says why it is sound.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason a deprecation must not change the signature is that a deprecation is
supposed to be a *non*-breaking change. If `deprecate` returned
`(...args: unknown[]) => unknown`, every consumer's build would break on the
version that added the warning — which is exactly the outcome the deprecation
period exists to avoid.

## Hint 2

The warn-once rule matters more than it looks. A deprecated function called in
a loop produces ten thousand identical lines, which trains everyone to filter
the message, which defeats the purpose. Real implementations key the "already
warned" flag on the message text so that the same deprecation warns once per
process no matter how many wrappers exist.

## Hint 3

The type-level half of a deprecation is the `@deprecated` JSDoc tag, which
editors render as a strikethrough and which no runtime wrapper can provide. The
complete deprecation is both: the tag so that the developer sees it while
writing, and the wrapper so that a build that already shipped tells somebody at
runtime. Neither alone is enough.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Four private helpers and one assembly function. Keep the surface computation,
the API diff, the version bump and the manifest inspection separate — they have
no shared state, and mixing them makes the sort at the end harder than it needs
to be.

## Hint 2

The manifest guard is the fiddly part:

```ts
const exportsField = candidate.manifest.exports;
const isObject =
  typeof exportsField === "object" &&
  exportsField !== null &&
  !Array.isArray(exportsField);
if (isObject) {
  const keys = Object.keys(exportsField as Record<string, unknown>);
  // ...first key decides subpath map vs conditions object
}
```

`typeof null === "object"` and arrays are objects — the same two traps as the
very first exercise of this volume.

## Hint 3

For the version, feed the changes from your diff into the bump function and
then into `nextVersion`. Doing it in one expression is fine and makes the data
flow obvious: diff, bump, apply.

Left to you: whether an empty `exports` object should produce the missing-`"."`
blocker. It has no first key, so the subpath-map test fails — decide whether
that is the behaviour you want and whether the prompt permits it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The blocker-versus-warning split is the design decision worth defending. A
leaked type and a broken exports map mean your users get a package that does
not work — those stop the release. A removed export means the release is a
major version, which is a fact rather than a fault. A gate that blocks on facts
gets disabled within a month.

## Hint 2

The version recommendation is a recommendation rather than an enforcement, and
that is deliberate too. A string-level diff cannot tell a widening from a
breaking change, so it over-reports majors. The right ergonomics are: suggest,
show the changes that led to the suggestion, and let a human override with a
note. Every tool that silently chose the version for people has been turned
off.

## Hint 3

If you build the real version of this, add one more thing the prompt omits:
run it against the *packed* tarball rather than the source tree. `npm pack`
produces exactly what a consumer receives, and the number of packages that pass
every check in the repository and ship a broken `dist` is not small. The gate
should test the artefact, not the intention.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`declare global` is only legal inside a module, and a file is a module when it
has at least one top-level `import` or `export`. This file has exports, so it
qualifies — but if you ever write an ambient file with no exports, `export {}`
at the bottom is the standard trick.

## Hint 2

The merge needs the `undefined`-skipping rule spelled out, because
`{ ...defaults, ...options }` does *not* do it — an explicit `undefined` in
`options` overwrites the default with `undefined`:

```ts
const merged = { ...chat.defaults };
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(options)) {
  if (value !== undefined) (merged as Record<string, unknown>)[key] = value;
}
```

## Hint 3

An interface with both a call signature and a construct signature is written as
two bare members:

```ts
interface F {
  (x: number): string;
  new (x: number): Instance;
}
```

No `function` keyword, no property name. It is the same syntax used for `Date`
in `lib.es5.d.ts`, which is worth opening once to see how the standard library
describes a callable-and-newable global.

Left to you: whether `openChat` should validate that `room` is a non-empty
string. The type says it is a string; the runtime is a legacy script that will
do something unhelpful with `""`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason `var` is required in `declare global` is a genuine language detail
rather than a quirk. `var` at the top level of a script creates a property on
the global object; `let` and `const` create a binding in the script scope that
is *not* a property of `globalThis`. The declaration mirrors that, so
`declare global { let X: T }` types the identifier and leaves
`globalThis.X` unknown.

## Hint 2

Notice the shape of the safety: the global is typed `LegacyChatStatic |
undefined`, not `LegacyChatStatic`. A script tag may not have loaded, may have
failed, may be blocked by an ad blocker. Declaring it as always-present is the
same lie as a hand-written `.d.ts` from the first sector of this volume, and
the `undefined` is what forces every consumer through your accessor.

## Hint 3

`defaults` is mutable in the interface and `version` is `readonly`, and that
asymmetry is a description of the real object rather than a preference. The
legacy script genuinely lets you assign to `defaults`; it genuinely does not
expect you to change `version`. A declaration file's job is to describe what is
true, including the parts you wish were not.
